name: Mark
subtitle: A Way Made of Scripture
howToRead: Mark opens by telling you how to read it: “As it is written in the prophets,” and then a fused word of Malachi and Isaiah about a messenger preparing the way of the Lord in the wilderness. The way — ὁδός — is the gospel’s spine, the road John clears, the road Jesus walks from the Jordan toward Jerusalem and the cross. Mark quotes Scripture sparingly compared to Matthew, but the whole narrative is built on it: the beloved Son of Psalm 2 and the bound son of Genesis 22 at the baptism, the rejected prophets of Israel, the parable of the vineyard read straight off Isaiah 5, the apocalypse of chapter 13 woven from Daniel, and a Passion narrated almost entirely in the words of the suffering psalms — the divided garments and mocking heads of Psalm 22, the vinegar of Psalm 69, the cry of dereliction itself. The chips beside each passage name the Scripture underneath it — solid for a formal quotation, dashed for an allusion, dotted for a fainter echo, ◇ for a figural pattern that borrows no words. A lighter chip and a trailing ? mark an echo that is faint or contested. Where Mark follows the Greek of the Septuagint against the Hebrew, both readings are shown.

pericopes.text: The beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: Mark's programmatic noun 'gospel/good news' (euangelion) leans on Isaiah's herald who publishes 'good news' that 'your God reigns.' Volume is conceptual rather than verbal in 1:1 itself, but recurrence is strong: Mark returns to Isaianic euangelizō language at 1:14-15 (the reign of God). Coherence is high since the whole Gospel frames itself as the announcement Isaiah anticipated.

echoes.text: You who tell good news to Zion, go up on a high mountain. You who tell good news to Jerusalem, lift up your voice with strength. Lift it up. Don’t be afraid. Say to the cities of Judah, “Behold, your God!”
echoes.note: Isaiah 40:9 pairs 'good tidings' with Zion's herald immediately before the 40:3 'voice in the wilderness' that Mark quotes in 1:3. The proximity of the two Isaiah loci makes it likely Mark heard 'gospel' from this same context. Volume is low in v.1 but the deliberate quotation of 40:3 two verses later raises availability and coherence.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: The Servant 'anointed to bring good news' supplies another Isaianic root for Mark's euangelion. Verbal contact is faint here and the link is largely thematic; included for maximal coverage because Mark's Jesus is the Spirit-anointed herald (cf. 1:10).

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The title 'Son of God' in the superscription anticipates the divine voice of 1:11, which quotes Psalm 2:7. Volume in v.1 is a single title, but recurrence within the chapter (and at 9:7; 15:39) gives the royal-sonship reading strong coherence. The superscription programmatically front-loads the enthronement language Mark unpacks at the baptism.

echoes.text: I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: Nathan's dynastic oracle ('I will be his father, he shall be my son') stands behind the messianic 'Son of God' title alongside Psalm 2. Verbal volume in Mark is minimal; the link is by way of the Davidic sonship tradition rather than direct citation, hence low and contested.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'The beginning' (archē) may evoke the Genesis incipit, casting Jesus' advent as a new creation. Volume is one word and many read 'beginning' merely as a heading for the narrative, so the echo is genuinely contested; coherence rises only if Mark intends a creation-typology, which 1:10-13 (Spirit, wilderness, wild beasts) may support.

pericopes.text: As it is written in the prophets, “Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you. The voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make ready the way of the Lord! Make his paths straight!’” John came baptizing in the wilderness and preaching the baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins. All the country of Judea and all those of Jerusalem went out to him. They were baptized by him in the Jordan river, confessing their sins. John was clothed with camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist. He ate locusts and wild honey. He preached, saying, “After me comes he who is mightier than I, the thong of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and loosen. I baptized you in water, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.”

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: Mark's 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way' is a near-verbatim citation of Malachi 3:1, though Mark misattributes the fused text to 'Isaiah.' Volume is maximal (sustained verbal repetition), and recurrence is confirmed by Mark 9:11-13, where the Elijah-messenger of Malachi is again applied to John. Coherence is total: the messenger prepares the way of the Lord.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send an angel before you, to keep you by the way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.
echoes.note: The opening clause 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face' matches Exodus 23:20 LXX (the angel guarding Israel on the wilderness road) even more closely than Malachi for the first half. Mark has conflated Exodus 23:20 with Malachi 3:1; the shared 'before your face' wording and new-Exodus 'way' imagery give high volume and coherence to a deliberate fusion.

echoes.text: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.
echoes.note: 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make ready the way of the Lord' quotes Isaiah 40:3 (LXX), the only part Mark's 'as written in Isaiah' formula actually names. Volume is maximal and the wilderness/way motif structures the whole prologue (John baptizes 'in the wilderness,' 1:4). The new-Exodus comfort-of-Zion context is highly coherent with Mark's gospel announcement.

echoes.text: They answered him, “He was a hairy man, and wearing a leather belt around his waist.” He said, “It is Elijah the Tishbite.”
echoes.note: John's garb of camel's hair and a leather belt around the waist deliberately mirrors Elijah, 'a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist' (2 Kings 1:8 LXX, zōnēn dermatinēn perthan identical phrase). High volume in a distinctive sartorial detail; recurrence at Mark 9:13 ('Elijah has come') confirms the identification. Coherence is strong: John is the returning Elijah of Malachi.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: Malachi 4:5 (3:23 MT) promises Elijah's return 'before the great day of the LORD'; Mark casts John in this role, fusing it with the messenger of Malachi 3:1. Verbal volume in 1:2-8 is indirect, but the Elijah dress (v.6) and Mark 9:11-13 make the figural identification explicit and recurrent. Coherence is the engine of the whole prologue.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that the prophets will each be ashamed of his vision, when he prophesies; neither will they wear a hairy mantle to deceive:
echoes.note: Zechariah 13:4 mentions prophets wearing 'a hairy mantle' as a deceptive sign; some see John's camel-hair garment drawing on the generic prophetic-mantle convention rather than Elijah specifically. Volume is low and the negative valence in Zechariah weakens coherence; included as a contested alternate source for the prophet's dress.

echoes.text: Even of these you may eat: any kind of locust, any kind of katydid, any kind of cricket, and any kind of grasshopper.
echoes.note: John's diet of locusts reflects the one insect category Leviticus 11:22 permits as clean food, anchoring his wilderness asceticism in Torah dietary law. The contact is a single permitted-food detail with no verbal borrowing, so the echo is faint and contested; it functions mainly to authenticate his wilderness piety.

pericopes.text: In those days, Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee, and was baptized by John in the Jordan. Immediately coming up from the water, he saw the heavens parting, and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. A voice came out of the sky, “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The heavenly voice 'You are my beloved Son' echoes the royal enthronement decree 'You are my Son' of Psalm 2:7. Volume is high (the opening clause is near-verbatim) and recurrence is strong (Mark 9:7; the title frames the Gospel). Coherence is maximal: the baptism functions as a messianic enthronement, declaring Jesus the Davidic king-son.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: 'In whom I am well pleased' draws on the Servant of Isaiah 42:1, 'my chosen, in whom my soul delights,' paired with the Spirit resting on him (v.10). Volume is high on the 'well pleased / delight' clause and the Spirit-endowment, and the fusion of royal Son (Ps 2) with suffering Servant (Isa 42) is a load-bearing Markan Christology. Coherence is high.

echoes.text: Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence,
echoes.note: Mark's distinctive 'the heavens being torn' (schizomenous) recalls Isaiah 64:1 LXX, 'O that you would rend the heavens and come down.' Volume rests on the violent verb 'tear,' which Mark uniquely chooses (vs. Matthew/Luke's 'opened') and reuses at the temple veil (15:38). Coherence is high: God rends the heavens to descend in the Spirit upon Jesus.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'Beloved Son' (agapētos) may invoke Isaac, 'your only/beloved son,' in the Aqedah of Genesis 22:2 LXX, foreshadowing the offered son. Volume is the single distinctive adjective agapētos (which LXX uses for Isaac), giving real verbal contact; recurrence at 9:7 and the passion's sacrificial logic raise coherence. Genuinely contested—agapētos may simply intensify 'Son.'

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: The Spirit descending over the baptismal waters may evoke the Spirit/wind hovering over the primordial waters of Genesis 1:2, framing the baptism as new creation. Volume is conceptual only (no 'dove' in Genesis), so the link is faint; some rabbinic traditions compared the Genesis Spirit to a bird, which marginally supports it. Contested.

echoes.text: Now in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth of the month, as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's inaugural vision opens with 'the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God,' a prophetic-commission topos that Mark's heaven-rending and Spirit-descent may share. Volume is low and the verb differs (open vs. tear), so this is a generic apocalyptic-opening echo rather than a targeted citation; included for completeness.

echoes.text: Then he remembered the days of old, Moses and his people, saying, Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? where is he who put his holy Spirit in their midst? who caused his glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moses? who divided the waters before them, to make himself an everlasting name? who led them through the depths, as a horse in the wilderness, so that they didn’t stumble? As the livestock that go down into […]
echoes.note: Isaiah 63 recalls God putting his Holy Spirit among his people at the Exodus through the sea, a new-Exodus matrix coherent with Jesus' Spirit-anointing at the Jordan. The contact is thematic (Spirit + water + sonship of Israel) rather than verbal, so volume is low; it strengthens the new-Exodus reading of the whole prologue.

pericopes.text: Immediately the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness. He was there in the wilderness forty days tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals; and the angels were serving him.

echoes.text: You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments, or not.
echoes.note: Jesus' forty days 'tempted' in the wilderness recapitulates Israel's forty years in which the LORD led them to test (peirazō) them. Volume is thematic (forty + wilderness + testing) rather than verbal, but the typology of the new Israel re-running the wilderness probation is coherent and recurrent in early Christian reading. Mark, unlike Q, gives no scriptural debate, so the link is figural.

echoes.text: He was there with Yahweh forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, nor drank water. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.
echoes.note: Moses' forty days and forty nights on Sinai (also Exodus 24:18) supplies one of the canonical 'forty days' fasts that Jesus' wilderness sojourn evokes. Volume is the shared numeral and wilderness setting; the Moses typology is coherent with Mark's broader new-Exodus framing, though Mark's brevity keeps it allusive rather than verbal.

echoes.text: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!” He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again. Yahweh’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty […]
echoes.note: Elijah's forty days in the wilderness, sustained by an angel who 'served' him with food, closely parallels Mark's 'forty days... and the angels were serving him.' Volume includes the shared forty days plus angelic ministration, a distinctive combination; given Mark's heavy Elijah typology (John as Elijah, 1:6), recurrence and coherence are notable.

echoes.text: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways. They will bear you up in their hands, so that you won’t dash your foot against a stone. You will tread on the lion and cobra. You will trample the young lion and the serpent underfoot.
echoes.note: Psalm 91 promises angelic guardianship and treading on lion and serpent unharmed; Mark's pairing of 'wild animals' and 'angels serving him' may reflect this protection motif. Volume is low and indirect (the psalm is explicit in the Q temptation, not Mark), so for Mark this is a contested thematic echo rather than a citation.

echoes.text: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat; The calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together; and a little child will lead them. The cow and the bear will graze. Their young ones will lie down together. The lion will eat straw like the ox. The nursing child will play near a cobra’s hole, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den. They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for […]
echoes.note: Jesus 'with the wild animals' may evoke the eschatological peace where beasts no longer harm, marking him as inaugurator of restored creation. Volume is purely thematic and the wild beasts in Mark could equally signal danger (cf. Ps 91), so the irenic-Eden reading is contested; included for the new-creation typology.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”
echoes.note: The new-Adam reading sees Jesus, tempted by Satan yet among the beasts and served by angels, reversing Adam's failure in the garden among the animals. Volume is conceptual (Satan as tempter, the beasts, paradise restored) with no verbal borrowing, so this Adam-Christ typology is faint and contested in Mark, who never names Adam.

pericopes.text: Now after John was taken into custody, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Good News of the Kingdom of God, and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and the Kingdom of God is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News.”

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: 'The kingdom of God is at hand' announced as 'good news' fulfills the herald of Isaiah 52:7 who proclaims good news and says 'Your God reigns.' Volume couples the distinctive verb euangelizō with the reign of God, both present here; recurrence binds it to 1:1's euangelion. Coherence is maximal—this is Mark's thesis statement drawn from Isaiah's gospel of God's kingship.

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: The expectation that 'the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed' supplies the apocalyptic content of Jesus' 'kingdom of God.' Volume is conceptual but the specific phrase 'kingdom of God/heaven' has its clearest Second-Temple anchor in Daniel; coherence with Mark's 'the time is fulfilled' (an apocalyptic timetable) is strong.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The everlasting dominion given to the 'one like a son of man' is the kingdom Mark's Jesus proclaims and later claims (Mark 13:26; 14:62). In 1:15 the contact is thematic—the inbreaking eternal kingdom—rather than verbal, but the recurrence of Daniel 7 across Mark gives the echo real weight here.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;
echoes.note: 'The time is fulfilled' resonates with Isaiah 61:2's 'the acceptable year of the LORD,' the proclamation of the eschatological jubilee by the Spirit-anointed herald (cf. Jesus' anointing at 1:10). Volume is moderate on the 'favorable/fulfilled time' motif; coherence with the gospel-of-God framing is good, though Mark does not quote it as Luke does.

echoes.text: Your doom has come to you, inhabitant of the land: the time has come, the day is near, a day of tumult, and not of joyful shouting, on the mountains.
echoes.note: Ezekiel 7:7,12 declare 'the time has come, the day is near,' a near-formula for Mark's 'the time is fulfilled.' Volume is the shared 'the time has come' idiom, but Ezekiel's announcement is judgment, not gospel, weakening coherence; included as a faint, contested verbal parallel.

pericopes.text: Passing along by the sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. Jesus said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men.” Immediately they left their nets, and followed him. Going on a little further from there, he saw James the son of Zebedee, and John, his brother, who were also in the boat mending the nets. Immediately he called them, and they left their father, Zebedee, in the boat with the hired servants, and went after him.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send for many fishermen, says Yahweh, and they shall fish them up; and afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks.
echoes.note: 'I will make you into fishers for men' draws on Jeremiah 16:16, 'I will send for many fishers... and they shall fish them.' Volume rests on the distinctive 'fishers of men' image, which is rare in scripture; coherence is the chief question because Jeremiah's fishers gather for judgment while Jesus' gather for salvation, a deliberate transvaluation. Distinctiveness makes the allusion likely.

echoes.text: It shall happen, that fishermen shall stand by it: from En Gedi even to En Eglaim shall be a place for the spreading of nets; their fish shall be after their kinds, as the fish of the great sea, exceeding many.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's vision of fishermen spreading nets along the life-giving temple river offers a more positive 'fishers' background than Jeremiah's judgment. Volume is low (no verbal contact beyond 'fishermen/nets') and the link is thematic, so it is a contested alternate backdrop to the call of the fishermen.

echoes.text: The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his holiness that behold, “The days shall come on you that they will take you away with hooks, and the last of you with fish hooks.
echoes.note: Amos 4:2 threatens that the people will be taken away 'with fishhooks,' another OT fishing-for-people image. Volume is faint and, like Jeremiah, the valence is judgment; included for maximal coverage of the 'catching people' metaphor though coherence with Jesus' summons is weak.

echoes.text: So he departed there, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing, with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed over to him, and cast his mantle on him. He left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?” He returned from following him, and took the yoke of oxen, and killed them, […]
echoes.note: The abrupt prophetic call—Jesus passing by, the brothers immediately leaving father and livelihood—mirrors Elijah's call of Elisha, who left his oxen and his father to follow. Volume lies in the shared call-narrative form (summons in the midst of work, leaving family/trade), and Mark's pervasive Elijah typology raises coherence and recurrence for the pattern, even without direct quotation.

pericopes.text: They went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath day he entered into the synagogue and taught. They were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as having authority, and not as the scribes. Immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out, saying, “Ha! What do we have to do with you, Jesus, you Nazarene? Have you come to destroy us? I know you who you are: the Holy One of God!” Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be quiet, and come out of him!” The unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying with a loud voice, came out of him. They were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, “What is this? A new teaching? For with authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him!” The report of him went out immediately everywhere into all the region of Galilee and its surrounding area.

echoes.text: They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron, Yahweh’s saint.
echoes.note: The demon's confession 'the Holy One of God' uses a title applied in Psalm 106:16 (LXX 105:16) to Aaron, 'the holy one of the LORD.' Volume is the shared distinctive title, but its referent differs sharply (Aaron vs. Jesus), so the link is contested; it may simply mark Jesus as the consecrated agent of God whose holiness repels the unclean spirit.

echoes.text: but he said to me, ‘Behold, you shall conceive, and bear a son; and now drink no wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing; for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.’”
echoes.note: Samson is to be 'a Nazirite/holy one of God from the womb' (Judges 13:7; 16:17 LXX 'hagios theou'), the closest verbal match to the demon's 'Holy One of God.' Volume on the exact phrase is real, but the Samson connection is thematically thin, so this is a contested lexical parallel for the title rather than a developed allusion.

echoes.text: Ah sinful nation, a people loaded with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children who deal corruptly! They have forsaken Yahweh. They have despised the Holy One of Israel. They are estranged and backward.
echoes.note: 'The Holy One of Israel,' Isaiah's signature divine title, may stand behind 'the Holy One of God' as a claim to Jesus' divine identity recognized by the demon. Volume is partial (Holy One + God/Israel) and the genitive differs, so coherence is suggestive but the link remains faint and contested.

pericopes.text: Immediately, when they had come out of the synagogue, they came into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. Now Simon’s wife’s mother lay sick with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. He came and took her by the hand, and raised her up. The fever left her, and she served them.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Jesus taking the sick woman 'by the hand' and raising her up loosely follows the Elijah/Elisha healing pattern (Elijah revives the widow's son). Volume is purely formal (prophet restores a stricken person), with no verbal borrowing in Mark's terse account, so this is a contested figural echo riding on Mark's broader Elijah typology.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha's raising of the Shunammite's son by personal touch offers another prophetic-healing template for Jesus' gesture of taking the hand and 'raising' the feverish woman. The contact is thematic and the language non-distinctive, so the echo is faint; included to register the prophet-healer typology underlying the miracle.

pericopes.text: At evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick, and those who were possessed by demons. All the city was gathered together at the door. He healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. He didn’t allow the demons to speak, because they knew him.

echoes.text: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
echoes.note: Mark's summary of Jesus healing 'all who were sick' and casting out demons resonates with the Servant who 'bore our infirmities,' the verse Matthew explicitly cites at this point. For Mark the link is unmarked and thematic, so volume is low and it is contested whether Mark intends the Servant-of-Isaiah reading here, though it coheres with the Isa 42 Servant motif of 1:11.

pericopes.text: Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there. Simon and those who were with him followed after him; and they found him, and told him, “Everyone is looking for you.” He said to them, “Let’s go elsewhere into the next towns, that I may preach there also, because I came out for this reason.” He went into their synagogues throughout all Galilee, preaching and casting out demons.

echoes.text: The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary: he wakens morning by morning, he wakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.
echoes.note: Jesus rising 'early in the morning' to a solitary place to pray faintly echoes the Servant who is wakened 'morning by morning' to hear and speak God's word. Volume is minimal (the morning-prayer motif) with no verbal borrowing, so this is a contested, low-confidence echo; it coheres only loosely with Mark's Servant Christology.

pericopes.text: A leper came to him, begging him, kneeling down to him, and saying to him, “If you want to, you can make me clean.” Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him, and said to him, “I want to. Be made clean.” When he had said this, immediately the leprosy departed from him, and he was made clean. He strictly warned him, and immediately sent him out, and said to him, “See you say nothing to anybody, but go show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing the things which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them.” But he went out, and began to proclaim it much, and to spread about the matter, so that Jesus could no more openly enter into a city, but was outside in desert places: and they came to him from everywhere.

echoes.text: “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp. The priest shall examine him, and behold, if the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper, then the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two living clean birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop.
echoes.note: Jesus' command to 'show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing the things which Moses commanded' directly invokes the leper's purification rite of Leviticus 14, where the cleansed person presents himself to the priest with the prescribed offerings. Volume is high (Mark names 'the things Moses commanded' for cleansing), coherence total, and the reference is explicit Torah citation in substance.

echoes.text: “The leper in whom the plague is shall wear torn clothes, and the hair of his head shall hang loose. He shall cover his upper lip, and shall cry, ‘Unclean! Unclean!’ All the days in which the plague is in him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall dwell alone. Outside of the camp shall be his dwelling.
echoes.note: The leper's condition—ritual uncleanness and exclusion from the community—presupposes the diagnostic law of Leviticus 13, the necessary backdrop to the cleansing of v.42. Volume is conceptual but the legal framework is unmistakably in view (the leper must be declared clean by a priest), and it coheres tightly with the offering command of v.44.

echoes.text: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]
echoes.note: The cleansing of a leper evokes Elisha's healing of Naaman, the paradigmatic OT leprosy cure by a prophet. Volume is the shared distinctive event (only Elisha cleanses a leper in the OT narratives) plus Mark's Elijah/Elisha typology; coherence is strong, and Luke 4:27 makes the Naaman link explicit, supporting its availability and recurrence in the tradition.

echoes.text: The cloud departed from over the Tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow. Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. Aaron said to Moses, “Oh, my lord, please don’t count this sin against us, in which we have done foolishly, and in which we have sinned. Let her not, I pray, be as one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb.” Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, “Heal her, God, I beg you!” Yahweh […]
echoes.note: Miriam's leprosy and Moses' intercession, with the priestly/Mosaic handling of her exclusion and restoration, sits in the background of leprosy as a divinely-managed impurity. Volume is low and the contact thematic rather than verbal, so this is a contested supporting echo to the Levitical leprosy frame.

pericopes.text: When he entered again into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was in the house. Immediately many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even around the door; and he spoke the word to them. Four people came, carrying a paralytic to him. When they could not come near to him for the crowd, they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on. Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.” But there were some of the scribes sitting there, and reasoning in their hearts, “Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you reason these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to tell the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Arise, and take up your bed, and walk?’ But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic— “I tell you, arise, take up your mat, and go to your house.” He arose, and immediately took up the mat, and went out in front of them all; so that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!”

echoes.text: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.
echoes.note: The scribes' objection "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (v.7) presupposes the prophetic axiom of Isa 43:25, "I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake." High volume on the distinctive theology that pardon of sin is God's sole prerogative; Mark stages Jesus' authority precisely against this exclusive divine claim. Recurrence is strong in Isaiah's forgiveness oracles (44:22).

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth, keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”
echoes.note: The covenant self-revelation of YHWH as the God "forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin" is the foundational text behind the scribes' assumption that forgiveness belongs to God alone. Thematic coherence is high: Jesus' pronouncement of forgiveness enacts a divine attribute scripturally reserved to the LORD. The verbal contact is via the shared lexeme of forgiving sin rather than direct quotation.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: "The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" (v.10) draws on Dan 7:13-14, where "one like a son of man" is given dominion and authority before the Ancient of Days. High distinctiveness in the title plus the keyword "authority" (exousia), which Mark recurs at 2:28 and the eschatological discourse (13:26). Mark transposes the heavenly investiture into earthly authority.

echoes.text: who forgives all your sins; who heals all your diseases;
echoes.note: "Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases" pairs forgiveness and healing exactly as Mark 2:1-12 does, where pardon is demonstrated by the cure of the paralytic. Thematic coherence is strong: the psalm makes the two divine acts a single benefaction, which is the logic of Jesus' "which is easier" challenge (v.9). Verbal volume is modest, carried by the forgiveness/healing pairing.

echoes.text: Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: "Then shall the lame man leap like a deer" anchors the healing of the paralytic in Isaiah's eschatological restoration, where bodily wholeness signals the inbreaking reign of God. Thematic coherence with Mark's miracle is high; the crowd's astonishment ("We never saw anything like this!", v.12) fits the new-thing motif of Isaiah 35 and 43. Verbal repetition is limited, so this is an echo rather than allusion.

echoes.text: Blessed is he whose disobedience is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man to whom Yahweh doesn’t impute iniquity, in whose spirit there is no deceit. When I kept silence, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy on me. My strength was sapped in the heat of summer. Selah. I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn’t hide my iniquity. I said, I will confess my transgressions to Yahweh, and you […]
echoes.note: The psalm links the blessedness of the one "whose transgression is forgiven" with the bodily wasting that lifts when sin is confessed and pardoned. This is the closest OT paradigm for Mark's premise that the paralytic's deeper need is forgiveness, healed alongside the body. Coherence is strong though the verbal contact is thematic.

echoes.text: But there is forgiveness with you, therefore you are feared.
echoes.note: "But there is forgiveness with you, that you may be feared" reinforces the scribal premise that pardon is a divine possession evoking reverence; the crowd's reaction is awe and glorifying God (v.12). Low volume and no verbal borrowing, but thematically coherent with the chapter's contest over who may forgive.

echoes.text: He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.
echoes.note: The scribes charge "blasphemies" (v.7); Lev 24:16 makes blasphemy of the Name a capital offense, supplying the legal background to their unspoken accusation. Coherence is high: Mark frames Jesus' forgiveness as an apparent usurpation of the divine Name that the Law guards. The link is conceptual rather than quoted.

echoes.text: The inhabitant won’t say, “I am sick.” The people who dwell therein will be forgiven their iniquity.
echoes.note: "No inhabitant will say, 'I am sick'; the people who dwell there will be forgiven their iniquity" joins healing and forgiveness as twin marks of Zion's restoration, exactly the combination Mark dramatizes. The echo is faint and verbally thin, but thematically apt to the pericope's fusion of the two.

pericopes.text: He went out again by the seaside. All the multitude came to him, and he taught them. As he passed by, he saw Levi, the son of Alphaeus, sitting at the tax office, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he arose and followed him. He was reclining at the table in his house, and many tax collectors and sinners sat down with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many, and they followed him. The scribes and the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with the sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why is it that he eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners?” When Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice" underlies Jesus' defense of eating with tax collectors and sinners and his mission "to call sinners." Mark does not quote it (unlike Matt 9:13), but the mercy-over-cult logic governs the table-fellowship dispute, making this a genuine thematic echo. Recurrence within the Synoptic tradition strengthens the case even where Mark leaves it implicit.

echoes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.
echoes.note: "I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed... but the fat and the strong I will destroy" matches Jesus' physician saying: he comes for the sick, not the healthy, for sinners, not the self-righteous. The shepherd-God who seeks the weak is reworked into Jesus' calling of Levi and the sinners. Coherence and the recurrence of the shepherd motif in Mark (6:34) support an allusion.

echoes.text: You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither have you bound up that which was broken, neither have you brought back that which was driven away, neither have you sought that which was lost; but with force and with rigor you have ruled over them.
echoes.note: The indictment of shepherds who did not heal the sick or seek the lost frames Jesus' physician aphorism (v.17) as a contrast to negligent leaders. The verbal contact is the sick/strayed sheep imagery rather than quotation, so an echo. It coheres with Mark's critique of the scribes and Pharisees.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: "The LORD looks on the heart" while man judges by outward appearance illuminates Jesus' choice of the tax collector Levi and his welcome of those the religious dismiss. Faint and verbally remote, but thematically coherent with the chapter's reversal of who is fit for God. Marked low and contested.

echoes.text: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars. She has prepared her meat. She has mixed her wine. She has also set her table. She has sent out her maidens. She cries from the highest places of the city: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” As for him who is void of understanding, she says to him, “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed! Leave your simple ways, and live. Walk in the way of […]
echoes.note: Wisdom's banquet invitation to the simple and those who lack sense offers a sapiential pattern for Jesus reclining at table with sinners and summoning them. The link rests on the meal-as-invitation-to-the-unworthy motif, with no verbal borrowing. Contested and low.

echoes.text: Is there no balm in Gilead? is there no physician there? why then isn’t the health of the daughter of my people recovered?
echoes.note: "Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there?" supplies the OT physician-for-the-sick imagery behind Jesus' aphorism in v.17. The shared healer/sickness vocabulary is suggestive though faint, and the prophetic question concerns the unhealed wound of God's people, coherent with Jesus' mission to sinners.

pericopes.text: John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting, and they came and asked him, “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples don’t fast?” Jesus said to them, “Can the groomsmen fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they can’t fast. But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then will they fast in that day. No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, or else the patch shrinks and the new tears away from the old, and a worse hole is made. No one puts new wine into old wineskins, or else the new wine will burst the skins, and the wine pours out, and the skins will be destroyed; but they put new wine into fresh wineskins.”

echoes.text: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: "As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you" supplies the OT bridegroom-as-God imagery Jesus claims for himself in the fasting dispute (v.19). The metaphor of the wedding feast as the time of joy when fasting is impossible is distinctively prophetic, and Mark's recurrence of the eschatological-banquet theme supports the allusion.

echoes.text: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.
echoes.note: Hosea's betrothal oracle, "I will betroth you to me forever," establishes the covenant marriage between God and his people behind the bridegroom saying. Jesus casting himself as bridegroom appropriates this YHWH-as-husband tradition; the wedding joy that suspends fasting coheres with Hosea's restored marriage. The link is thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Gather the people. Sanctify the assembly. Assemble the elders. Gather the children, and those who nurse from breasts. Let the bridegroom go out of his room, and the bride out of her room.
echoes.note: "Let the bridegroom leave his room" amid a summons to fasting and assembly provides a Second-Temple resonance for the juxtaposition of bridegroom and fasting that Mark inverts. The verbal contact is the rare "bridegroom" lexeme in a fasting context, but the sense is opposite, so a faint contested echo.

echoes.text: For your Maker is your husband; Yahweh of Armies is his name: and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer; the God of the whole earth shall he be called. For Yahweh has called you as a wife forsaken and grieved in spirit, even a wife of youth, when she is cast off,” says your God.
echoes.note: "Your Maker is your husband" continues the prophetic marriage metaphor that legitimates Jesus' bridegroom self-identification. No verbal borrowing, but it reinforces the availability of the God-as-husband tradition Jesus draws on. Contested and low.

echoes.text: I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will make you wear sackcloth on all your bodies, and baldness on every head. I will make it like the mourning for an only son, and its end like a bitter day.
echoes.note: "I will turn your feasts into mourning" anticipates the day when the bridegroom is "taken away" and the guests will fast (v.20). The reversal of feast to mourning matches Mark's prediction of grief, an echo carried by theme rather than wording. Low and contested.

echoes.text: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?
echoes.note: The bridegroom "taken away" (v.20) may glance at the servant who "was taken away" (cut off from the land of the living), hinting at the passion. Verbal overlap on the being-taken-away language is suggestive but slight, so a faint contested echo with possible passion typology.

echoes.text: Behold, my breast is as wine which has no vent; like new wineskins it is ready to burst.
echoes.note: "My belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst" is the closest OT image to Jesus' new-wine/old-skins parable (v.22). The shared bursting-new-wineskins picture gives a sapiential source for the figure, though Jesus applies it to the incompatibility of the new order with the old. Marked low.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they broke, although I was a husband to them, says Yahweh. But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in […]
echoes.note: The new-cloth and new-wine sayings figure the incompatibility of the inbreaking kingdom with the old order, typologically resonant with Jeremiah's new covenant that supersedes the broken one. There is no verbal borrowing, only a structural correspondence between new wine and new covenant. Listed as figural and contested.

pericopes.text: He was going on the Sabbath day through the grain fields, and his disciples began, as they went, to pluck the ears of grain. The Pharisees said to him, “Behold, why do they do that which is not lawful on the Sabbath day?” He said to them, “Did you never read what David did, when he had need, and was hungry—he, and those who were with him? How he entered into God’s house when Abiathar was high priest, and ate the show bread, which is not lawful to eat except for the priests, and gave also to those who were with him?” He said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

echoes.text: Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came to meet David trembling, and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no man with you?” David said to Ahimelech the priest, “The king has commanded me a business, and has said to me, ‘Let no man know anything of the business about which I send you, and what I have commanded you; and I have appointed the young men to such and such a place.’ Now therefore what is under your hand? Give me five loaves […]
echoes.note: Jesus' question "Did you never read what David did, when he had need... how he entered the house of God... and ate the show bread" (vv.25-26) directly retells 1 Sam 21:1-6. High volume: the showbread, David's hunger, and the unlawfulness for non-priests are all reproduced. Mark's reference to Abiathar (vs. Ahimelech in the source) is the well-known crux but confirms the deliberate citation.

echoes.text: “You shall take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes of it: two tenth parts of an ephah shall be in one cake. You shall set them in two rows, six on a row, on the pure gold table before Yahweh. You shall put pure frankincense on each row, that it may be to the bread for a memorial, even an offering made by fire to Yahweh. Every Sabbath day he shall set it in order before Yahweh continually. It is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting […]
echoes.note: The show bread (Bread of the Presence) and its rule that only the priests may eat it (v.26) come from Lev 24:5-9. Mark presupposes this legislation to make the David precedent meaningful: human need overrides cultic restriction. High coherence and verbal contact on "show bread" and "lawful... except for the priests."

echoes.text: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
echoes.note: "The Sabbath was made for man" (v.27) appeals to the creation ordinance where God rests and hallows the seventh day for humanity's sake. Distinctive theology: Sabbath is grounded in creation, not merely Sinai, which supports Jesus' claim that it serves man. Strong thematic coherence with the original institution of rest.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: The Decalogue Sabbath command, with its creation rationale, is the law the Pharisees invoke against the disciples' grain-plucking (v.24). Jesus does not abolish but reinterprets it: "the Sabbath was made for man." High coherence; the dispute over what is "lawful on the Sabbath" presupposes this command.

echoes.text: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic Sabbath command, with its humanitarian rationale (so servants may rest), reinforces Jesus' principle that the Sabbath exists for human benefit. The man-centered framing in v.27 coheres especially with Deuteronomy's emphasis on rest for people. Allusion via the Sabbath legislation cited in the dispute.

echoes.text: When you come into your neighbor’s standing grain, then you may pluck the ears with your hand; but you shall not move a sickle to your neighbor’s standing grain.
echoes.note: "When you come into your neighbor's standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hand" legitimates the disciples' action itself (v.23); the Pharisees object only to the Sabbath timing, not the plucking. This law shows the disciples were not stealing, sharpening the dispute as purely about Sabbath observance. Verbal contact on plucking ears of standing grain.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: "The Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath" (v.28) again invokes the Danielic figure given universal dominion, here extended to lordship over the sacred day. The keyword authority/lordship recurs from v.10, binding the chapter's two Son of Man sayings to Dan 7:13-14. High distinctiveness in the title and the claim of comprehensive authority.

echoes.text: You shall keep the Sabbath therefore; for it is holy to you. Everyone who profanes it shall surely be put to death; for whoever does any work therein, that soul shall be cut off from among his people.
echoes.note: "You shall keep the Sabbath... whoever profanes it shall be put to death" supplies the gravity behind the Pharisees' charge that the disciples do "what is not lawful" (v.24). The capital seriousness of Sabbath violation explains the intensity of the objection. Echo by legal background rather than quotation.

echoes.text: While the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. Those who found him gathering sticks brought him to Moses and Aaron, and to all the congregation. They put him in custody, because it had not been declared what should be done to him. Yahweh said to Moses, “The man shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall stone him with stones outside of the camp.” All the congregation brought him […]
echoes.note: The narrative of the man executed for gathering sticks on the Sabbath illustrates the rigorist reading of Sabbath labor the Pharisees apply to grain-plucking. It supplies a precedent for treating such acts as forbidden work, against which Jesus' humane principle is set. Faint, contested echo via the work-on-Sabbath theme.

echoes.text: And Mattathias and his friends knew it, and they mourned over them exceedingly. And one said to another, If we all do as our kindred have done, and fight not against the Gentiles for our lives and our ordinances, they will now quickly destroy us from off the earth. And they took counsel on that day, saying, whoever shall come against us to battle on the Sabbath day, let us fight against him, and we shall in no wise all die, as our kindred died in the […]
echoes.note: The Maccabean decision that preserving life overrides strict Sabbath rest establishes a Second-Temple precedent that human need can qualify Sabbath law, the very logic of Jesus' argument. As an available pre-Markan deuterocanonical source it strengthens the plausibility of "the Sabbath was made for man." The contact is conceptual, not verbal, so an echo.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: The mercy-not-sacrifice principle that frames the table dispute (2.2) also undergirds the Sabbath argument: human need (hunger) outweighs ritual strictness. The recurrence of the same theme across both controversy stories supports a faint thematic echo here. Low and contested.

pericopes.text: He entered again into the synagogue, and there was a man there who had his hand withered. They watched him, whether he would heal him on the Sabbath day, that they might accuse him. He said to the man who had his hand withered, “Stand up.” He said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath day to do good, or to do harm? To save a life, or to kill?” But they were silent. When he had looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored as healthy as the other. The Pharisees went out, and immediately conspired with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.

echoes.text: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]
echoes.note: The Sabbath conflict presupposes the Decalogue Sabbath command, which in Deuteronomy's form roots the day in liberation and mercy ('that your servant may rest'). Jesus' 'is it lawful to do good?' reframes the commandment toward the merciful, life-giving intent the text already carries. High thematic coherence with the Deuteronomic humanitarian rationale.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: The other Decalogue form of the Sabbath law stands directly behind the legal dispute over Sabbath healing. Availability and recurrence are strong; the verbal echo is to the command itself rather than to specific words of the verse.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil.
echoes.note: Jesus' antithesis 'to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill' mirrors the Deuteronomic covenant choice 'I have set before you life and death, good and evil.' The paired good/evil, life/death structure suggests a deliberate framing of Sabbath observance as a covenant life-or-death decision. Thematic coherence is high though no verbatim quotation.

echoes.text: Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: 'Grieved at the hardening of their hearts' echoes Isaiah's prophecy of a people whose heart is made fat and unresponsive, a motif Mark deploys elsewhere for the obtuse. The vocabulary of hardened heart (porosis) recurs in Mark for opponents and disciples, raising recurrence and coherence.

echoes.text: I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: The hardening-of-heart language evokes the Exodus Pharaoh tradition, where God hardens, or Pharaoh hardens, the heart against the works of God. Mark's opponents resist a manifest sign as Pharaoh resisted the plagues. Faint and thematic, marked contested.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: 'Is it lawful to do good?' aligns with the prophetic priority of mercy over cultic/ritual scruple ('I desire mercy, not sacrifice'). The healing-over-Sabbath logic coheres with Hosea's critique, though Mark does not cite it. Low volume, contested.

echoes.text: When the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar in Bethel, Jeroboam put out his hand from the altar, saying, “Seize him!” His hand, which he put out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back again to himself. The altar also was split apart, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by Yahweh’s word. The king answered the man of God, “Now entreat the favor […]
echoes.note: Jeroboam's hand withered and then restored offers an OT precedent of a withered/restored hand in a charged cultic confrontation. The verbal link (withered hand, restoration) is suggestive but the contexts differ sharply; possible figural resonance only.

pericopes.text: Jesus withdrew to the sea with his disciples, and a great multitude followed him from Galilee, from Judea, from Jerusalem, from Idumaea, beyond the Jordan, and those from around Tyre and Sidon. A great multitude, hearing what great things he did, came to him. He spoke to his disciples that a little boat should stay near him because of the crowd, so that they wouldn’t press on him. For he had healed many, so that as many as had diseases pressed on him that they might touch him. The unclean spirits, whenever they saw him, fell down before him, and cried, “You are the Son of God!” He sternly warned them that they should not make him known.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The gathering of crowds from Idumaea, Tyre, Sidon and beyond the Jordan hints at the eschatological ingathering of the nations to the Servant who is a light to them. The named Gentile-adjacent regions raise coherence with Isaiah's universal scope, though the link is thematic, not verbal.

echoes.text: He sends his word, and heals them, and delivers them from their graves.
echoes.note: The mass healing of the afflicted who press to touch him echoes the psalm's 'he sent his word and healed them.' Recurrence of the healing-deliverance motif in the Psalms supports coherence; volume is low.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The unclean spirits' cry 'You are the Son of God' draws on the royal/messianic 'Son' tradition rooted in the enthronement psalm, already echoed at Jesus' baptism in Mark. Recurrence within Mark and availability of the title in Second Temple messianism strengthen the connection.

pericopes.text: He went up into the mountain, and called to himself those whom he wanted, and they went to him. He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach, and to have authority to heal sicknesses and to cast out demons: Simon, to whom he gave the name Peter; James the son of Zebedee; John, the brother of James, and he called them Boanerges, which means, Sons of Thunder; Andrew; Philip; Bartholomew; Matthew; Thomas; James, the son of Alphaeus; Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot; and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him. He came into a house.

echoes.text: Moses wrote all Yahweh’s words, and rose up early in the morning, and built an altar under the mountain, and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.
echoes.note: Jesus goes up the mountain and constitutes twelve, evoking Moses building twelve pillars for the twelve tribes at Sinai. The mountain ascent plus the number twelve makes the covenant-foundation typology strong; the appointment of twelve is widely read as Israel's eschatological reconstitution. High coherence and availability.

echoes.text: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his blessing.
echoes.note: The deliberate count of twelve maps onto the twelve sons/tribes of Jacob, signaling the renewal of the twelve-tribe people around Jesus. Availability is total and the symbolism of twelve is unmistakable in a Jewish frame.

echoes.text: The stones shall be according to the names of the children of Israel, twelve, according to their names; like the engravings of a signet, everyone according to his name, they shall be for the twelve tribes.
echoes.note: The twelve stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes on the high priest's breastpiece reinforce the tribal symbolism of the named Twelve listed individually here. The naming of each disciple parallels the named tribal stones. Coherence is good though the echo is to the institution of twelve, not specific words.

echoes.text: With you there shall be a man of every tribe; everyone head of his fathers’ house. These are the names of the men who shall stand with you: Of Reuben: Elizur the son of Shedeur. Of Simeon: Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai. Of Judah: Nahshon the son of Amminadab. Of Issachar: Nethanel the son of Zuar. Of Zebulun: Eliab the son of Helon. Of the children of Joseph: Of Ephraim: Elishama the son of Ammihud. Of Manasseh: Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur. Of […]
echoes.note: The selection of named tribal representatives, one set apart from each tribe to lead, parallels Jesus naming twelve leaders for the renewed Israel. The list-of-names form and representative function support coherence.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, that they may stand there with you. I will come down and talk with you there. I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you not bear it yourself alone.
echoes.note: Moses appointing leaders to share his authority/spirit prefigures Jesus appointing the Twelve to share his authority to preach and cast out demons. The delegation-of-authority motif coheres; verbal contact is faint.

echoes.text: When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned, and flame will not scorch you.
echoes.note: 'Sons of Thunder' (Boanerges) may resonate with the storm/thunder theophany imagery applied to God's voice and zeal; thunder is a recurrent divine-presence symbol (Sinai, Psalm 29). The naming is suggestive but the OT anchor is diffuse, so marked contested and low.

echoes.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lower part of the mountain. Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked […]
echoes.note: The mountain setting where the people are gathered and authority is conferred recalls the Sinai theophany with its thunder; the 'Sons of Thunder' epithet may draw on this. Faint, thematic, contested.

pericopes.text: The multitude came together again, so that they could not so much as eat bread. When his friends heard it, they went out to seize him: for they said, “He is insane.” The scribes who came down from Jerusalem said, “He has Beelzebul,” and, “By the prince of the demons he casts out the demons.” He summoned them, and said to them in parables, “How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. If a house is divided against itself, that house cannot stand. If Satan has risen up against himself, and is divided, he can’t stand, but has an end. But no one can enter into the house of the strong man to plunder, unless he first binds the strong man; and then he will plunder his house. Most certainly I tell you, all sins of the descendants of man will be forgiven, including their blasphemies with which they may blaspheme; but whoever may blaspheme against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is subject to eternal condemnation.” —because they said, “He has an unclean spirit.”

echoes.text: Shall the plunder be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captives be delivered? But thus says Yahweh, “Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away, and the plunder of the terrible shall be delivered; for I will contend with him who contends with you, and I will save your children.
echoes.note: The strong-man parable, binding the strong man to plunder his house, closely tracks Isaiah's 'shall the prey be taken from the mighty?... I will contend... and save your children.' The vocabulary of the strong/mighty one and plunder/spoil maps onto the saying, and the theme of God liberating captives from a powerful captor gives high coherence. Strong volume for an OT background to the exorcism logic.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'He shall divide the spoil with the strong' supplies the plunder-of-the-strong imagery underlying v.27. The Servant's victory and dividing of spoil coheres with Jesus despoiling Satan's house; an alternative or supplement to Isaiah 49.

echoes.text: He delivered me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me; for they were too mighty for me.
echoes.note: Deliverance 'from my strong enemy' parallels the binding of the strong man; the psalmist is rescued from a mightier foe by God's power. Thematic coherence with the rescue-from-the-strong motif; low volume.

echoes.text: Now the Spirit of Yahweh departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from Yahweh troubled him. Saul’s servants said to him, “See now, an evil spirit from God troubles you. Let our lord now command your servants who are before you, to seek out a man who is a skillful player on the harp. It shall happen, when the evil spirit from God is on you, that he shall play with his hand, and you shall be well.” Saul said to his servants, “Provide me now a man who can play […]
echoes.note: The Beelzebul charge and the question 'how can Satan cast out Satan?' play against OT traditions where an evil spirit from the Lord can be soothed, distinguishing genuine deliverance from collusion. Faint background to the exorcism dispute.

echoes.text: Elijah came near to all the people, and said, “How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” The people answered him not a word.
echoes.note: Baal/Beelzebul nomenclature derives from the lord-of-the-house/lord-of-flies deity polemicized in Kings; the scribes' charge weaponizes a pagan-deity name with deep OT polemical history (Ahaziah's inquiry of Baal-zebub in 2 Kings 1). Provides the name's availability and connotation.

echoes.text: “‘But the soul who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native-born or a foreigner, the same blasphemes Yahweh. That soul shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised Yahweh’s word, and has broken his commandment, that soul shall utterly be cut off. His iniquity shall be on him.’”
echoes.note: The unforgivable, eternally-condemning blasphemy against the Spirit echoes the Torah's 'high-handed' sin that cuts a person off with no atonement, the one defiant offense excluded from forgiveness. Coherence with the deliberate-sin-without-pardon category is strong.

echoes.text: Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli, that the iniquity of Eli’s house shall not be removed with sacrifice nor offering forever.”
echoes.note: 'The iniquity of Eli's house shall not be atoned for by sacrifice forever' offers an OT precedent for a sin barred from forgiveness, paralleling the never-forgiven blasphemy. Thematic, low volume.

echoes.text: But they rebelled, and grieved his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them.
echoes.note: 'They rebelled and grieved his holy Spirit, so he turned to be their enemy' is one of the rare OT texts naming the Holy Spirit and a rebellion against it. Attributing the Spirit's work to an unclean spirit (v.30) is precisely grieving/blaspheming the holy Spirit; availability of the exact phrase is notable.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”
echoes.note: The Spirit's striving with humanity that does not abide forever offers a faint backdrop to a limit on forgiveness when the Spirit is rejected. Low volume and contested.

pericopes.text: His mother and his brothers came, and standing outside, they sent to him, calling him. A multitude was sitting around him, and they told him, “Behold, your mother, your brothers, and your sisters are outside looking for you.” He answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” Looking around at those who sat around him, he said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother.”

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: Levi's blessing praises those who say of father, mother and brothers 'I do not know them,' keeping covenant over kin, exactly the relativizing of natural family for the sake of God's word that Jesus enacts. Strong thematic coherence with redefining kinship around obedience to God.

echoes.text: He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. Moses said, “Consecrate yourselves today to Yahweh, yes, every man against his son, and against […]
echoes.note: The Levites' willingness to act against brother and son to do the Lord's will is invoked as covenant fidelity over blood ties, paralleling 'whoever does the will of God is my brother.' Thematic, low volume.

echoes.text: I delight to do your will, my God. Yes, your law is within my heart.”
echoes.note: 'I delight to do your will, O my God' anchors the climactic criterion of kinship: doing the will of God. The will-of-God obedience theme has strong recurrence in the Psalter and high coherence with Jesus' redefinition of family.

echoes.text: I will declare your name to my brothers. In the midst of the assembly, I will praise you.
echoes.note: 'I will declare your name to my brothers' supplies a Davidic-righteous-sufferer model of a community of brothers gathered around the one who does God's will. Faint, but Psalm 22 is heavily mined by Mark's passion, raising recurrence.

pericopes.text: Again he began to teach by the seaside. A great multitude was gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat in the sea, and sat down. All the multitude were on the land by the sea. He taught them many things in parables, and told them in his teaching, “Listen! Behold, the farmer went out to sow, and as he sowed, some seed fell by the road, and the birds came and devoured it. Others fell on the rocky ground, where it had little soil, and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of soil. When the sun had risen, it was scorched; and because it had no root, it withered away. Others fell among the thorns, and the thorns grew up, and choked it, and it yielded no fruit. Others fell into the good ground, and yielded fruit, growing up and increasing. Some produced thirty times, some sixty times, and some one hundred times as much.” He said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: Isaiah's image of rain and seed that gives bread and accomplishes God's purpose underwrites the sower parable's logic that the sown word inevitably bears fruit. Thematic coherence is strong (word = seed that does not return empty), and the harvest-yield climax in 4:8 mirrors Isaiah's effective word. Volume is moderate since Mark does not cite, but the recurrence of the word-as-seed motif across early Christian tradition supports availability.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's 'Break up your fallow ground, and don't sow among thorns' supplies the precise agricultural antithesis of good soil versus thorn-choked ground seen in 4:7-8. The shared sowing-among-thorns image gives thematic coherence, though volume is faint and the wording is conventional farming language widely available in the prophets.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
