echoes.note: Hosea's 'Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness; break up your fallow ground' joins sowing and reaping as a covenant-fruit metaphor coherent with the parable's yield. The connection is thematic rather than verbal, and the sowing/harvest pairing is a stock prophetic idiom, so it remains faint.

echoes.text: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both will be equally good.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's counsel to sow seed without knowing which will prosper resonates with the indiscriminate scattering across four soils in 4:4-8. The thematic coherence (uncertain outcome of sowing) is real but the image is proverbial, lowering volume and distinctiveness.

echoes.text: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.
echoes.note: Isaac's hundredfold harvest as a sign of divine blessing offers a scriptural precedent for the climactic 'one hundred times' yield in 4:8. The hundredfold motif is distinctive enough to register, though Mark gives no other Isaac signals, keeping recurrence and volume low.

pericopes.text: He said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

echoes.text: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: The summons 'Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear' inverts Deuteronomy's complaint that the LORD has not given Israel 'ears to hear,' setting up the hardening theme made explicit at 4:12. Thematic coherence with the eyes/ears-of-perception tradition is strong and recurs across Isaiah and Jeremiah, supporting the link even without verbatim citation.

echoes.text: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of the rebellious house, who have eyes to see, and don’t see, who have ears to hear, and don’t hear; for they are a rebellious house.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's rebellious house 'which have ears to hear, and don't hear' supplies nearly the exact idiom of the call to hearing in 4:9 and 4:23. The verbal overlap (ears to hear) and shared context of obstinate non-perception give good volume and coherence with Mark's hardening motif.

echoes.text: ‘Hear now this, foolish people, and without understanding; who have eyes, and don’t see; who have ears, and don’t hear:
echoes.note: Jeremiah's 'who have eyes, and don't see; who have ears, and don't hear' belongs to the same prophetic cluster Mark draws on for the ears-to-hear refrain. It reinforces recurrence within the Isaiah 6 family of hardening texts that frames the whole parables discourse.

pericopes.text: When he was alone, those who were around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. He said to them, “To you is given the mystery of the Kingdom of God, but to those who are outside, all things are done in parables, that ‘seeing they may see, and not perceive; and hearing they may hear, and not understand; lest perhaps they should turn again, and their sins should be forgiven them.’”

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: Mark 4:12 directly quotes Isaiah's commission ('seeing they may see, and not perceive; hearing they may hear, and not understand; lest they should turn and be forgiven'), with the wording closer to the Targum's 'be forgiven' than the MT/LXX 'be healed.' This is the chapter's central formal citation: high volume, explicit, and thematically governing the entire purpose-of-parables saying.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:
echoes.note: The disclosure of 'the mystery of the Kingdom of God' in 4:11 echoes Daniel's revealed 'mystery' (raz) of the coming kingdom that God makes known to the elect while it stays hidden from outsiders. The apocalyptic mystery-revelation vocabulary is distinctive and coherent with Mark's insider/outsider divide, giving solid thematic and verbal warrant.

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: Daniel's vision of the God of heaven setting up an indestructible kingdom underlies Mark's 'Kingdom of God' language as a revealed eschatological secret. Recurrence of the Danielic kingdom motif throughout Mark strengthens the coherence even though 4:11 cites no text.

echoes.text: For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers. All vision has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one who is educated, saying, “Read this, please”; and he says, “I can’t, for it is sealed:” and the book is delivered to one who is not educated, saying, “Read this, please”; and he says, “I can’t read.” The Lord said, “Because […]
echoes.note: Isaiah's theme of God sealing prophetic vision and giving a spirit of stupor so the people cannot understand parallels the deliberate withholding of perception in 4:11-12. It belongs to the same hardening tradition as Isaiah 6 and reinforces its recurrence, though Mark does not draw on its specific wording.

echoes.text: I will open my mouth in a parable. I will utter dark sayings of old,
echoes.note: The psalmist's 'I will open my mouth in a parable' connects parabolic speech with hidden things 'from of old' (so used in Matthew's redaction of this material). For Mark the link is faint and indirect, registering only as thematic coherence between parable-speech and concealed mysteries.

pericopes.text: He said to them, “Don’t you understand this parable? How will you understand all of the parables? The farmer sows the word. The ones by the road are the ones where the word is sown; and when they have heard, immediately Satan comes, and takes away the word which has been sown in them. These in the same way are those who are sown on the rocky places, who, when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with joy. They have no root in themselves, but are short-lived. When oppression or persecution arises because of the word, immediately they stumble. Others are those who are sown among the thorns. These are those who have heard the word, and the cares of this age, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful. Those which were sown on the good ground are those who hear the word, and accept it, and bear fruit, some thirty times, some sixty times, and some one hundred times.”

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: The interpretation that 'the farmer sows the word' (4:14) makes explicit the Isaianic identification of God's effective word with seed that produces fruit. The allegory's insistence that the word bears thirty/sixty/hundredfold (4:20) coheres tightly with Isaiah's word that accomplishes its purpose and does not return empty.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.
echoes.note: The thorn-choked seed that 'becomes unfruitful' (4:18-19) recalls Jeremiah's warning not to sow among thorns, here moralized into the cares and riches that choke the word. The agricultural antithesis is coherent but the language is conventional, keeping it faint.

echoes.text: He that loves gold shall not be justified; And he that follows destruction shall himself have his fill of it. Many have been given over to ruin for the sake of gold; And their perdition meets them face to face. It is a stumbling block to those who sacrifice to it; And every fool shall be taken therewith.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's warning that the lover of gold will not be justified and that riches are a stumbling block coheres with 'the deceitfulness of riches' that chokes the word in 4:19. The wisdom-tradition critique of wealth supplies a Second-Temple backdrop, though the connection is thematic rather than cited.

pericopes.text: He said to them, “Is the lamp brought to be put under a basket or under a bed? Isn’t it put on a stand? For there is nothing hidden, except that it should be made known; neither was anything made secret, but that it should come to light. If any man has ears to hear, let him hear.”

echoes.text: The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.
echoes.note: Proverbs' 'The spirit of man is the LORD's lamp, searching all his innermost parts' supplies a lamp-as-revelation image coherent with the saying that what is hidden must come to light (4:22). The lamp metaphor for disclosure of inner things gives thematic coherence, though Mark cites nothing and lamp imagery is widespread.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's conviction that God will bring every hidden work into judgment matches the principle 'there is nothing hidden, except that it should be made known' (4:22). The eschatological disclosure of the concealed is thematically coherent, though the wording is independent.

echoes.text: he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.
echoes.note: Daniel's praise that God 'reveals the deep and secret things' and that 'light dwells with him' resonates with the hidden-to-be-revealed/come-to-light pairing in 4:22, continuing the chapter's Danielic mystery-revelation vocabulary. The link is thematic and reinforces recurrence within the discourse.

pericopes.text: He said to them, “Take heed what you hear. With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you, and more will be given to you who hear. For whoever has, to him will more be given, and he who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away from him.”

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: The measure-for-measure principle that 'with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you' (4:24) draws on the wisdom logic of reciprocal recompense found in Proverbs' teaching that what one gives the LORD repays. The retributive-measure motif is coherent though proverbial and not specifically cited.

echoes.text: Instruct a wise man, and he will be still wiser. Teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.
echoes.note: The saying 'to him who has, more will be given' (4:25) parallels Proverbs' wisdom-multiplication theme ('Give to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser'). The principle that receptivity yields increase is thematically coherent with the surrounding hearing-discourse, though faint.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;
echoes.note: Daniel's God who 'gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding' offers a Second-Temple precedent for the have/have-not multiplication of 4:25. The connection is thematic and reinforces the chapter's Danielic coloring, but remains faint.

pericopes.text: He said, “The Kingdom of God is as if a man should cast seed on the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, he doesn’t know how. For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the fruit is ripe, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: The harvest climax 'he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come' (4:29) closely echoes Joel's 'Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe.' The verbal overlap of sickle-and-ripe-harvest is distinctive (high volume) and coheres with Mark's eschatological framing of the kingdom's arrival as a reaping, making this the pericope's strongest link.

echoes.text: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so. The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
echoes.note: The earth bearing fruit 'of itself' (automate)—blade, ear, full grain (4:28)—recalls the creation account of the earth bringing forth vegetation yielding seed after its kind. The motif of the earth's God-given autonomous fertility is thematically coherent, though Mark gives no verbal citation.

echoes.text: “‘When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not wholly reap the corners of your field, neither shall you gather the gleanings of your harvest.
echoes.note: The image of grain ripening to harvest draws on the broader Torah harvest framework, but the link is generic. Included for maximality; volume and distinctiveness are low and the coherence is only with the agricultural setting.

pericopes.text: He said, “How will we liken the Kingdom of God? Or with what parable will we illustrate it? It’s like a grain of mustard seed, which, when it is sown in the earth, though it is less than all the seeds that are on the earth, yet when it is sown, grows up, and becomes greater than all the herbs, and puts out great branches, so that the birds of the sky can lodge under its shadow.”

echoes.text: in the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it; and it shall produce boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches shall they dwell.
echoes.note: The mustard plant that puts out 'great branches, so that the birds of the sky can lodge under its shadow' (4:32) reworks Ezekiel's noble cedar planted on the mountain under which 'all birds of every wing' dwell in the shadow of its branches. The branches-shadow-birds-nesting cluster is verbally and thematically tight (high volume), and the imperial-tree-as-kingdom motif coheres with Mark's kingdom parable.

echoes.text: The leaves of it were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all: the animals of the field had shadow under it, and the birds of the sky lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
echoes.note: Nebuchadnezzar's tree whose branches shelter the beasts and in which 'the birds of the sky lived' supplies the proverbial great-tree-with-nesting-birds image behind 4:32. The recurrence of this kingdom-tree topos (Daniel 4:21 repeats it) gives strong availability and coherence with the contrast between the tiny seed and the sheltering kingdom.

echoes.text: All the birds of the sky made their nests in its boughs; and under its branches all the animals of the field gave birth to their young; and all great nations lived under its shadow.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's Assyrian cedar in whose boughs 'all the birds of the sky made their nests' and under whose shadow great nations lived belongs to the same world-tree tradition Mark evokes. The shared birds-nest-in-the-shadow image reinforces recurrence across the prophetic kingdom-tree corpus.

echoes.text: whose leaves were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all; under which the animals of the field lived, and on whose branches the birds of the sky had their habitation:
echoes.note: The reprise of the tree 'in whose branches the birds of the sky lived' restates the Danielic kingdom-tree, strengthening the topos behind 4:32 by recurrence within a single source. Its function is to confirm the availability of the great-tree-as-dominion symbol rather than to add new wording.

echoes.text: The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.
echoes.note: The psalm's 'birds of the sky' that nest by the branches and sing reflects the same creation-poetic image of birds lodging in foliage. It is a faint, generic parallel that adds coherence to the nesting-birds detail but lacks the kingdom-tree distinctiveness of Ezekiel and Daniel.

pericopes.text: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. Without a parable he didn’t speak to them; but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.

echoes.text: I will open my mouth in a parable. I will utter dark sayings of old,
echoes.note: The summary that Jesus spoke 'without a parable he didn't speak to them' resonates with the psalmist's 'I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings of old.' The link between exclusive parabolic teaching and revealed/concealed wisdom is thematically coherent, though for Mark it is faint and uncited.

pericopes.text: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let’s go over to the other side.” Leaving the multitude, they took him with them, even as he was, in the boat. Other small boats were also with him. A big wind storm arose, and the waves beat into the boat, so much that the boat was already filled. He himself was in the stern, asleep on the cushion, and they woke him up, and told him, “Teacher, don’t you care that we are dying?” He awoke, and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” The wind ceased, and there was a great calm. He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?” They were greatly afraid, and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”

echoes.text: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their […]
echoes.note: The storm-stilling sequence—seafarers in distress, a stormy wind lifting the waves, a cry to the LORD, and his making 'the storm a calm, so that its waves are still'—maps closely onto 4:37-39. The verbal echo of the LORD stilling waves into calm is distinctive (high volume) and thematically frames Jesus exercising divine prerogative over the sea.

echoes.text: But Yahweh sent out a great wind on the sea, and there was a mighty storm on the sea, so that the ship was likely to break up. Then the mariners were afraid, and every man cried to his god. They threw the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten the ship. But Jonah had gone down into the innermost parts of the ship, and he was laying down, and was fast asleep. So the ship master came to him, and said to him, “What do you mean, sleeper? Arise, […]
echoes.note: The scene of a prophet asleep in the boat during a great storm, woken by terrified sailors fearing death, with the sea growing calm once he acts, closely parallels 4:37-41. The shared narrative structure (sleeping figure, fear of perishing, calmed sea, awe-struck question) gives strong volume and coherence, with Jesus surpassing Jonah by commanding rather than being thrown overboard.

echoes.text: You rule the pride of the sea. When its waves rise up, you calm them.
echoes.note: 'You rule the pride of the sea. When its waves rise up, you still them' attributes to YHWH precisely the sea-rebuking power Jesus wields in 4:39. The distinctive divine-warrior motif of mastering the chaotic sea makes this a strong echo undergirding the disciples' question 'Who then is this?'

echoes.text: who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, and the turmoil of the nations.
echoes.note: God's stilling of 'the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves' supplies the same sea-mastery vocabulary applied to Jesus in 4:39. It reinforces the recurrence of the YHWH-stills-the-sea topos across the Psalter that frames the miracle's Christological force.

echoes.text: He rebuked the Red Sea also, and it was dried up; so he led them through the depths, as through a desert.
echoes.note: God's 'rebuke' of the Red Sea so that it dried up supplies the rebuke-of-the-sea verb (epitimao) used in 4:39, framing the calming as a divine-warrior subjugation of chaotic waters. The shared rebuking-the-sea motif gives good coherence with Mark's exodus-tinged sea command.

echoes.text: He rebukes the sea, and makes it dry, and dries up all the rivers. Bashan languishes, and Carmel; and the flower of Lebanon languishes.
echoes.note: Nahum's God who 'rebukes the sea, and makes it dry' provides another instance of the divine rebuke of the waters behind Jesus' command 'Peace! Be still!' (4:39). It strengthens the recurrence of the sea-rebuke tradition, though it is not specifically cited.

echoes.text: “Or who shut up the sea with doors, when it broke out of the womb, when I made clouds its garment, and wrapped it in thick darkness, marked out for it my bound, set bars and doors, and said, ‘Here you may come, but no further. Here your proud waves shall be stayed?’
echoes.note: The LORD's setting bounds for the sea—'thus far shall you come, but no further; and here shall your proud waves be stayed'—portrays the creator's unique authority over the deep that Jesus assumes in 4:39-41. The coherence with the disciples' awe at one who commands wind and sea is strong, supporting the figural Christology.

echoes.text: At your rebuke they fled. At the voice of your thunder they hurried away.
echoes.note: The waters fleeing at God's rebuke in the creation-psalm adds to the cluster of texts where the deity's voice masters the sea, coherent with Jesus' verbal command. It is a faint reinforcement of the sea-rebuke topos rather than a distinct source.

echoes.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety.
echoes.note: The psalmist's peaceful sleep in trust—'I will both lay down and sleep in peace'—offers a faint counterpoint to Jesus asleep amid the storm (4:38), portraying serene confidence in God. The link is thematic and weak, included for maximality.

echoes.text: Again, one preparing to sail, and about to journey over raging waves, Calleth upon a piece of wood more rotten than the vessel that carries him; For that vessel the hunger for gains devised, And a craftsman, even wisdom, built it; And your providence, O Father, guideth it along, Because even in the sea you gave a way, And in the waves a sure path, Shewing that you can save out of every danger, That so even without are a man may put to sea;
echoes.note: Wisdom's portrait of God's providence guiding the sea-voyager safely through the waves provides a Second-Temple backdrop to deliverance from a storm at sea (4:37-39). It contributes thematic coherence and availability, but the connection is general rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: They came to the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes. When he had come out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit met him out of the tombs. He lived in the tombs. Nobody could bind him any more, not even with chains, because he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been torn apart by him, and the fetters broken in pieces. Nobody had the strength to tame him. Always, night and day, in the tombs and in the mountains, he was crying out, and cutting himself with stones. When he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and bowed down to him, and crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have I to do with you, Jesus, you Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, don’t torment me.” For he said to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!” He asked him, “What is your name?” He said to him, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” He begged him much that he would not send them away out of the country. Now on the mountainside there was a great herd of pigs feeding. All the demons begged him, saying, “Send us into the pigs, that we may enter into them.” At once Jesus gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered into the pigs. The herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea, and they were drowned in the sea. Those who fed them fled, and told it in the city and in the country. The people came to see what it was that had happened. They came to Jesus, and saw him who had been possessed by demons sitting, clothed, and in his right mind, even him who had the legion; and they were afraid. Those who saw it declared to them what happened to him who was possessed by demons, and about the pigs. They began to beg him to depart from their region. As he was entering into the boat, he who had been possessed by demons begged him that he might be with him. He didn’t allow him, but said to him, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you, and how he had mercy on you.” He went his way, and began to proclaim in Decapolis how Jesus had done great things for him, and everyone marveled.

echoes.text: who sit among the graves, and lodge in the secret places; who eat pig’s flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;
echoes.note: Isaiah indicts the rebellious people who 'sit among the graves and lodge in the secret places, who eat swine's flesh.' Mark's demoniac dwelling among the tombs (vv.2-3,5) coupled with the herd of swine (vv.11-13) gives a remarkably dense convergence of both motifs — graves and pigs — that no other OT text combines. High Volume and Thematic Coherence: both passages concern unclean, rebellious figures marked off from covenant life, met by a God who reveals himself to those not seeking him (Isa 65:1).

echoes.text: a people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens, and burning incense on bricks;
echoes.note: Continues the Isaiah 65 oracle: a people 'who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens.' The demoniac's defiant, self-destructive crying out night and day (v.5) coheres with Isaiah's portrait of provocation and cultic impurity. Strengthens the recurrence of the Isaiah 65 background already secured by v.4.

echoes.text: who say, Stand by yourself, don’t come near to me, for I am holier than you. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burns all the day.
echoes.note: The unclean of Isaiah say 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you' — a perverse holiness that defiles. The demoniac's cry 'What have I to do with you... do not torment me' (v.7) and the swine's contagion echo the ironic uncleanness-as-holiness of Isa 65:5, where God calls such people 'a smoke in my nostrils.' Thematic coherence within the same oracle reinforces the allusion.

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: The drowning of the unclean spirits in the sea (v.13) and the larger Markan motif of mastering the deep (preceding stilling of the storm) draws on the chaos-waters over which God's spirit broods at creation. The sea as the locus into which disorder is cast is faintly evocative of the primeval deep, but the connection is thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its strength when the morning appeared; and the Egyptians fled against it. Yahweh overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea. The waters returned, and covered the chariots and the horsemen, even all Pharaoh’s army that went in after them into the sea. There remained not so much as one of them.
echoes.note: 'Legion' — a Roman military term — and the herd's headlong rush into the sea where they are drowned (v.13) figurally re-enacts the destruction of Pharaoh's host swallowed by the sea. The numbering ('about two thousand'), the military diction, and the drowning of an enemy army in water echo the Exodus deliverance. Mark casts Jesus' exorcism as a new-Exodus liberation from an occupying force, a coherence many read in the Gerasene narrative.

echoes.text: Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to Yahweh, and said, “I will sing to Yahweh, for he has triumphed gloriously. The horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.
echoes.note: The Song of the Sea celebrates that horse and rider were thrown into the sea. The drowning of Legion's host (v.13) resonates with this triumph-song over a defeated army cast into the waters, supporting the new-Exodus reading; faint and thematic, dependent on the Exodus 14 figural link.

echoes.text: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High.
echoes.note: The demoniac addresses Jesus as 'Son of the Most High God' (v.7), using El Elyon, the divine title first given by Melchizedek (Gen 14:18-20). The Septuagintal 'God Most High' is a recurrent OT designation (Ps 78:35; Dan 3:26) and here, on Gentile lips, signals recognition of Israel's God by an outsider/unclean source. Strong Availability and Volume for the title.

echoes.text: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace: he spoke and said, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, you servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here. Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out of the midst of the fire.
echoes.note: Nebuchadnezzar calls the three 'servants of the Most High God' — the same Greek title used by the demoniac (v.7) and characteristic of Gentile recognition of Israel's God in the LXX. The pattern of a pagan figure confessing 'the Most High God' coheres with Mark's setting in Gentile Decapolis. Recurrence of the title in Daniel strengthens the figural background.

echoes.text: Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron,
echoes.note: Psalm 107 describes those who 'sat in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in affliction and irons,' whom God delivers. The demoniac bound with chains and fetters, dwelling in deathly tombs and broken loose (vv.3-4), evokes this portrait of the captive freed by divine mercy. The same Psalm's later stilling of the storm (107:29) parallels Mark's preceding pericope, supporting recurrence; nonetheless verbal contact is faint.

echoes.text: “Whoever in the open field touches one who is slain with a sword, or a dead body, or a bone of a man, or a grave, shall be unclean seven days.
echoes.note: The Torah's gravest corpse-uncleanness law marks anyone touching a grave or the dead as defiled seven days. The demoniac's permanent residence among the tombs (vv.2-3,5) renders him maximally unclean by this standard, which Mark heightens by adjoining the swine. Thematic coherence with the wider Markan concern for purity boundaries crossed by Jesus.

echoes.text: The pig, because he has a split hoof, and is cloven-footed, but doesn’t chew the cud, he is unclean to you. Of their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch; they are unclean to you.
echoes.note: Swine are the paradigmatic unclean animal: 'of their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch.' The great herd of pigs (vv.11-13) signals the Gentile, unclean territory and supplies the fitting receptacle for unclean spirits. The legal designation of swine grounds the narrative's purity logic and reinforces the Isaiah 65:4 swine motif.

pericopes.text: When Jesus had crossed back over in the boat to the other side, a great multitude was gathered to him; and he was by the sea. Behold, one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, came; and seeing him, he fell at his feet, and begged him much, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Please come and lay your hands on her, that she may be made healthy, and live.” He went with him, and a great multitude followed him, and they pressed upon him on all sides. A certain woman, who had an issue of blood for twelve years, and had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse, having heard the things concerning Jesus, came up behind him in the crowd, and touched his clothes. For she said, “If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well.” Immediately the flow of her blood was dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her affliction. Immediately Jesus, perceiving in himself that the power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd, and asked, “Who touched my clothes?” His disciples said to him, “You see the multitude pressing against you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” He looked around to see her who had done this thing. But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had been done to her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth. He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease.”

echoes.text: “‘If a woman has a discharge of her blood many days not in the time of her period, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her period; all the days of the discharge of her uncleanness shall be as in the days of her period: she is unclean. Every bed whereon she lies all the days of her discharge shall be to her as the bed of her period: and everything whereon she sits shall be unclean, as the uncleanness of her period. Whoever touches these things […]
echoes.note: The woman 'with an issue of blood' (v.25) embodies the Levitical zavah: a woman with a discharge beyond her period is unclean all the days of the flow, and whatever and whoever she touches becomes unclean. Her touching Jesus' garment (v.27) inverts the expected contagion — purity flows outward rather than impurity inward. Very high Volume and Thematic Coherence; the legal background is essential to the scene's meaning.

echoes.text: “‘If a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood, she shall be in her impurity seven days: and whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening.
echoes.note: The baseline menstrual-impurity law ('seven days she shall be in her impurity, and whoever touches her shall be unclean') frames the chronic twelve-year condition (v.25). Establishes that the woman is perpetually outside normal social and cultic contact, deepening the audacity of her approach in the crowd.

echoes.text: The priest shall offer the one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering; and the priest shall make atonement for her before Yahweh for the uncleanness of her discharge.
echoes.note: The law's resolution requires the priest to make atonement 'for her unclean discharge,' after which she is clean. Jesus' word 'be cured of your disease' (v.34) functions as the priestly declaration of restored cleanness, the discharge being 'dried up' (v.29). Thematic coherence: Jesus enacts the role the Levitical system assigns to atonement and priestly verdict.

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (kanaph)' — the same term denotes the hem/corner of a garment. The woman seeks healing by touching the edge of Jesus' clothes (vv.27-28), and Matthew/Luke specify the kraspedon (tassel). Faint but evocative: healing located in the garment's edge resonates with Malachi's healing 'in the wings.'

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;
echoes.note: The command to wear tassels on the corners of garments as reminders of the commandments stands behind the Synoptic detail of touching the hem (here generalized as 'his clothes,' v.27). The healing power located in the garment's fringe gains resonance from the sanctity Torah attaches to the tassel; faint in Mark, who omits the tassel itself.

echoes.text: As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
echoes.note: Contact with Elisha's bones revives a corpse — power transmitted by touch from a holy person even involuntarily. The woman's cure by touching Jesus' garment, with power 'gone out from him' (v.30), echoes the prophetic motif of healing virtue conveyed through physical contact. Thematic, supporting the Elijah-Elisha typology that pervades the chapter.

pericopes.text: While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue ruler’s house saying, “Your daughter is dead. Why bother the Teacher any more?” But Jesus, when he heard the message spoken, immediately said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Don’t be afraid, only believe.” He allowed no one to follow him, except Peter, James, and John the brother of James. He came to the synagogue ruler’s house, and he saw an uproar, weeping, and great wailing. When he had entered in, he said to them, “Why do you make an uproar and weep? The child is not dead, but is asleep.” They ridiculed him. But he, having put them all out, took the father of the child, her mother, and those who were with him, and went in where the child was lying. Taking the child by the hand, he said to her, “Talitha cumi!” which means, being interpreted, “Girl, I tell you, get up!” Immediately the girl rose up and walked, for she was twelve years old. They were amazed with great amazement. He strictly ordered them that no one should know this, and commanded that something should be given to her to eat.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah raises the widow of Zarephath's son: he goes in to where the child lies, acts privately, and 'the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived,' then Elijah presents the living child. Mark's raising of Jairus' daughter — entering where the child lay (v.40), the restoring word, the return to life (v.42) — is patterned on this paradigmatic prophetic resurrection. Strong Volume and recurrence within the chapter's Elijah-Elisha typology.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha raises the Shunammite's son: he enters alone with the dead child, shuts the door (cf. Jesus putting out the mourners, v.40), and the child revives; the mother falls at his feet (cf. Jairus, v.22). The closest single template for Jairus' daughter — privacy, exclusion of others, parental supplication, and bodily resurrection of a child — making the Elisha narrative a primary subtext.

echoes.text: He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
echoes.note: Elisha's bodily, hands-on revival ('he put his mouth on his mouth... the flesh of the child grew warm') resonates with Jesus 'taking the child by the hand' (v.41). The motif of resurrection effected by the prophet's physical contact strengthens the Elisha typology beyond the structural parallels already noted in 4:32-37.

echoes.text: Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the room into the house, and delivered him to his mother; and Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives.”
echoes.note: Elijah 'gave him to his mother' after the raising; Jesus likewise restores the child to her parents and orders that she be given food (v.43), confirming bodily life. The return-to-the-parent motif and the demonstration of real restored life cohere closely with the Elijah pattern.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Jesus' euphemism 'the child is not dead, but is asleep' (v.39) trades on the OT/Second-Temple metaphor of death as sleep from which the dead awake, classically formulated in Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake.' The raising functions as a proleptic sign of resurrection hope; thematic and verbal contact through the sleep-of-death idiom.

echoes.text: He said, “Swear to me,” and he swore to him. Israel bowed himself on the bed’s head.
echoes.note: Death-as-sleep language (e.g., the patriarchs 'sleeping with their fathers,' a recurrent OT idiom) underlies Jesus' 'she is asleep' (v.39), prompting the mourners' ridicule because they hear only literal sleep. Faint, depending on the broader idiom rather than a single text; cited to register the OT availability of the metaphor.

echoes.text: For his anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.
echoes.note: 'Weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning' — the turning of mourning into rejoicing at a child's restoration loosely echoes the psalm's reversal from lament to deliverance, set against the 'weeping and great wailing' (v.38) Jesus overturns. Thematic only; included as a faint coherence with the chapter's reversal of death into life.

pericopes.text: He went out from there. He came into his own country, and his disciples followed him. When the Sabbath had come, he began to teach in the synagogue, and many hearing him were astonished, saying, “Where did this man get these things?” and, “What is the wisdom that is given to this man, that such mighty works come about by his hands? Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary, and brother of James, Joses, Judah, and Simon? Aren’t his sisters here with us?” They were offended at him. Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country, and among his own relatives, and in his own house.” He could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people, and healed them. He marveled because of their unbelief. He went around the villages teaching.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says Yahweh concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, saying, You shall not prophesy in Yahweh’s name, that you not die by our hand;
echoes.note: Jeremiah's own townsmen of Anathoth seek his life, the classic instance of a prophet rejected by his native place. Jesus' aphorism that a prophet lacks honor 'in his own country' and 'among his own relatives' coheres thematically with Jeremiah's hometown opposition. Recurrence of the rejected-prophet pattern across the OT strengthens the figural reading.

echoes.text: For even your brothers, and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you; even they have cried aloud after you: don’t believe them, though they speak beautiful words to you.
echoes.note: Jeremiah is warned that even his brothers and his father's house deal treacherously with him. Mark's specification 'among his own relatives, and in his own house' closely tracks this kin-and-household betrayal motif. The verbal overlap of 'house' and 'kindred' makes the echo more than generic.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah laments rejection by his own people Israel despite his prophetic word, part of the OT type of the lone unhonored prophet. The thematic coherence with Jesus' rejection at Nazareth supports a faint echo, though no verbal link exists. Marked contested as a pattern-level resonance only.

echoes.text: He said to me, Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, to a nation of rebels who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me even to this very day. The children are impudent and stiff-hearted: I am sending you to them; and you shall tell them, Thus says the Lord Yahweh. They, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house), yet shall know that there has been a prophet […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel is sent to a rebellious house that will not listen, and is told to speak 'whether they hear or refuse to hear.' Jesus' marveling at their unbelief and inability to do mighty works mirrors the prophet sent to obstinate kin. The commissioning-to-the-resistant pattern coheres with Mark's portrait.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: The Servant is 'despised and rejected' and not esteemed. Nazareth's being 'offended' at Jesus faintly anticipates the despised-Servant motif Mark develops toward the passion. Low confidence and contested: thematic only, no verbal contact here.

pericopes.text: He called to himself the twelve, and began to send them out two by two; and he gave them authority over the unclean spirits. He commanded them that they should take nothing for their journey, except a staff only: no bread, no wallet, no money in their purse, but to wear sandals, and not put on two tunics. He said to them, “Wherever you enter into a house, stay there until you depart from there. Whoever will not receive you nor hear you, as you depart from there, shake off the dust that is under your feet for a testimony against them. Assuredly, I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city!” They went out and preached that people should repent. They cast out many demons, and anointed many with oil who were sick, and healed them.

echoes.text: This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.
echoes.note: Israel eats the Passover with staff in hand, sandals on feet, dressed for urgent departure. The Twelve are likewise equipped with a staff and sandals only, traveling light and ready, evoking the Exodus-haste posture. The shared cluster of staff + sandals supports the allusion despite the differing inventory of permitted items.

echoes.text: Then he said to Gehazi, “Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my staff in your hand, and go your way. If you meet any man, don’t greet him; and if anyone greets you, don’t answer him again. Then lay my staff on the face of the child.”
echoes.note: Elisha sends Gehazi with staff in hand on an urgent prophetic errand, not to greet anyone on the way. The sending of agents bearing a staff, with authority over life and sickness, coheres with the Elijah/Elisha framing of the mission of the Twelve who heal and anoint. Recurrence of the prophet-sends-disciple type strengthens this.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: Elijah lodges in a single household (the widow of Zarephath) and is sustained there, a model of the prophet received into one house. Jesus' instruction to stay in one house until departure resonates faintly with this prophetic hospitality pattern. Contested, thematic coherence only.

echoes.text: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.
echoes.note: Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his garment as a prophetic sign-act of curse against those who break covenant. The disciples' shaking off the dust 'for a testimony against them' enacts the same symbolic withdrawal-and-witness gesture. The shared performative testimony-against-the-faithless motif supports the allusion.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky. He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground.
echoes.note: The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah is explicitly named by Jesus as the benchmark of judgment for towns that reject the messengers. This is a direct invocation of the OT narrative as the measure of eschatological accountability. High confidence given the named cities.

echoes.text: Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets, and said to him, “Put your belt on your waist, take this vial of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth Gilead. When you come there, find Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi, and go in, and make him arise up from among his brothers, and carry him to an inner room. Then take the vial of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, ‘Thus says Yahweh, “I have anointed you king over Israel.”’ Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha dispatches a member of the prophetic guild with anointing oil to act in Yahweh's name. The Twelve who 'anointed many with oil' for healing faintly echo prophetic anointing as a delegated sign-act. Contested and thematic; the OT oil here anoints a king, not the sick.

echoes.text: Then Amos answered Amaziah, “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet’s son; but I was a herdsman, and a farmer of sycamore figs; and Yahweh took me from following the flock, and Yahweh said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’
echoes.note: Amos is a layman taken from his ordinary work and sent to prophesy, paralleling the commissioning of ordinary disciples to preach repentance. The send-the-unlikely-prophet motif coheres but lacks verbal contact. Marked contested.

pericopes.text: King Herod heard this, for his name had become known, and he said, “John the Baptizer has risen from the dead, and therefore these powers are at work in him.” But others said, “He is Elijah.” Others said, “He is a prophet, or like one of the prophets.” But Herod, when he heard this, said, “This is John, whom I beheaded. He has risen from the dead.” For Herod himself had sent out and arrested John, and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, for he had married her. For John said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” Herodias set herself against him, and desired to kill him, but she couldn’t, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe. When he heard him, he did many things, and he heard him gladly. Then a convenient day came, that Herod on his birthday made a supper for his nobles, the high officers, and the chief men of Galilee. When the daughter of Herodias herself came in and danced, she pleased Herod and those sitting with him. The king said to the young lady, “Ask me whatever you want, and I will give it to you.” He swore to her, “Whatever you shall ask of me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.” She went out, and said to her mother, “What shall I ask?” She said, “The head of John the Baptizer.” She came in immediately with haste to the king, and asked, “I want you to give me right now the head of John the Baptizer on a platter.” The king was exceedingly sorry, but for the sake of his oaths, and of his dinner guests, he didn’t wish to refuse her. Immediately the king sent out a soldier of his guard, and commanded to bring John’s head, and he went and beheaded him in the prison, and brought his head on a platter, and gave it to the young lady; and the young lady gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard this, they came and took up his corpse, and laid it in a tomb.

echoes.text: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword. Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!”
echoes.note: Jezebel, the powerful queen, vows to kill the prophet Elijah, who is identified in this very passage (v. 15) with the figure expected to return. Herodias' relentless desire to kill John, the Elijah-figure, replays the Jezebel-versus-prophet conflict. Strong thematic coherence and recurrence, reinforced by Mark's explicit Elijah identification.

echoes.text: After these things, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard, which was in Jezreel, hard by the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. Ahab spoke to Naboth, saying, “Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a garden of herbs, because it is near to my house; and I will give you for it a better vineyard than it. Or, if it seems good to you, I will give you its worth in money.” Naboth said to Ahab, “May Yahweh forbid me, that I should give the inheritance of my […]
echoes.note: Jezebel manipulates a royal feast and oath/legal machinery to bring about Naboth's death while the weak king Ahab acquiesces. Herodias engineers John's execution through her daughter at a banquet while a reluctant Herod yields, a deliberate Ahab-Jezebel-Naboth typology. The wicked-queen-orchestrates-judicial-murder pattern is tightly coherent.

echoes.text: Then the king asked her, “What would you like, queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you even to the half of the kingdom.”
echoes.note: Ahasuerus, at a banquet, offers Esther her request 'up to half of my kingdom,' the exact royal-oath formula Herod swears to the dancing girl (also Esther 5:6; 7:2). The verbal correspondence is precise and distinctive, making this a near-quotation of the Persian-court motif. High volume and recurrence within Esther.

echoes.text: for it was so, when Jezebel cut off the prophets of Yahweh, that Obadiah took one hundred prophets, and hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water.)
echoes.note: Jezebel cuts off (kills) the prophets of Yahweh while Obadiah hides them, establishing the queen-as-prophet-killer. John's beheading at the queen's instigation reprises this. The Elijah-cycle background that Mark foregrounds strengthens the echo.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife. It is your brother’s nakedness.
echoes.note: John's charge, 'It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife,' directly invokes the Levitical prohibition against uncovering the nakedness of a brother's wife. The legal ground of John's rebuke is this statute (cf. Lev 20:21). The verbal and legal correspondence is explicit.

echoes.text: “‘If a man takes his brother’s wife, it is an impurity. He has uncovered his brother’s nakedness. They shall be childless.
echoes.note: This statute declares it 'impurity' for a man to take his brother's wife, the precise offense John names against Herod for marrying Herodias. Together with Lev 18:16 it furnishes the explicit legal basis of the prophet's condemnation. Direct invocation of Torah.

echoes.text: The king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah, and carry him back to Amon the governor of the city, and to Joash the king’s son. Say, ‘Thus says the king, “Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I come in peace.”’”
echoes.note: King Ahab imprisons the prophet Micaiah for speaking an unwelcome word. Herod's binding John in prison for his unwelcome rebuke replays the king-imprisons-truthful-prophet motif. Contested, thematic coherence within the Kings prophetic cycle.

echoes.text: Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchijah the king’s son, that was in the court of the guard: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. In the dungeon there was no water, but mire; and Jeremiah sank in the mire. Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a eunuch, who was in the king’s house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon (the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin), Ebedmelech went out of the king’s house, and spoke to […]
echoes.note: Jeremiah is imprisoned by officials while a vacillating king Zedekiah privately respects yet fails to protect him. Herod's fearing and gladly hearing John yet failing to save him mirrors the weak-king-and-imprisoned-prophet dynamic. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: The fear of man proves to be a snare, but whoever puts his trust in Yahweh is kept safe.
echoes.note: The fear of human opinion becomes a snare. Herod's capitulation 'for the sake of his oaths and of his dinner guests' illustrates this proverbial snare of social fear. Wisdom-thematic resonance only; contested.

echoes.text: Jephthah vowed a vow to Yahweh, and said, “If you will indeed deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, then it shall be, that whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, it shall be Yahweh’s, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering.” So Jephthah passed over to the children of Ammon to fight against them; and Yahweh delivered them into his hand. He struck them from Aroer until you come […]
echoes.note: Jephthah's rash vow forces him to a deadly act he regrets, the king-bound-by-his-oath tragedy. Herod, 'exceedingly sorry' yet bound 'for the sake of his oaths,' replays this rash-vow type. Contested, thematic and structural parallel without verbal link.

echoes.text: On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he made a feast for all his servants, and he lifted up the head of the chief cup bearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants. He restored the chief cup bearer to his position again, and he gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand; but he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
echoes.note: Pharaoh's birthday feast becomes the occasion of an execution, the only other clear OT royal birthday banquet ending in death. Herod's birthday supper culminating in beheading faintly recalls this. Low confidence, contested resonance.

pericopes.text: The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught. He said to them, “You come apart into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat. They went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves. They saw them going, and many recognized him and ran there on foot from all the cities. They arrived before them and came together to him. Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses prays for a successor so Israel will not be 'as sheep which have no shepherd,' the precise phrase Mark applies to the crowd. Jesus stepping in to teach is cast as the Moses-appointed shepherd over a leaderless people. Verbal correspondence and thematic coherence make this a strong allusion.

echoes.text: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let them each return to his house in peace.’”
echoes.note: Micaiah sees Israel 'scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd' because their king-shepherd has failed. With Herod's failure as shepherd-king just narrated, Mark's shepherdless-sheep description points pointedly to this text. Strong verbal and thematic fit.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered.
echoes.note: Ezekiel indicts Israel's shepherds and says the flock was 'scattered, because there was no shepherd,' promising that God himself will shepherd them. Jesus' compassion and teaching enact Yahweh's promised shepherding of the abandoned flock. High thematic coherence with the immediately preceding failure of Herod.

echoes.text: For the teraphim have spoken vanity, and the diviners have seen a lie; and they have told false dreams. They comfort in vain. Therefore they go their way like sheep. They are oppressed, because there is no shepherd.
echoes.note: The people 'wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd' because false guidance has failed them. Mark's shepherdless crowd resonates with Zechariah's diagnosis. Verbal overlap on the shepherdless-sheep image supports a solid allusion, though Numbers/Ezekiel are nearer.

echoes.text: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: The leader is to 'go out before them and come in before them,' guiding their movements, language Mark's narrative of the crowd's pursuit and Jesus' going-out-to-teach faintly mirrors. Reinforces the Moses-successor framing of v.34. Contested as a secondary layer of the same Numbers context.

echoes.text: On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening. When Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he did to the people, he said, “What is this thing that you do for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning to evening?” Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God. When they have a matter, they come to me, and I judge […]
echoes.note: Moses is so pressed by the people seeking him that he has no respite, prompting Jethro's counsel to share the load. The crowds giving Jesus and the Twelve 'no leisure so much as to eat' faintly recalls the overburdened-mediator scene. Contested, thematic only.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: Woe to shepherds who scatter the flock; God will gather his scattered sheep and raise true shepherds. The shepherdless crowd that Jesus gathers and teaches coheres with this oracle of regathering. Recurrence of the false-shepherd/true-shepherd theme strengthens the echo.

pericopes.text: When it was late in the day, his disciples came to him, and said, “This place is deserted, and it is late in the day. Send them away, that they may go into the surrounding country and villages, and buy themselves bread, for they have nothing to eat.” But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” They asked him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread, and give them something to eat?” He said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go see.” When they knew, they said, “Five, and two fish.” He commanded them that everyone should sit down in groups on the green grass. They sat down in ranks, by hundreds and by fifties. He took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed and broke the loaves, and he gave to his disciples to set before them, and he divided the two fish among them all. They all ate, and were filled. They took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and also of the fish. Those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.

echoes.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]
echoes.note: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, his servant objects at the inadequacy, all eat and there is food left over, with a word of the LORD that they shall eat and have some left. The structure of Mark's feeding (objection, insufficient bread, all filled, surplus gathered) closely follows this Elisha miracle. The strongest single source-text by structural correspondence.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not. It shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare that which they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.” Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, “At evening, then you shall know that Yahweh has brought […]
echoes.note: God feeds Israel with manna in the wilderness so that 'they gathered, some more, some less... and they had no lack,' all eating to sufficiency. The desert-feeding of the multitude evokes the manna provision, with the 'deserted place' setting reinforcing the wilderness typology. High thematic coherence and recurrence in Israel's memory.

echoes.text: Yes, they spoke against God. They said, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Behold, he struck the rock, so that waters gushed out, and streams overflowed. Can he give bread also? Will he provide flesh for his people?” Therefore Yahweh heard, and was angry. A fire was kindled against Jacob, anger also went up against Israel, because they didn’t believe in God, and didn’t trust in his salvation. Yet he commanded the skies above, and opened the doors […]
echoes.note: Israel asks 'Can God spread a table in the wilderness?' and God rains food so 'they ate and were well filled.' Mark's 'they all ate, and were filled' in a deserted place answers the psalm's challenge. The verbal echo of eating-and-being-filled in the desert supports a solid allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
echoes.note: The shepherd LORD makes his flock 'lie down in green pastures.' Mark's striking detail that the people sit on the 'green grass' immediately after the shepherdless-sheep statement links the feeding to the shepherd-feeds-his-flock psalm. The unusual 'green' notation strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil. My cup runs over.
echoes.note: 'You prepare a table before me'; the shepherd-host who provides a meal coheres with Jesus feeding the crowd after the shepherd motif. Contested, secondary to the green-pastures echo of v.2. Thematic resonance only.

echoes.text: Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens. Let them judge the people at all times. It shall be that every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves. So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you. If you will […]
echoes.note: Moses organizes Israel into groups over 'thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens' at Jethro's counsel. The crowd seated 'in groups... by hundreds and by fifties' deliberately arranges the people in the Mosaic wilderness-camp formation. The hundreds-and-fifties ordering is a distinctive verbal echo.

echoes.text: Moses was angry with the officers of the army, the captains of thousands and the captains of hundreds, who came from the service of the war.
echoes.note: Israel's host is officered by 'commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds,' the wilderness military ordering. The ranked seating by hundreds and fifties faintly evokes the ordered camp/army of Israel. Contested, reinforces the Exodus 18 echo.

echoes.text: Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets to Elisha, saying, “Your servant my husband is dead. You know that your servant feared Yahweh. Now the creditor has come to take for himself my two children to be slaves.” Elisha said to her, “What shall I do for you? Tell me: what do you have in the house?” She said, “Your handmaid has nothing in the house, except a pot of oil.” Then he said, “Go, borrow containers from of all your […]
echoes.note: Elisha multiplies a widow's small jar of oil to overflowing abundance. The Elisha-cycle motif of a prophet multiplying scarce food/provision reinforces the dominant 2 Kings 4:42-44 allusion. Contested, recurrence within the same prophetic cycle.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: Elijah's word causes a widow's flour and oil not to fail through a famine. The prophet-makes-meager-food-suffice pattern coheres with the feeding miracle. Contested, faint Elijah/Elisha background to the loaves.

pericopes.text: Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat, and to go ahead to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he himself sent the multitude away. After he had taken leave of them, he went up the mountain to pray. When evening had come, the boat was in the midst of the sea, and he was alone on the land. Seeing them distressed in rowing, for the wind was contrary to them, about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea, and he would have passed by them, but they, when they saw him walking on the sea, supposed that it was a ghost, and cried out; for they all saw him, and were troubled. But he immediately spoke with them, and said to them, “Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.” He got into the boat with them; and the wind ceased, and they were very amazed among themselves, and marveled; for they hadn’t understood about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.

echoes.text: He alone stretches out the heavens, and treads on the waves of the sea.
echoes.note: God alone 'treads upon the waves of the sea,' an act reserved to the Creator. Jesus walking on the sea enacts this exclusively divine prerogative, presenting him in the role Job ascribes to God alone. The verbal correspondence (walking/treading on the sea) is precise and theologically loaded.

echoes.text: Your way was through the sea; your paths through the great waters. Your footsteps were not known.
echoes.note: 'Your way was in the sea, your paths in the great waters,' celebrating God's saving passage through the sea at the Exodus. Jesus' path across the water reprises Yahweh's mastery of the deep in deliverance. Strong thematic coherence with the divine sea-crossing motif.

echoes.text: He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.” He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.” Yahweh also said, “Behold, there is a place by me, and you shall stand on the rock. It will happen, while my glory passes by, that I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and will cover you with my […]
echoes.note: Yahweh makes his glory 'pass by' Moses, the technical theophanic 'passing by.' Mark's odd note that Jesus 'would have passed by them' uses this theophany verb, signaling a divine self-disclosure on the water. The distinctive 'pass by' language anchors the allusion.

echoes.text: He said, “Go out, and stand on the mountain before Yahweh.” Behold, Yahweh passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains, and broke in pieces the rocks before Yahweh; but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake.
echoes.note: Yahweh 'passed by' Elijah at Horeb in a theophany of wind and stillness. The same passing-by-of-God motif, paired with wind that ceases, undergirds Jesus' sea epiphany. Reinforces the Exodus 33-34 theophany reading; medium because Exodus is the primary lexical source.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: God reveals his name 'I AM' (egō eimi) to Moses. Jesus' self-identification 'It is I' (egō eimi) on the water, joined to the theophanic passing-by, evokes the divine Name as reassurance. The phrase plus the do-not-be-afraid formula marks a deliberate I-AM theophany.

echoes.text: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their […]
echoes.note: Those at sea in distress cry out, and God stills the storm so the waves are hushed and he brings them to harbor. Mark's distressed rowers, contrary wind, and the wind ceasing when Jesus enters the boat closely follow this psalm's sea-rescue script. Strong structural and thematic correspondence.

echoes.text: who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, and the turmoil of the nations.
echoes.note: God 'stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves.' The wind ceasing at Jesus' presence enacts this divine sea-calming prerogative. Reinforces the Job 9 and Psalm 107 cluster; contested as a secondary witness.

echoes.text: You rule the pride of the sea. When its waves rise up, you calm them.
echoes.note: 'You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them.' Jesus' calming of the wind and waves manifests this sovereign rule over the sea. Recurrence of the God-rules-the-sea theme across the Psalter strengthens the echo.

echoes.text: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned, and flame will not scorch you.
echoes.note: Yahweh says 'Fear not... when you pass through the waters I will be with you,' joining the do-not-fear oracle to passage through the waters. Jesus' 'Don't be afraid' amid the sea echoes this salvation-oracle pattern. Contested but thematically apt to the I-AM theophany.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of Yahweh; awake, as in the days of old, the generations of ancient times. Isn’t it you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the monster? Isn’t it you who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep; who made the depths of the sea a way for the redeemed to pass over?
echoes.note: God's arm dries the sea and makes a way for the redeemed to pass over, recalling the Exodus mastery of the deep. Jesus' walking on and crossing the sea faintly reprises this redemption-through-the-deep imagery. Contested, low verbal contact.

echoes.text: You trampled the sea with your horses, churning mighty waters.
echoes.note: 'You trampled the sea with your horses, the surging of mighty waters,' a theophany of God treading the sea in deliverance. Jesus treading the sea faintly echoes this divine-warrior imagery. Low confidence, contested.

pericopes.text: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret, and moored to the shore. When they had come out of the boat, immediately the people recognized him, and ran around that whole region, and began to bring those who were sick, on their mats, to where they heard he was. Wherever he entered, into villages, or into cities, or into the country, they laid the sick in the marketplaces, and begged him that they might touch just the fringe of his garment; and as many as touched him were made well.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;
echoes.note: Israelites are commanded to wear tassels (the 'fringe') on the corners of their garments as a mark of holiness and remembrance of the commandments. The sick seeking to touch the 'fringe' of Jesus' garment invokes this distinctively Israelite tasseled hem. The specific 'fringe' term grounds the allusion.

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: 'The sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in its wings (hem/corners),' a promise of eschatological healing associated with the garment's corners/wings. The crowds healed by touching Jesus' garment-fringe evoke this healing-in-the-hem promise. Medium confidence given the wordplay on 'wings/corners' (kanaph) shared with the tassel.
