echoes.text: As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
echoes.note: Mere contact with Elisha's bones restores life, the OT motif of healing power conveyed by touching the prophet or his remains. The healing transmitted by touching Jesus' garment coheres with this contact-with-the-holy-one healing pattern. Contested, thematic resonance only.

echoes.text: He brought me back to the door of the house; and behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward; (for the forefront of the house was toward the east;) and the waters came down from under, from the right side of the house, on the south of the altar. Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me round by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east; and behold, there ran […]
echoes.note: Healing flows out from the temple/sanctuary to wherever the water reaches, an outward-radiating healing presence. Jesus moving through villages and country with healing extending to all who touch him faintly mirrors this radiating-healing motif. Low confidence, contested.

pericopes.text: Then the Pharisees, and some of the scribes gathered together to him, having come from Jerusalem. Now when they saw some of his disciples eating bread with defiled, that is, unwashed, hands, they found fault. (For the Pharisees, and all the Jews, don’t eat unless they wash their hands and forearms, holding to the tradition of the elders. They don’t eat when they come from the marketplace, unless they bathe themselves, and there are many other things, which they have received to hold to: washings of cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and couches.) The Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why don’t your disciples walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat their bread with unwashed hands?”

echoes.text: “You shall also make a basin of brass, and its base of brass, in which to wash. You shall put it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and you shall put water in it. Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet in it. When they go into the Tent of Meeting, they shall wash with water, that they not die; or when they come near to the altar to minister, to burn an offering made by fire to Yahweh. So they shall wash their hands and their […]
echoes.note: The Pharisaic 'tradition of the elders' on washing hands before eating develops from priestly ablution law, where Aaron and his sons must wash hands and feet before approaching the altar. Mark frames the dispute against this Torah backdrop of ritual purity, though the hand-washing of laypeople before ordinary meals is an extension beyond the written commandment, which is precisely Jesus' point. Availability and thematic coherence are strong; verbal volume is faint.

echoes.text: On whatever any of them falls when they are dead, it shall be unclean; whether it is any vessel of wood, or clothing, or skin, or sack, whatever vessel it is, with which any work is done, it must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it will be clean. Every earthen vessel, into which any of them falls, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it. All food which may be eaten, that on which water comes, shall be […]
echoes.note: The catalogue of washings of cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and couches echoes Leviticus' rules on vessels rendered unclean by contact and requiring rinsing or breaking. Mark's parenthetical ethnography (7:3-4) presupposes this purity system as the matrix for the elders' tradition. The coherence is high though no single verse is quoted.

echoes.text: “‘Whoever he who has the discharge touches, without having rinsed his hands in water, he shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the evening. “‘The earthen vessel, which he who has the discharge touches, shall be broken; and every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water.
echoes.note: Leviticus 15 makes hands a vector of impurity (one with a discharge who has not rinsed his hands conveys uncleanness) and prescribes rinsing vessels of wood and breaking those of clay. This is among the few Torah texts tying hand-rinsing to purity, plausibly seeding the elders' extension to all meals. Faint and contested but availability is genuine.

pericopes.text: He answered them, “Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. But in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’ “For you set aside the commandment of God, and hold tightly to the tradition of men—the washing of pitchers and cups, and you do many other such things.” He said to them, “Full well do you reject the commandment of God, that you may keep your tradition. For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother;’and, ‘He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him be put to death.’ But you say, ‘If a man tells his father or his mother, “Whatever profit you might have received from me is Corban, that is to say, given to God”;’ then you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or his mother, making void the word of God by your tradition, which you have handed down. You do many things like this.”

echoes.text: The Lord said, “Because this people draws near with their mouth and with their lips to honor me, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught;
echoes.note: Formal citation introduced 'as it is written': 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' Mark follows the LXX, whose 'teaching as doctrines the commandments of men' supplies the polemical hinge against human tradition that the Hebrew lacks. Maximal volume, recurrence, and thematic coherence; this is the load-bearing OT text of the pericope.
echoes.lxxText: And the Lord has said, This people draw nigh to me with their mouth, and they honour me with their lips, but their heart is far from me: but in vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
echoes.note: Jesus cites the Decalogue commandment 'Honor your father and your mother' (attributed to Moses) as the divine command that Corban casuistry nullifies. Direct verbal quotation; the antithesis between this commandment and the tradition is the argument's spine.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic form of the honor-parents commandment is an equally valid source for 'Honor your father and your mother,' since Mark's citation could draw on either Decalogue. Listed as a parallel availability alongside Exodus 20:12; the verbal match is exact in both.

echoes.text: “Anyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.
echoes.note: The paired citation 'He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him be put to death' quotes the capital statute of Exodus 21:17, reinforcing the gravity of the command being voided. Mark's wording tracks the LXX (kakologon). High volume and direct verbal correspondence.

echoes.text: “‘For everyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death: he has cursed his father or his mother; his blood shall be upon him.
echoes.note: Leviticus 20:9 ('everyone who curses his father or mother shall be put to death') is a near-identical alternate source for the death-penalty clause and may stand behind Mark alongside Exodus 21:17. Strong availability; offered as parallel attestation.

echoes.text: When a man vows a vow to Yahweh, or swears an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.
echoes.note: The Corban dispute turns on the binding force of a vow dedicating property to God; Numbers 30 is the Torah's law of vows ('he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth'). Jesus' charge is that scribal handling of such irrevocable vows is used to override the prior duty to parents, so the vow legislation is the legal substrate of the controversy. Thematic coherence high; verbal volume moderate.

echoes.text: When you vow a vow to Yahweh your God, you shall not be slack to pay it; for Yahweh your God will surely require it of you; and it would be sin in you. But if you refrain from making a vow, it shall be no sin in you. You shall observe and do that which has gone out of your lips. Whatever you have vowed to Yahweh your God as a freewill offering, which you have promised with your mouth, you must do.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's vow law ('when you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay to pay it... that which has gone out of your lips you shall keep') reinforces the irrevocability that makes Corban exploitable. A secondary witness to the vow background behind 7:11-12.

echoes.text: “‘If it is an animal, of which men offer an offering to Yahweh, all that any man gives of such to Yahweh becomes holy. He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change animal for animal, then both it and that for which it is changed shall be holy. If it is any unclean animal, of which they do not offer as an offering to Yahweh, then he shall set the animal before the priest; and the priest shall […]
echoes.note: Leviticus 27 governs things devoted/dedicated to the LORD (cherem and votive gifts), the legal category 'Corban, that is, given to God' invokes. Mark's transliterated technical term presupposes this dedication law; the abuse is treating a thing as devoted to bar a creditor-parent. Availability genuine, volume faint.

pericopes.text: He called all the multitude to himself, and said to them, “Hear me, all of you, and understand. There is nothing from outside of the man, that going into him can defile him; but the things which proceed out of the man are those that defile the man. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear!” When he had entered into a house away from the multitude, his disciples asked him about the parable. He said to them, “Are you thus without understanding also? Don’t you perceive that whatever goes into the man from outside can’t defile him, because it doesn’t go into his heart, but into his stomach, then into the latrine, thus purifying all foods?” He said, “That which proceeds out of the man, that defiles the man. For from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, sexual sins, murders, thefts, covetings, wickedness, deceit, lustful desires, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and defile the man.”

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: Jesus relocates defilement to the heart: 'from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts.' Genesis 6:5 ('every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually') is the foundational OT diagnosis of the heart as the source of evil intent. Strong thematic coherence; the vice-list in 7:21-22 unpacks this anthropology.

echoes.text: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.
echoes.note: The post-flood verdict that 'the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth' parallels Mark's claim that evil proceeds from within the heart. Together with Genesis 6:5 it supplies the Torah's most explicit teaching that defilement is interior and inborn, cohering with Jesus' redefinition of purity.

echoes.text: The heart is deceitful above all things, and it is exceedingly corrupt: who can know it?
echoes.note: Jeremiah's 'the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately corrupt' is the prophetic locus classicus for the heart as the seat of hidden defilement, matching Jesus' catalogue of deceit, covetousness, and wickedness emerging from within. High thematic coherence with the heart/exterior antithesis driving the pericope.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]
echoes.note: Mark's editorial gloss 'thus he declared all foods clean' (7:19) directly engages the dietary code of Leviticus 11 distinguishing clean from unclean animals. Jesus' saying that nothing entering from outside can defile reframes and relativizes precisely this food legislation; the food laws are the explicit object of the controversy. Volume and coherence both high.

echoes.text: You shall not eat any abominable thing. These are the animals which you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the chamois. Every animal that parts the hoof, and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, that may you eat. Nevertheless these you shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of those who have the hoof cloven: the camel, the hare, and the […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy 14 is the parallel statute of clean and unclean foods that, with Leviticus 11, constitutes the dietary law Jesus' pronouncement on foods addresses. Equally available as the OT food-purity background to 'purifying all foods.'

echoes.text: “‘Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who eats any kind of blood, I will set my face against that soul who eats blood, and will cut him off from among his people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel, “No person […]
echoes.note: Leviticus 17's blood and carcass prohibitions extend the ingestion-as-defilement logic Jesus overturns. A secondary witness to the food-purity system at stake; fainter than Leviticus 11 / Deuteronomy 14.

echoes.text: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.
echoes.note: Duplicate-domain note: the 'evil from youth' verdict also undergirds the comprehensiveness of the vice-list (adulteries, murders, thefts, covetings), framing human sin as welling up from the heart rather than contracted from without. Retained as a low echo on the catalog itself.

echoes.text: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.
echoes.note: 'Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it are the issues of life' anticipates Mark's image of what 'proceeds out of' the person from the heart. Wisdom availability; verbal contact ('proceeds out') is suggestive but faint.

echoes.text: Exalt not yourself, lest you fall, And bring dishonor upon your soul; And so the Lord will reveal your secrets, And will cast you down in the midst of the congregation; Because you came not to the fear of the Lord, And your heart was full of deceit.
echoes.note: Ben Sira repeatedly contrasts outward show with the heart and warns against hypocrisy ('exalt not yourself... the Lord will reveal your secrets'), part of the Second-Temple wisdom milieu locating defilement in interior disposition. Deuterocanonical availability supporting the heart-purity theme; contested and faint.

echoes.text: Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing; and he cry to Yahweh against you, and it be sin to you.
echoes.note: Mark's vice 'an evil eye' (ophthalmos poneros) is a Semitic idiom for stinginess/grudging that appears in Deuteronomy 15:9 ('your eye be evil against your poor brother'). The phrase in the vice-list plausibly draws on this OT idiom for ungenerous malice. Idiomatic availability; volume faint.

pericopes.text: From there he arose, and went away into the borders of Tyre and Sidon. He entered into a house, and didn’t want anyone to know it, but he couldn’t escape notice. For a woman, whose little daughter had an unclean spirit, having heard of him, came and fell down at his feet. Now the woman was a Greek, a Syrophoenician by race. She begged him that he would cast the demon out of her daughter. But Jesus said to her, “Let the children be filled first, for it is not appropriate to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” But she answered him, “Yes, Lord. Yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” He said to her, “For this saying, go your way. The demon has gone out of your daughter.” She went away to her house, and found the child having been laid on the bed, with the demon gone out.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: Jesus' withdrawal to the region of Tyre and Sidon and his healing of a Gentile woman's child recalls Elijah's sojourn with the Sidonian widow of Zarephath, whose son he restored, the paradigm of an Israelite prophet bringing life to a Gentile woman of that very coastland. Geographic and typological coherence is strong; the Sidonian-widow precedent frames the boundary-crossing mercy.

echoes.text: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”
echoes.note: The 'children first... then the dogs' logic enacts the order of salvation in which blessing comes to Israel first and through Israel to the nations ('in you all families of the earth shall be blessed'). The Syrophoenician's faith anticipates the Abrahamic extension of blessing beyond Israel. Figural and contested, but thematically coherent with election-then-overflow.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The servant's mission to be 'a light to the nations' so that salvation reaches the ends of the earth resonates with the children's bread overflowing to a Gentile. Mark's narrative geography (Tyre, Decapolis) participates in the prophetic vision of the nations drawn in; faint figural availability.

echoes.text: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.
echoes.note: Jesus' priority 'let the children be filled first' presupposes Israel's status as God's chosen children/people set apart from the nations (Deuteronomy 7's election language). The exchange negotiates that elect-Israel-first economy; availability strong, verbal volume faint.

echoes.text: For dogs have surrounded me. A company of evildoers have enclosed me. They have pierced my hands and feet.
echoes.note: The 'dogs' metaphor for Gentiles draws on a stock OT pejorative (e.g., 'dogs have surrounded me'), here softened to household pups under the table. The idiom's OT background gives the insult-and-reversal its bite. Lexical availability; contested and faint.

pericopes.text: Again he departed from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and came to the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the region of Decapolis. They brought to him one who was deaf and had an impediment in his speech. They begged him to lay his hand on him. He took him aside from the multitude, privately, and put his fingers into his ears, and he spat, and touched his tongue. Looking up to heaven, he sighed, and said to him, “Ephphatha!” that is, “Be opened!” Immediately his ears were opened, and the impediment of his tongue was released, and he spoke clearly. He commanded them that they should tell no one, but the more he commanded them, so much the more widely they proclaimed it. They were astonished beyond measure, saying, “He has done all things well. He makes even the deaf hear, and the mute speak!”

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: The healing of a deaf man with a speech impediment, climaxing in 'he makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak,' enacts Isaiah's eschatological promise: 'then the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped... and the tongue of the mute shall sing.' Mark signals the messianic age dawning; volume, recurrence (cf. Isa 29:18; 42:18), and thematic coherence are all high.

echoes.text: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
echoes.note: The crowd's acclamation 'he has done all things well' (panta kalos pepoieken) echoes the creation refrain that God saw all he had made and it was 'very good' (LXX kala lian), casting Jesus' restorative work as a new creation. The verbal contact (kalos / kala) and theme of God making/doing all things well give the allusion real volume.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness. The humble also will increase their joy in Yahweh, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
echoes.note: 'In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and the eyes of the blind shall see' reinforces the deaf-hearing motif of Isaiah 35 and ties back to the chapter's earlier Isaiah 29:13 citation, giving recurrence within the same prophetic source. The opening of ears is the visible sign of the promise.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?
echoes.note: 'Who makes a man mute, or deaf... Is it not I, the LORD?' grounds the claim that making the deaf hear and the mute speak is a divine prerogative. The crowd's wonder implicitly attributes to Jesus a work Yahweh claims as his own. Thematic coherence high; specific verbal volume moderate.

echoes.text: “Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see.
echoes.note: 'Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see' belongs to the cluster of Isaianic deaf/mute imagery animating this healing. A secondary witness reinforcing recurrence within Isaiah; fainter than 35:5-6.

echoes.text: Because wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, And made the tongues of babes to speak clearly.
echoes.note: 'Wisdom opened the mouth of the mute, and made the tongues of infants speak clearly' (of the Exodus deliverance) is a Second-Temple text pairing divine wisdom with the loosing of mute tongues, resonant with Jesus loosing the tongue so the man 'spoke clearly.' Deuterocanonical availability; contested and faint.

echoes.text: For then I will purify the lips of the peoples, that they may all call on Yahweh’s name, to serve him shoulder to shoulder.
echoes.note: 'For then I will restore to the peoples a pure speech' offers an eschatological loosing-of-tongues motif consonant with the man speaking plainly in the Gentile Decapolis. Geographic-thematic resonance; very faint and contested.

pericopes.text: In those days, when there was a very great multitude, and they had nothing to eat, Jesus called his disciples to himself, and said to them, “I have compassion on the multitude, because they have stayed with me now three days, and have nothing to eat. If I send them away fasting to their home, they will faint on the way, for some of them have come a long way.” His disciples answered him, “From where could one satisfy these people with bread here in a deserted place?” He asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.” He commanded the multitude to sit down on the ground, and he took the seven loaves. Having given thanks, he broke them, and gave them to his disciples to serve, and they served the multitude. They had a few small fish. Having blessed them, he said to serve these also. They ate, and were filled. They took up seven baskets of broken pieces that were left over. Those who had eaten were about four thousand. Then he sent them away. Immediately he entered into the boat with his disciples, and came into the region of Dalmanutha.

echoes.text: They took their journey from Elim, and all the congregation of the children of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departing out of the land of Egypt. The whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron in the wilderness; and the children of Israel said to them, “We wish that we had died by the hand of Yahweh in the land of Egypt, […]
echoes.note: The feeding of the four thousand in a 'deserted place' (v.4) reprises the manna narrative: God satisfies a hungry multitude with bread in the wilderness. Volume is high via the desert setting and the disciples' incredulous 'from where' question, which echoes Israel's manna astonishment ('What is it?'). Mark's wilderness feedings deliberately retell the Exodus provision in messianic key.

echoes.text: Yes, they spoke against God. They said, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Behold, he struck the rock, so that waters gushed out, and streams overflowed. Can he give bread also? Will he provide flesh for his people?” Therefore Yahweh heard, and was angry. A fire was kindled against Jacob, anger also went up against Israel, because they didn’t believe in God, and didn’t trust in his salvation. Yet he commanded the skies above, and opened the doors […]
echoes.note: The disciples' 'From where could one satisfy these people with bread here in a deserted place?' answers, in the negative, Israel's taunt 'Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?' (Ps 78:19), which the psalm then resolves with manna ('bread of the mighty', v.25). Coherence with Mark's wilderness-feeding theology is strong, and the verbal frame of doubting provision in the desert is close.

echoes.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]
echoes.note: Elisha's feeding of a hundred men from limited loaves, with leftovers remaining 'according to the word of the LORD,' is the closest prophetic prototype: insufficient bread, a doubting attendant ('How can I set this before a hundred?'), miraculous satiety, and surplus. Mark frames Jesus as the prophet-greater-than-Elisha, and the surplus motif (seven baskets) recalls the same pattern.

echoes.text: Where could I get meat to give to all this people? For they weep to me, saying, ‘Give us meat, that we may eat.’ I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me. If you treat me this way, please kill me right now, if I have found favor in your sight; and don’t let me see my wretchedness.” Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over […]
echoes.note: Moses' protest 'Where am I to get meat to give to all this people?' (Num 11:13) and the doubt that flesh could be found in the wilderness underlies the disciples' helpless question in v.4. Coherence with the wilderness-provision frame is high; this is a recurrent grumbling-and-provision pattern Mark draws upon.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines. He will destroy in this mountain the surface of the covering that covers all peoples, and the veil that is spread over all nations. He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, […]
echoes.note: The eschatological banquet on the mountain where God 'makes for all peoples a feast of rich food' may color Mark's second feeding, traditionally read as extending to Gentile territory (the Decapolis). The volume is faint but coherent with Mark's movement of the bread to outsiders.

echoes.text: They wandered in the wilderness in a desert way. They found no city to live in. Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted in them. Then they cried to Yahweh in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses, he led them also by a straight way, that they might go to a city to live in. Let them praise Yahweh for his loving kindness, for his wonderful works to the children of men! For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with […]
echoes.note: The psalm describes the hungry and faint wandering 'in a desert waste' whom the LORD 'satisfies' and 'fills with good things.' The verbal cluster of wilderness, fainting, hunger, and satisfaction overlaps the scene (note v.3 'faint on the way'), though without distinctive enough wording to rise above echo.

pericopes.text: The Pharisees came out and began to question him, seeking from him a sign from heaven, and testing him. He sighed deeply in his spirit, and said, “Why does this generation seek a sign? Most certainly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.” He left them, and again entering into the boat, departed to the other side.

echoes.text: All the congregation of the children of Israel traveled from the wilderness of Sin, by their journeys, according to Yahweh’s commandment, and encamped in Rephidim; but there was no water for the people to drink. Therefore the people quarreled with Moses, and said, “Give us water to drink.” Moses said to them, “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test Yahweh?” The people were thirsty for water there; and the people murmured against Moses, and said, “Why […]
echoes.note: The Pharisees 'testing' Jesus by demanding a sign from heaven inverts Massah/Meribah, where Israel 'tested the LORD' by demanding proof ('Is the LORD among us or not?'). Mark casts the sign-seekers as the new wilderness generation that puts God to the test; the testing-in-the-desert motif coheres with the feeding context just preceding.

echoes.text: You shall not tempt Yahweh your God, as you tempted him in Massah.
echoes.note: 'You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah' provides the legal-theological frame for Jesus' refusal: the sign-demand is itself the forbidden testing. Coherence is strong with v.11's language of peirazo (testing).

echoes.text: Don’t harden your heart, as at Meribah, as in the day of Massah in the wilderness, when your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my work. Forty long years I was grieved with that generation, and said, “It is a people that errs in their heart. They have not known my ways.” Therefore I swore in my wrath, “They won’t enter into my rest.”
echoes.note: Jesus' deep sigh and verdict that 'no sign will be given to this generation' echoes the psalm's oracle against the wilderness generation: 'Harden not your hearts as at Meribah... For forty years I loathed that generation.' The 'this generation' rebuke and divine grief/loathing are tightly coherent, and Mark develops the hardened-heart theme in v.17.

echoes.text: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
echoes.note: The Song of Moses brands Israel 'a perverse and crooked generation' whose corruption is 'no longer his children's.' Jesus' indictment of 'this generation' draws on this prophetic vocabulary for a faithless cohort that demands proof yet will not believe.

echoes.text: He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.
echoes.note: 'They are a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness'—God hides his face from them. The motif of a faithless 'generation' from which God withholds himself directly parallels Jesus withholding the sign and departing (v.13).

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “How long will this people despise me? and how long will they not believe in me, for all the signs which I have worked among them?
echoes.note: 'How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, for all the signs which I have done?' frames the wilderness generation that, despite signs, refuses faith—precisely the dynamic Jesus laments before the sign-seekers.

pericopes.text: They forgot to take bread; and they didn’t have more than one loaf in the boat with them. He warned them, saying, “Take heed: beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and the yeast of Herod.” They reasoned with one another, saying, “It’s because we have no bread.” Jesus, perceiving it, said to them, “Why do you reason that it’s because you have no bread? Don’t you perceive yet, neither understand? Is your heart still hardened? Having eyes, don’t you see? Having ears, don’t you hear? Don’t you remember? When I broke the five loaves among the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” They told him, “Twelve.” “When the seven loaves fed the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” They told him, “Seven.” He asked them, “Don’t you understand, yet?”

echoes.text: This day shall be to you for a memorial, and you shall keep it a feast to Yahweh: throughout your generations you shall keep it a feast by an ordinance forever. “‘Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even the first day you shall put away yeast out of your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel. In the first day there shall be to you a holy convocation, and in the […]
echoes.note: The warning to 'beware of the yeast/leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod' trades on the Passover prohibition of leaven, where leaven symbolizes corruption to be purged. The figural valence of leaven as pervasive moral contamination is rooted in the unleavened-bread legislation.

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: Jesus' rebuke 'Having eyes, don't you see? Having ears, don't you hear?' directly applies Isaiah's commission oracle of a people who see but do not perceive and hear but do not understand. Mark already cited this text at 4:12; recurrence and verbal closeness make this a strong, deliberate appropriation now turned on the disciples themselves.

echoes.text: ‘Hear now this, foolish people, and without understanding; who have eyes, and don’t see; who have ears, and don’t hear:
echoes.note: 'Hear this, O foolish and senseless people, who have eyes but do not see, who have ears but do not hear'—the near-exact phrasing of Jesus' double question. Jeremiah's indictment of a hardened, uncomprehending people supplies the prophetic template; the verbal volume is very high.

echoes.text: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of the rebellious house, who have eyes to see, and don’t see, who have ears to hear, and don’t hear; for they are a rebellious house.
echoes.note: 'Son of man, you dwell in the midst of a rebellious house, who have eyes to see but do not see, ears to hear but do not hear, for they are a rebellious house.' This is the other classic seeing-not/hearing-not oracle, paired with hardness; its conjunction with rebellion coheres with Mark's hardened-heart charge in v.17.

echoes.text: Moses called to all Israel, and said to them: Your eyes have seen all that Yahweh did in the land of Egypt to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land; the great trials which your eyes saw, the signs, and those great wonders. But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: Moses tells Israel they saw the signs in Egypt 'yet to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears to hear.' This explicitly links failure to perceive God's mighty works (the feedings) with an ungiven heart—exactly Jesus' point that the disciples fail to remember the loaves.

echoes.text: O Yahweh, why do you make us to err from your ways, and harden our heart from your fear? Return for your servants’ sake, the tribes of your inheritance.
echoes.note: 'Why do you harden our hearts so that we do not fear you?' supplies the hardened-heart vocabulary that Jesus levels at the disciples ('Is your heart still hardened?'). The motif is recurrent in Mark (6:52), grounding the charge in prophetic lament over insensate Israel.

echoes.text: Don’t harden your heart, as at Meribah, as in the day of Massah in the wilderness,
echoes.note: 'Harden not your hearts' carries forward from the sign-seeking pericope; the disciples' hardened hearts place them within the same warned-against wilderness generation that fails to read God's provision (the manna/loaves).

pericopes.text: He came to Bethsaida. They brought a blind man to him, and begged him to touch him. He took hold of the blind man by the hand, and brought him out of the village. When he had spit on his eyes, and laid his hands on him, he asked him if he saw anything. He looked up, and said, “I see men; for I see them like trees walking.” Then again he laid his hands on his eyes. He looked intently, and was restored, and saw everyone clearly. He sent him away to his house, saying, “Don’t enter into the village, nor tell anyone in the village.”

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened'—the healing of the blind man at Bethsaida enacts Isaiah's promise of eschatological restoration. Mark positions this sign as a figural opening of eyes that frames the disciples' partial sight; volume and coherence with the surrounding seeing/not-seeing motif are high.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: 'In that day...out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see'—paired in Isaiah with the deaf hearing, this restoration oracle undergirds the staged healing. The Isaianic blindness/sight complex is the controlling intertext for the whole pericope's placement.

echoes.text: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations; to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant is given 'to open the eyes that are blind,' a commissioning that Mark sees fulfilled in Jesus' physical opening of blind eyes as a sign of his servant-messiahship—coherent with the suffering Son of Man developed just after (v.31).

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: The two-stage cure—first blurred ('men like trees walking'), then clear sight—dramatizes the half-perceiving condition diagnosed by Isaiah's seeing-but-not-perceiving oracle. Mark figures the disciples' gradual, incomplete recognition of Jesus through the man's gradual healing; the structural coherence is strong even without verbal quotation.

echoes.text: The eyes of those who see will not be dim, and the ears of those who hear will listen.
echoes.note: 'The eyes of those who see will not be closed, and the ears of those who hear will listen' belongs to the cluster of restoration-of-sight oracles that Mark's healing actualizes. Faint but within the recurrent Isaianic field.

pericopes.text: Jesus went out, with his disciples, into the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do men say that I am?” They told him, “John the Baptizer, and others say Elijah, but others: one of the prophets.” He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ.” He commanded them that they should tell no one about him.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The popular guess that Jesus is 'Elijah' draws directly on Malachi's promise to send Elijah before the great day of the LORD; the expectation of Elijah redivivus frames the crowd's christological speculation. Mark develops Elijah typology around John the Baptizer.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The opinion that Jesus is 'one of the prophets' resonates with the promise of a prophet 'like Moses' whom God would raise up; the prophet-like-Moses expectation is part of the matrix the crowd's answers reflect, sharpened by Mark's Moses/wilderness typology in the feedings.

echoes.text: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: Peter's confession 'You are the Christ' (the Anointed) actualizes the royal vocabulary of Psalm 2, where the nations rage against 'the LORD and his Anointed.' Mark's Christ-title carries the Davidic-king freight of this enthronement psalm, which surfaces explicitly at Jesus' trial and baptism.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: The title 'Christ' invokes the Davidic covenant promise of an anointed son whose throne is established forever. Coherence with Mark's Son-of-David theme (10:47) supports reading the confession against the Nathan oracle, though the link here is conceptual rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise again. He spoke to them openly. Peter took him, and began to rebuke him. But he, turning around, and seeing his disciples, rebuked Peter, and said, “Get behind me, Satan! For you have in mind not the things of God, but the things of men.”

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we […]
echoes.note: That 'the Son of Man must suffer many things... and be killed' draws on the Servant who was 'despised and rejected,' 'a man of sorrows,' who bore suffering and was 'cut off.' The necessity (dei) of redemptive suffering coheres with Isaiah 53's vicarious death; this is the foundational suffering-text behind Mark's passion predictions.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: 'Be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes' anticipates the rejected-stone of Psalm 118, which Mark quotes explicitly at 12:10 ('the stone the builders rejected'). The specific language of rejection by the leadership maps onto the builders' rejection, making this a deliberate, recurrent intertext.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The self-designation 'Son of Man' derives from Daniel's vision of 'one like a son of man' who comes with the clouds and receives dominion. Mark's title is recurrent and load-bearing; though here paired paradoxically with suffering, the Danielic figure of vindicated dominion underlies the whole Son-of-Man complex.

echoes.text: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”
echoes.note: The motif of the righteous one despised and rejected ('a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind') feeds the suffering-Son-of-Man pattern; Mark draws heavily on Psalm 22 for the passion (15:34, 15:24), so its presence behind the first prediction is coherent and recurrent.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After three days rise again' may echo Hosea's 'after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up.' The third-day-resurrection language is plausibly drawn from this oracle of restoration, a connection later interpreters made explicit.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: 'Get behind me, Satan!' resonates with Zechariah's vision where 'the LORD rebuke you, O Satan' is spoken against the accuser. The act of rebuking the satan/adversary who opposes God's purpose coheres verbally and conceptually with Jesus' rebuke of Peter as voicing 'the things of men.'

pericopes.text: He called the multitude to himself with his disciples, and said to them, “Whoever wants to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wants to save his life will lose it; and whoever will lose his life for my sake and the sake of the Good News will save it. For what does it profit a man, to gain the whole world, and forfeit his life? For what will a man give in exchange for his life? For whoever will be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man also will be ashamed of him, when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'When he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels' renders the Son of Man's coming in Daniel's vision, where the one like a son of man comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days to receive glory and an everlasting kingdom. The conjunction of Son of Man, coming, and glory is a direct appropriation.

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him' supplies the entourage of 'holy angels/holy ones' accompanying the divine advent. Mark's coming Son of Man 'with the holy angels' draws on this theophany of God arriving with his holy retinue for judgment.

echoes.text: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
echoes.note: The throne-and-myriads scene—'thousand thousands served him'—reinforces the angelic-attendant imagery of the Son of Man's glorious advent in v.38. Coherent with the Danielic court of judgment that frames being 'ashamed' before the coming one.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough, That he should live on forever, that he should not see corruption.
echoes.note: 'For what will a man give in exchange for his life?' closely parallels the psalm's reflection that no one can 'give to God a ransom for his life... for the redemption of their soul is costly.' The wisdom logic that life cannot be bought back with wealth underlies vv.36-37.

echoes.text: What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?
echoes.note: 'What does it profit a man, to gain the whole world?' echoes Qoheleth's recurring 'What profit (yitron) has a man of all his toil?'—the wisdom idiom of weighing profit against the vanity of worldly gain. Faint but coherent with the saying's sapiential cast.

echoes.text: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
echoes.note: 'This adulterous and sinful generation' reprises the Song of Moses' 'perverse and crooked generation,' tying the audience of Jesus' words to the faithless wilderness cohort already invoked in the sign-seeking pericope. The recurrence of the 'generation' label within Mark 8 strengthens the link.

echoes.text: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts;
echoes.note: The charge 'adulterous... generation' draws on the prophetic figure of Israel as an unfaithful, adulterous spouse (Hosea's central metaphor), framing the present generation's unbelief as covenant infidelity. Faint, but within the prophetic adultery-as-apostasy tradition.

pericopes.text: He said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, there are some standing here who will in no way taste death until they see the Kingdom of God come with power.”

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Jesus' promise that some standing here will see 'the Kingdom of God come with power' draws on Daniel's vision of dominion, glory, and an everlasting kingdom given to the one like a son of man. The conjunction of kingdom and divine power coheres with Daniel's eschatological enthronement scene. Recurrence of Danielic son-of-man and kingdom language throughout Mark strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: The God of heaven setting up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed and that breaks all others supplies the apocalyptic backdrop for a kingdom arriving 'with power.' The volume is faint and the verbal overlap general, but the coherence with Mark's kingdom proclamation is real.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The good news that 'your God reigns' lies behind Markan kingdom-arrival language. The link to 9:1 specifically is faint and rests on the shared royal-reign theme rather than verbal contact.

pericopes.text: After six days Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John, and brought them up onto a high mountain privately by themselves, and he was changed into another form in front of them. His clothing became glistening, exceedingly white, like snow, such as no launderer on earth can whiten them. Elijah and Moses appeared to them, and they were talking with Jesus. Peter answered Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good for us to be here. Let’s make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” For he didn’t know what to say, for they were very afraid. A cloud came, overshadowing them, and a voice came out of the cloud, “This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.” Suddenly looking around, they saw no one with them any more, except Jesus only.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.
echoes.note: The Sinai theophany supplies Mark's frame: the glory of the LORD settled on the mountain, the cloud covered it six days, and on the seventh day God called to Moses out of the cloud. Mark's 'after six days,' the high mountain, the overshadowing cloud, and the voice from the cloud reproduce this cluster with high volume and tight coherence. The Transfiguration is staged as a new Sinai.

echoes.text: Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain.
echoes.note: Moses goes up the mountain and the cloud covers it, the immediate setting for the giving of the covenant. Mark's ascent of three named companions onto a high mountain into a cloud reactivates this Sinai ascent. The recurrence of mountain-and-cloud theophany makes the availability and coherence criteria strong.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him.
echoes.note: When Moses came down from Sinai the skin of his face shone because he had talked with God, so that the people were afraid. Jesus' garments becoming dazzling white and the disciples' fear echo the transfigured radiance of Moses, while transposing the glory from reflected to inherent. The Moses-glory pattern is reinforced by Moses' actual presence on the mountain.

echoes.text: Yahweh descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: The LORD descended in the cloud and stood with Moses and proclaimed his name. The descending cloud and the divine voice in Mark cohere with this Sinai descent, reinforcing the Moses typology already active through Moses' appearance.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The heavenly voice 'This is my beloved Son' draws on the royal-enthronement decree 'You are my Son.' The divine sonship language frames Jesus as the messianic king. Recurrence of Psalm 2 at the baptism (Mark 1:11) and here establishes a Markan inclusio of divine attestation.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: Moses promises a prophet like himself whom God will raise up, and commands 'to him you shall listen.' The heavenly 'Listen to him' verbally echoes this command, and the presence of Moses on the mountain makes the prophet-like-Moses identification pointed. Volume and coherence are both strong.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: 'Behold my servant, my chosen, in whom my soul delights' stands behind the beloved-Son acclamation, blending servant election with sonship. The Markan voice fuses Psalm 2 royal sonship with Isaianic servant language. The servant motif coheres with the suffering Son of Man that immediately follows.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: God's command to Abraham regarding 'your son, your only son, whom you love' supplies the Aqedah resonance behind 'my beloved Son.' The Greek agapetos echoes the Septuagint of Isaac, linking divine sonship to sacrificial offering, which coheres with Mark's passion theme. The connection is suggestive rather than verbally exact.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: Elijah's appearance on the mountain activates the expectation that Elijah will come before the day of the LORD, made explicit in 9:11-13. His presence beside Moses pairs Law and Prophets as witnesses to Jesus. The motif is developed verbally in the following pericope.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The messenger sent to prepare the way contributes to the Elijah-forerunner complex evoked by Elijah's presence. The link here is indirect, mediated through Mark's broader Elijah typology.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Elijah's being taken up to heaven by chariot explains why he, like Moses (whose death and burial were hidden), is available to appear on the mountain rather than being among the dead. The translation traditions of both figures underwrite their eschatological reappearance. Coherence with Jewish expectation is strong though the verbal contact is nil.

echoes.text: So Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab, according to Yahweh’s word.
echoes.note: Moses' death on Mount Nebo with no known grave fed traditions of his assumption, making his appearance alongside Elijah intelligible. The faint link supports the availability of Moses as a heavenly witness. It rests on later interpretive tradition rather than the text alone.

echoes.text: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire.
echoes.note: The clothing white as snow in Daniel's vision of the Ancient of Days lies behind Mark's description of garments dazzling white beyond any launderer's whitening. The apocalyptic-glory vocabulary transfers heavenly radiance onto Jesus. Volume is moderate and coheres with Mark's son-of-man Christology.

echoes.text: As Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, Yahweh’s glory appeared in the cloud.
echoes.note: The glory of the LORD appearing in the cloud in the wilderness contributes to the cloud-glory motif overshadowing the disciples. The general theophanic cloud is shared, though Exodus 24 is the primary source. A faint reinforcing echo.

echoes.text: You shall dwell in booths seven days. All who are native-born in Israel shall dwell in booths,
echoes.note: Peter's proposal to make three booths (skenai) may draw on the Feast of Booths command to dwell in temporary shelters, evoking eschatological feast and divine dwelling. The link is contested and may be incidental to Peter's confusion. If intended, it ties the theophany to Sukkot's hope of God's tabernacling presence.

echoes.text: It will happen that everyone who is left of all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up from year to year to worship the King, Yahweh of Armies, and to keep the feast of tents.
echoes.note: Zechariah's vision of all nations keeping the Feast of Booths when the LORD becomes king supplies a possible eschatological-Sukkot backdrop to Peter's tents. The connection is faint and depends on reading the booths motif eschatologically. It coheres with the kingdom-with-power saying of 9:1.

pericopes.text: As they were coming down from the mountain, he commanded them that they should tell no one what things they had seen, until after the Son of Man had risen from the dead. They kept this saying to themselves, questioning what the “rising from the dead” meant. They asked him, saying, “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” He said to them, “Elijah indeed comes first, and restores all things. How is it written about the Son of Man, that he should suffer many things and be despised? But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they have also done to him whatever they wanted to, even as it is written about him.”

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The scribal teaching that 'Elijah must come first' directly reflects Malachi's promise to send Elijah before the great and terrible day of the LORD. Jesus affirms and reinterprets this expectation, identifying the returned Elijah with John the Baptist. Verbal and thematic volume is high.

echoes.text: He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
echoes.note: Elijah's task to 'turn the hearts' and so restore relationships underlies Jesus' phrase that Elijah 'restores all things.' The restoration motif is drawn directly from Malachi's commission. Coherence with the forerunner role is exact.

echoes.text: Who was recorded for reproofs in their seasons, To pacify anger, before it brake forth into wrath; To turn the heart of the father to the son, And to restore the tribes of Jacob.
echoes.note: Sirach interprets Malachi, saying Elijah is ready to calm wrath, turn the heart of the father to the son, and restore the tribes of Jacob. Jesus' wording that Elijah 'restores all things' tracks Sirach's restorationist gloss more closely than Malachi alone, demonstrating Second-Temple availability. This is a key deuterocanonical witness to the expectation Mark engages.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: Jesus' question 'how is it written about the Son of Man, that he should suffer many things and be despised' draws on the servant who is despised and rejected by men. The suffering-and-despised pairing matches Isaiah's fourth servant song closely. Mark grounds the passion in this Scripture as 'written.'

echoes.text: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
echoes.note: The servant who bears griefs and is esteemed stricken reinforces the 'suffer many things' clause. The vicarious-suffering theme coheres with Mark's repeated passion predictions. Volume is moderate alongside the stronger 53:3 contact.

echoes.text: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people.
echoes.note: The sufferer 'despised by the people' supplies a scriptural template for the Son of Man being 'despised.' Mark's passion narrative repeatedly draws on Psalm 22, making its recurrence a strong coherence indicator. The verbal contact on contempt strengthens the echo.

echoes.text: Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!”
echoes.note: Jezebel's threat to kill Elijah, who flees for his life, stands behind 'they have also done to him whatever they wanted,' applied to John the Baptist's persecution and death. The historical Elijah's suffering at royal hands prefigures the returned Elijah's fate. Coherence with the rejected-prophet pattern is strong.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah's lament that the Israelites have killed the prophets and seek his life reinforces the pattern that the forerunner suffers as the prophets did. The link to 'done to him whatever they wanted' is thematic. It supports reading John's death through an Elijah lens.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The title 'Son of Man,' twice used in this pericope, derives from Daniel's heavenly figure, here paradoxically joined to suffering. Mark fuses Danielic exaltation with Isaianic suffering. The recurrence of the title throughout Mark anchors the Danielic source.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: The rejected stone supplies a scriptural pattern of the chosen one being despised and rejected, coherent with the Son of Man being 'set at nought.' Mark cites this psalm later (12:10), making its availability and recurrence plausible. The contact here is faint.

pericopes.text: Coming to the disciples, he saw a great multitude around them, and scribes questioning them. Immediately all the multitude, when they saw him, were greatly amazed, and running to him greeted him. He asked the scribes, “What are you asking them?” One of the multitude answered, “Teacher, I brought to you my son, who has a mute spirit; and wherever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams at the mouth, and grinds his teeth, and wastes away. I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they weren’t able.” He answered him, “Unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I bear with you? Bring him to me.” They brought him to him, and when he saw him, immediately the spirit convulsed him, and he fell on the ground, wallowing and foaming at the mouth. He asked his father, “How long has it been since this has come to him?” He said, “From childhood. Often it has cast him both into the fire and into the water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us, and help us.” Jesus said to him, “If you can believe, all things are possible to him who believes.” Immediately the father of the child cried out with tears, “I believe. Help my unbelief!” When Jesus saw that a multitude came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to him, “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him, and never enter him again!” Having cried out, and convulsed greatly, it came out of him. The boy became like one dead; so much that most of them said, “He is dead.” But Jesus took him by the hand, and raised him up; and he arose. When he had come into the house, his disciples asked him privately, “Why couldn’t we cast it out?” He said to them, “This kind can come out by nothing, except by prayer and fasting.”

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, “Go, get down; for your people, who you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves!
echoes.note: Jesus descending the mountain to find a disordered crowd and disputing scribes parallels Moses descending Sinai to find Israel corrupted around the golden calf. The 'faithless generation' rebuke echoes the wilderness apostasy. The narrative staging reinforces the Moses-on-the-mountain typology of the preceding scene.

echoes.text: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
echoes.note: Jesus' address 'O faithless generation' draws on the Song of Moses, which calls Israel a 'perverse and crooked generation' that has dealt corruptly and is not faithful. The generation-rebuke vocabulary is distinctively Deuteronomic. Mark frames the unbelieving crowd in covenant-lawsuit terms.

echoes.text: He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.
echoes.note: God hides his face from 'a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness,' precisely the charge of faithlessness Jesus levels. The pairing of 'generation' with unbelief tracks this verse closely. It deepens the Song-of-Moses backdrop to the rebuke.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “How long will this people despise me? and how long will they not believe in me, for all the signs which I have worked among them?
echoes.note: God's lament 'how long will this people despise me, and how long will they not believe' matches Jesus' double 'how long shall I be with you... how long shall I bear with you' aimed at unbelief. The wilderness-unbelief motif coheres with the faithless-generation theme. Volume is moderate.

echoes.text: “How long shall I bear with this evil congregation, that murmur against me? I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel, which they murmur against me.
echoes.note: God's 'how long shall I bear with this evil congregation' supplies the bearing-with-unbelief vocabulary in Jesus' complaint. The wilderness murmuring pattern reinforces the Deuteronomy 32 frame. A faint reinforcing echo.

echoes.text: I am poured out like water. All my bones are out of joint. My heart is like wax; it is melted within me.
echoes.note: The boy 'like one dead' so that bystanders said 'He is dead,' followed by being raised up, faintly evokes the psalm of one poured out like water and brought to the dust of death yet vindicated. The death-to-life movement coheres with the resurrection foreshadowing of the chapter. Contact is thematic and low-volume.

echoes.text: He stretched himself on the child three times, and cried to Yahweh, and said, “Yahweh my God, please let this child’s soul come into him again.”
echoes.note: Elijah raising the widow's apparently dead son, after which the child revived, supplies an Elijah-resurrection template behind Jesus taking the boy by the hand and raising him so that he arose. Given the chapter's Elijah typology, the link has some coherence. Verbal contact is slight.

echoes.text: He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm.
echoes.note: Elisha reviving the Shunammite's dead son extends the prophetic resuscitation pattern that frames Jesus' raising of the boy. The motif of a prophet restoring a child reinforces the scene's prophetic resonance. The connection is faint and pattern-based.

pericopes.text: They went out from there, and passed through Galilee. He didn’t want anyone to know it. For he was teaching his disciples, and said to them, “The Son of Man is being handed over to the hands of men, and they will kill him; and when he is killed, on the third day he will rise again.” But they didn’t understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: The Son of Man being 'handed over to the hands of men' echoes the servant whom the LORD delivered up for iniquity; the Septuagint's language of being given over underlies Mark's passion prediction. The vicarious handing-over coheres with Mark's Isaianic passion theme. Recurrence across the passion predictions strengthens it.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The servant 'poured out his soul to death' and 'was numbered with the transgressors,' having been delivered up. Mark's 'delivered into the hands of men... they will kill him' tracks the servant's being given over to death. The betrayal-and-death sequence aligns with the song's climax.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up' is the most likely scriptural source for 'on the third day he will rise again.' The third-day resurrection timing coheres with the formulaic passion predictions. Volume is moderate; the verbal 'third day' contact is notable.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The title 'Son of Man' carries Danielic weight even when joined to betrayal and death, fusing exaltation with suffering. The recurrence across Mark's passion predictions establishes the Danielic source. Here the paradox of the heavenly figure killed is sharpest.

pericopes.text: He came to Capernaum, and when he was in the house he asked them, “What were you arguing among yourselves on the way?” But they were silent, for they had disputed one with another on the way about who was the greatest. He sat down, and called the twelve; and he said to them, “If any man wants to be first, he shall be last of all, and servant of all.” He took a little child, and set him in their midst. Taking him in his arms, he said to them, “Whoever receives one such little child in my name, receives me, and whoever receives me, doesn’t receive me, but him who sent me.”

echoes.text: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
echoes.note: The dispute about who is greatest and Jesus' reversal that the first must be last and servant of all coheres with wisdom warnings that pride goes before destruction and humility precedes honor. The link is thematic rather than verbal. It situates the teaching in the OT wisdom reversal of status.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh teaches wisdom. Before honor is humility.
echoes.note: 'Before honor is humility' provides a wisdom backdrop to the last-shall-be-first saying and the embrace of the child. The contact is general and pattern-based. It reinforces the OT roots of Jesus' status reversal.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: The servant who justifies many through humble service supplies a faint figural backdrop to 'servant of all.' The connection is thematic and depends on Mark's wider servant Christology. Low volume.

pericopes.text: John said to him, “Teacher, we saw someone who doesn’t follow us casting out demons in your name; and we forbade him, because he doesn’t follow us.” But Jesus said, “Don’t forbid him, for there is no one who will do a mighty work in my name, and be able quickly to speak evil of me. For whoever is not against us is on our side. For whoever will give you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you are Christ’s, most certainly I tell you, he will in no way lose his reward.

echoes.text: A young man ran, and told Moses, and said, “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp!”
echoes.note: John's complaint about an outsider casting out demons in Jesus' name, and the demand to forbid him, closely parallels Joshua's plea that Moses forbid Eldad and Medad from prophesying outside the tent. Jesus' refusal to forbid mirrors Moses' magnanimous reply. The structural and thematic parallel is striking.

echoes.text: Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his chosen men, answered, “My lord Moses, forbid them!”
echoes.note: Joshua's 'My lord Moses, forbid them' is answered by Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets. Mark casts the disciples as Joshua and Jesus as the larger-hearted Moses who will not restrict the Spirit's work. The parallel reinforces the Moses typology running through the chapter.

echoes.text: Moses said to him, “Are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all Yahweh’s people were prophets, that Yahweh would put his Spirit on them!”
echoes.note: Moses' 'Would that all the LORD's people were prophets' anticipates Jesus' inclusive 'whoever is not against us is for us.' The generous expansion of authorized agency is shared. The echo completes the Eldad-and-Medad parallel.

pericopes.text: Whoever will cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if he were thrown into the sea with a millstone hung around his neck. If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter into life maimed, rather than having your two hands to go into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire, ‘where their worm doesn’t die, and the fire is not quenched.’ If your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter into life lame, rather than having your two feet to be cast into Gehenna, into the fire that will never be quenched— ‘where their worm doesn’t die, and the fire is not quenched.’ If your eye causes you to stumble, cast it out.
