The pairing of love-of-God with the relativizing of burnt offerings closely matches Hosea's formula.

echoes.text: How shall I come before Yahweh, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will Yahweh be pleased with thousands of rams? With tens of thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience? The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: Micah's contrast between multiplied burnt offerings and the real requirement to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God supplies the same prophetic logic the scribe applies. It belongs to the recurrent prophetic critique that ethical love outweighs sacrifice, reinforcing the scribe's verdict.

echoes.text: Only take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law which Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, to love Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”
echoes.note: Joshua's exhortation to love the Lord, walk in his ways, and serve him 'with all your heart and all your soul' echoes the Shema's totalizing love-language that Jesus quotes. As a near-verbatim restatement of Deuteronomy's command, it shows the formula's currency but adds little beyond the primary citation.

pericopes.text: Jesus responded, as he taught in the temple, “How is it that the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? For David himself said in the Holy Spirit, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.”’ Therefore David himself calls him Lord, so how can he be his son?” The common people heard him gladly.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: Jesus quotes verbatim 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet,' attributing it to David 'in the Holy Spirit.' This is the pericope's formal citation, the entire argument about the Messiah being David's Lord turns on it.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: The premise that the Christ is 'the son of David' rests on the Davidic covenant promise that God will raise up David's offspring and be a father to him. The scribal expectation Jesus interrogates is generated by Nathan's oracle, making it the necessary background to the riddle even though it is not quoted.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: The 'footstool' / subjugation-of-enemies-under-the-feet motif overlaps with Psalm 8's 'you have put all things under his feet.' The enthronement imagery of dominion beneath the feet belongs to a recurring royal/messianic cluster that interpreters frequently read alongside Psalm 110.

pericopes.text: In his teaching he said to them, “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk in long robes, and to get greetings in the marketplaces, and the best seats in the synagogues, and the best places at feasts: those who devour widows’ houses, and for a pretense make long prayers. These will receive greater condemnation.”

echoes.text: “You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child. If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.
echoes.note: Jesus condemns scribes who 'devour widows' houses,' invoking the covenant's strict protection of widows: God hears the cry of any widow afflicted and his wrath burns against the oppressor. The exploitation of widows is precisely the sin the Torah threatens with divine vengeance, grounding the prophetic 'greater condemnation.'

echoes.text: Woe to those who decree unrighteous decrees, and to the writers who write oppressive decrees; to deprive the needy from justice, and to rob the poor among my people of their rights, that widows may be their plunder, and that they may make the fatherless their prey!
echoes.note: Isaiah pronounces woe on those who make widows their prey and rob the needy of justice, the same predatory devouring of widows Jesus denounces. The prophetic woe-against-widow-plunderers tradition supplies both the indictment and the eschatological judgment Jesus announces.

echoes.text: You shall not deprive the foreigner or the fatherless of justice, nor take a widow’s clothing in pledge;
echoes.note: The Torah's prohibition against perverting justice due the widow or taking her garment in pledge frames widows as the paradigmatic protected class. Jesus' charge that the scribes devour widows' houses presupposes this legal duty of care that they have inverted.

echoes.text: I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against the perjurers, and against those who oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and who deprive the foreigner of justice, and don’t fear me,” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: Malachi names those who oppress the widow among the wrongdoers God will swiftly judge. The pairing of widow-oppression with imminent divine reckoning parallels Jesus' 'these will receive greater condemnation,' reinforcing the prophetic-judgment frame.

echoes.text: He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall?
echoes.note: Ben Sira insists God does not ignore the supplication of the widow nor her tears running down her cheek, and will repay her oppressor. This Second-Temple wisdom text, available to Mark's milieu, coheres with the indictment of those who profit from widows.

pericopes.text: Jesus sat down opposite the treasury, and saw how the multitude cast money into the treasury. Many who were rich cast in much. A poor widow came, and she cast in two small brass coins, which equal a quadrans coin. He called his disciples to himself, and said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, this poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury, for they all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on.”

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: The poor widow who gives 'all that she had to live on' strongly recalls the widow of Zarephath who, at Elijah's word, spends her last handful of meal trusting God for provision. The shared figure of a destitute widow giving her entire remaining sustenance makes this the closest narrative analogue and likely a deliberate typological echo.

echoes.text: “‘All the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is Yahweh’s. It is holy to Yahweh.
echoes.note: The treasury-offering setting and the contrast between giving from abundance versus giving all evoke the Torah's regulation of dedicated gifts and tithes. The widow's total gift outdoes proportional giving, implicitly measuring devotion against the cultic baseline of the tithe.

echoes.text: When you reap your harvest in your field, and have forgotten a sheaf in the field, you shall not go again to get it. It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow; that Yahweh your God may bless you in all the work of your hands. When you beat your olive tree, you shall not go over the boughs again. It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow. When you harvest your vineyard, you shall not glean it after […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's gleaning laws structurally cast the widow as a recipient of charity, not a donor; Mark inverts the expectation by showing the widow as giver, which heightens the pathos of her poverty against the Torah's assumption that widows need provision rather than provide it.

echoes.text: But Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one comes into Yahweh’s house: and the priests who kept the threshold put therein all the money that was brought into Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: The temple treasury chest where money was cast, established in Jehoiada's reform, is the institutional backdrop of the scene. Mark's 'treasury' and the act of casting coins into it presuppose this cultic apparatus, a faint but concrete OT realia echo.

pericopes.text: As he went out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Teacher, see what kind of stones and what kind of buildings!” Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone on another, which will not be thrown down.”

echoes.text: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.
echoes.note: Jesus' oracle that not one stone of the temple will be left on another reprises the classic prophetic threat that Zion will be plowed as a field and the temple mount become a wooded height. Micah's word is itself remembered in Jeremiah 26:18 as a precedent for temple-doom prophecy, giving recurrence; the volume (a prophet announcing the sanctuary's ruin) is strong and the coherence with Jeremiah 7 below is tight.

echoes.text: then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's temple sermon threatens to make 'this house like Shiloh' and Jerusalem a curse, the OT template for a prophet predicting the sanctuary's destruction and being put on trial for it. Mark frames Jesus in exactly this Jeremianic role, and the temple-saying becomes evidence at his trial (Mark 14:58), so the figural coherence is high.

echoes.text: therefore will I do to the house which is called by my name, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
echoes.note: The threat to do to 'this house which is called by my name' as was done to Shiloh undergirds the prediction that the great buildings will fall. Mark elsewhere quotes Jeremiah 7:11 ('den of robbers') at the temple cleansing, establishing recurrence of this chapter in the temple-confrontation narrative.

echoes.text: Now, please consider from this day and backward, before a stone was laid on a stone in Yahweh’s temple.
echoes.note: The disciples' marveling at 'what stones, what buildings' inverts Haggai's prophecy of glory for the rebuilt house ('stone laid upon stone'); Jesus' reversal of stone-on-stone may play against the temple-construction language of the post-exilic prophets. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’
echoes.note: The Deuteronomistic warning that if Israel forsakes the LORD 'this house will become a heap of ruins; everyone who passes will be appalled' supplies the covenantal logic for the temple's fall as judgment. Coherence with the prophetic temple-doom tradition is strong, though the specific 'stone on stone' idiom comes from Micah.

pericopes.text: As he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked him privately, “Tell us, when will these things be? What is the sign that these things are all about to be fulfilled?”

echoes.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
echoes.note: Jesus delivers the apocalyptic discourse seated on the Mount of Olives 'opposite the temple,' the very mountain where Zechariah says the LORD's feet will stand on the day of the LORD and the mount will split. The setting is freighted with eschatological geography, lending figural coherence to a discourse about the day of the LORD, though Mark does not cite the verse.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory went up from the midst of the city, and stood on the mountain which is on the east side of the city.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's glory of the LORD departs the doomed temple and halts on 'the mountain east of the city,' i.e., Olivet; Jesus pronouncing the temple's destruction from that same eastern mountain may echo the departure-of-the-glory motif. Faint and dependent on topographical identification.

echoes.text: One said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, How long shall it be to the end of these wonders? I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be […]
echoes.note: The disciples' double question — 'when will these things be, and what is the sign that all is about to be accomplished?' — closely tracks Daniel's question to the man clothed in linen, 'how long until the end of these wonders?' and the answer measuring the time of the end. Mark's eschatological timetable is structured by Daniel 12, giving this opening question strong Danielic coherence.

echoes.text: He said, Behold, I will make you know what shall be in the latter time of the indignation; for it belongs to the appointed time of the end.
echoes.note: Daniel's 'I will tell you what will happen at the latter end of the indignation, for it pertains to the appointed time of the end' parallels the disciples' request to be told the sign of the consummation. The vocabulary of an 'appointed time of the end' shapes the whole discourse.

pericopes.text: Jesus, answering, began to tell them, “Be careful that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and will lead many astray. “When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, don’t be troubled. For those must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places. There will be famines and troubles. These things are the beginning of birth pains.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:
echoes.note: 'These things must happen' (Greek dei genesthai) verbally echoes Daniel 2:28 LXX, 'what must come to pass in the latter days,' the programmatic statement of apocalyptic necessity. Mark adopts Daniel's deterministic 'must' to frame the wars and disasters as the divinely fixed sequence before the end.

echoes.text: I will stir up the Egyptians against the Egyptians, and they will fight everyone against his brother, and everyone against his neighbor; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.
echoes.note: 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom' closely reproduces Isaiah's oracle, 'I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians... kingdom against kingdom.' The paired idiom of nation/kingdom conflict is distinctive enough (high volume) to mark deliberate use of Isaiah's day-of-the-LORD imagery of internecine collapse.

echoes.text: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.
echoes.note: 'Nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every distress' supplies the same nation-against-nation formula combined with God-sent 'trouble,' matching Mark's 'troubles.' The Chronicler's portrait of God-ordained civil chaos coheres with the apocalyptic catalogue.

echoes.text: They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame.
echoes.note: 'The beginning of birth pains' draws on Isaiah's day-of-the-LORD oracle against Babylon where men are 'in anguish like a woman in labor.' Birth-pang imagery for eschatological tribulation is a recurrent prophetic topos (Isaiah 26:17; Jeremiah 22:23; Hosea 13:13), and Isaiah 13 also supplies the cosmic darkening cluster echoed later in 13:24, strengthening coherence.

echoes.text: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Like a woman with child... cries out in her pangs, so were we before you, O LORD' is part of the proto-apocalyptic Isaiah Apocalypse (chs. 24-27) that supplies Mark with resurrection-and-tribulation imagery. The labor-pang figure for the people's distress before deliverance coheres tightly with Mark's 'beginning of birth pains.'

echoes.text: Inhabitant of Lebanon, who makes your nest in the cedars, how greatly to be pitied you will be when pangs come on you, the pain as of a woman in travail!
echoes.note: 'How you will groan when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor' applies the birth-pang figure specifically to Jerusalem/Judah's coming judgment, the very referent of Mark 13. The recurrence of the labor metaphor across the prophets for the city's doom supports its presence here.

echoes.text: The sorrows of a travailing woman will come on him. He is an unwise son; for when it is time, he doesn’t come to the opening of the womb.
echoes.note: 'The pangs of childbirth come for him' as an image of Ephraim's crisis adds to the prophetic stock of birth-pang imagery behind Mark's phrase. Faint, included for recurrence within the tradition rather than distinctive verbal contact.

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
echoes.note: The warning 'do not be led astray' by 'many who come in my name' echoes Deuteronomy's law against the prophet or dream-diviner who arises to 'lead you astray' (LXX planao) from the LORD. The same planao verb and the testing-of-Israel motif recur in 13:22, indicating Deuteronomy 13 as a structuring subtext for the deception warnings.

echoes.text: I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: 'Wonders in the heavens and on the earth' before the day of the LORD lies behind the catalogue of cosmic and terrestrial signs (wars, earthquakes); Joel is quoted heavily in early Christian eschatology and resurfaces in Mark's darkening of sun and moon in 13:24. Faint here, marked for recurrence.

echoes.text: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land; and I will shake all nations. The precious things of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land, and all nations' supplies a prophetic precedent for cosmic-political upheaval (kingdoms, shaking) preceding the end. The 'shaking' language returns in 13:25 ('powers shaken'), giving the cluster coherence.

pericopes.text: But watch yourselves, for they will deliver you up to councils. You will be beaten in synagogues. You will stand before rulers and kings for my sake, for a testimony to them. The Good News must first be preached to all the nations. When they lead you away and deliver you up, don’t be anxious beforehand, or premeditate what you will say, but say whatever will be given you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. “Brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child. Children will rise up against parents, and cause them to be put to death. You will be hated by all men for my name’s sake, but he who endures to the end, the same will be saved.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: Daniel's little horn that 'wears out the saints of the Most High' for an appointed time supplies the apocalyptic pattern of the faithful handed over to persecuting authorities before vindication. Mark's councils, beatings, and kings before whom believers stand instantiate the saints' tribulation under hostile rulers, a Danielic frame the discourse repeatedly invokes.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: 'Brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child; children will rise against parents' is a near-verbatim use of Micah 7:6, 'the son treats the father with contempt... a man's enemies are the men of his own household.' The family-rending of the eschatological crisis is drawn directly from Micah's lament over a society in moral collapse; high volume and distinctiveness.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: 'The gospel must first be preached to all the nations' draws on the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth,' the Isaianic universalism behind the worldwide proclamation. The 'must' (eschatological necessity) plus the nations theme coheres with Isaiah's mission oracles.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The mandate that the good news be proclaimed 'to all the nations' echoes the dominion given to the one like a son of man, that 'all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him.' Since Mark 13:26 explicitly invokes Daniel 7:13, the universal-nations note here likely draws on the same vision's worldwide scope.

echoes.text: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'I will speak of your testimonies before kings and not be ashamed' faintly parallels standing 'before rulers and kings... for a testimony.' The righteous-sufferer-before-rulers motif is diffuse in the Psalter; low confidence, included for the testimony-before-kings overlap.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak. Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh. Then Yahweh stretched out his hand, and touched my mouth; and Yahweh said to me, “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.
echoes.note: The promise 'do not be anxious what you will say... it is not you who speak but the Holy Spirit' echoes the LORD's commission to Jeremiah, 'do not say I am only a youth... I have put my words in your mouth,' the prophetic-inspiration topos. The assurance of divinely given speech before hostile powers follows the call-narrative pattern.

echoes.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”
echoes.note: 'I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak' is the foundational promise of God-supplied speech for a reluctant messenger, directly behind 'say whatever is given you in that hour.' The Moses-commissioning of inspired speech reinforces the Jeremiah parallel.

echoes.text: Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days. But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.
echoes.note: 'He who endures to the end will be saved' resonates with Daniel's beatitude on the one who waits and reaches the end of the days ('blessed is he who waits... you shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days'). The endurance-to-the-end-yields-deliverance logic is Danielic apocalyptic, coherent with Mark's framework.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: Daniel's promise that 'your people shall be delivered, everyone found written in the book' stands behind the eschatological 'will be saved.' The deliverance of the faithful remnant through the unequaled tribulation (cited explicitly at 13:19) frames the salvation of the endurer here.

pericopes.text: But when you see the abomination of desolation,spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing where it ought not (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let him who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter in, to take anything out of his house. Let him who is in the field not return back to take his cloak. But woe to those who are with child and to those who nurse babies in those days! Pray that your flight won’t be in the winter. For in those days there will be oppression, such as there has not been the like from the beginning of the creation which God created until now, and never will be. Unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the chosen ones, whom he picked out, he shortened the days.

echoes.text: He shall make a firm covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease; and on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate; and even to the full end, and that determined, shall wrath be poured out on the desolate.
echoes.note: 'The abomination of desolation' is a formal citation, named as 'spoken of by Daniel the prophet.' Daniel 9:27's 'abomination that makes desolate' upon the wing of the temple is the source phrase; Mark's masculine participle 'standing where it ought not' personalizes the desolator. The highest-volume Danielic anchor of the discourse.

echoes.text: Forces shall stand on his part, and they shall profane the sanctuary, even the fortress, and shall take away the continual burnt offering, and they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.
echoes.note: Daniel 11:31's forces that 'profane the temple... and set up the abomination that makes desolate' supplies the historical referent (Antiochus' altar to Zeus) reapplied to a future profanation. Mark's 'standing where it ought not' (i.e., in the holy place) directly tracks this temple-desecration sense.

echoes.text: From the time that the continual burnt offering shall be taken away, and the abomination that makes desolate set up, there shall be one thousand two hundred ninety days.
echoes.note: Daniel 12:11 dates 'the abomination that makes desolate set up' to the countdown of the end (1,290 days), tying the phrase to the eschatological timetable Mark is expounding. The recurrence of the exact phrase across Daniel 9, 11, and 12 underwrites Mark's explicit appeal to 'Daniel the prophet.'

echoes.text: And on the fifteenth day of Chislev, in the hundred and forty and fifth year, they built an abomination of desolation upon the altar, and in the cities of Judah on every side they built idol altars.
echoes.note: 1 Maccabees 1:54 narrates the fulfillment of Daniel, 'they erected a desolating sacrilege on the altar of burnt offering,' giving the concrete Second-Temple referent for the phrase. As a deuterocanonical witness to how 'abomination of desolation' was understood, it supplies the interpretive backdrop ('let the reader understand') for Mark's reuse.

echoes.text: And he and his sons fled into the mountains, and forsook all that they had in the city.
echoes.note: 'Mattathias and his sons fled to the mountains' at the persecution provides the precise precedent for 'let those in Judea flee to the mountains.' The Maccabean flight from the desolating sacrilege is the paradigmatic response Mark commands, making this a strong situational echo within the same desolation script.

echoes.text: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”
echoes.note: 'Flee to the mountains... do not look back, do not stop' (the angels to Lot at Sodom) underlies the urgent flight commands — not going back from the roof or field for possessions. The Sodom-escape pattern of immediate, possession-abandoning flight before judgment coheres with Mark's instructions (cf. Luke's explicit 'remember Lot's wife').

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: 'Tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of creation... and never will be' closely renders Daniel 12:1, 'a time of trouble such as never has been since there was a nation till that time.' The unequaled-distress formula is distinctive and explicitly Danielic, the climactic tribulation before the deliverance of the elect.

echoes.text: A day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness. As the dawn spreading on the mountains, a great and strong people; there has never been the like, neither will there be any more after them, even to the years of many generations.
echoes.note: Joel's day of the LORD is 'a day of darkness... such as has never been from of old, nor will be again after,' an unequaled-day formula parallel to Daniel 12:1 and reused by Mark. Joel supplies both the superlative-distress idiom and (in 2:10, 31) the sun-moon darkening cluster Mark deploys at 13:24, strengthening coherence.

echoes.text: There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has not been, nor shall be any more.
echoes.note: 'A great cry... such as there has never been, nor ever will be again' (the plague of the firstborn) is an early instance of the unequaled-event formula that Daniel and Joel inherit. Faint, included as the deep background of the 'never before, never again' superlative.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one says, ‘Don’t destroy it, for a blessing is in it:’ so will I do for my servants’ sake, that I may not destroy them all. I will bring a seed out of Jacob, and out of Judah an inheritor of my mountains; and my chosen shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there.
echoes.note: The shortening of the days 'for the sake of the elect, whom he chose' resonates with Isaiah's promise to preserve a remnant 'for my servants' sake, that I may not destroy them all.' The mercy-for-the-chosen logic that mitigates total destruction parallels Mark's 'unless the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh would be saved.'

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: 1 Enoch speaks of the days being shortened/disordered in the time of the sinners, a Second-Temple apocalyptic motif of cosmic time foreshortened in the last crisis. The pseudepigraphal parallel to 'he shortened the days' suggests a shared apocalyptic idiom rather than direct dependence; marked contested.

pericopes.text: Then if anyone tells you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or, ‘Look, there!’ don’t believe it. For there will arise false christs and false prophets, and will show signs and wonders, that they may lead astray, if possible, even the chosen ones. But you watch. “Behold, I have told you all things beforehand.

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
echoes.note: 'False prophets will arise and show signs and wonders to lead astray' reproduces Deuteronomy's test: the prophet who 'gives a sign or wonder' and it comes to pass, yet leads you after other gods, is testing whether you love the LORD. The pairing of 'signs and wonders' with seductive false prophecy and the verb 'lead astray' (planao) is distinctively Deuteronomic.

echoes.text: That prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death, because he has spoken rebellion against Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to draw you aside out of the way which Yahweh your God commanded you to walk in. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's verdict that such a prophet has 'spoken to lead you astray from the LORD your God' underlies Mark's 'that they may lead astray, if possible, even the elect.' The danger to even the faithful elect echoes the law's concern that the whole community could be seduced by validated false signs.

echoes.text: But the prophet who speaks a word presumptuously in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.” You may say in your heart, “How shall we know the word which Yahweh has not spoken?” When a prophet speaks in Yahweh’s name, if the thing doesn’t follow, nor happen, that is the thing which Yahweh has not spoken. The prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You shall not be afraid of him.
echoes.note: The law on the presumptuous prophet who speaks in the LORD's name without commission supplements the false-prophet warning. Less verbally specific than Deuteronomy 13, included for the recurrent false-prophet legislation behind Mark's 'false christs and false prophets.'

echoes.text: “For from their least even to their greatest, everyone is given to covetousness; and from the prophet even to the priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed also the hurt of my people superficially, saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ when there is no peace.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's polemic against prophets who 'have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying peace, peace, when there is no peace' supplies the prophetic stock of deceiving prophets in a doomed Jerusalem. Faint and thematic rather than verbal; coheres with Mark's setting of false messianic claims amid the city's crisis.

pericopes.text: But in those days, after that oppression, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will be falling from the sky, and the powers that are in the heavens will be shaken. Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. Then he will send out his angels, and will gather together his chosen ones from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of the sky.

echoes.text: For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.
echoes.note: 'The sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light' is near-verbatim from Isaiah 13:10, 'the sun will be dark at its rising and the moon will not shed its light,' the day-of-the-LORD oracle against Babylon. The catastrophic dimming of the luminaries is the lead element of Mark's cosmic-collapse cluster; highest volume in the constellation.

echoes.text: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
echoes.note: 'The stars will be falling from heaven and the powers of the heavens will be shaken' draws on Isaiah 34:4, 'all the host of heaven shall rot away, the skies roll up like a scroll, all their host fall.' Mark's falling stars and shaken heavenly powers reproduce Isaiah's cosmic-judgment imagery (LXX 'the powers of the heavens shall melt').

echoes.text: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.
echoes.note: 'The sun and moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining' (also 2:31, 3:15) is a primary source for Mark's three-element luminary collapse. Joel's day-of-the-LORD theophany combines earth-quaking, heaven-trembling, and darkened sun/moon/stars, matching Mark's whole cluster and reinforcing the multiply-attested character of the imagery.

echoes.text: When I shall extinguish you, I will cover the heavens, and make its stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of the sky will I make dark over you, and set darkness on your land, says the Lord Yahweh.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's lament over Pharaoh: 'I will cover the heavens and darken their stars; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of heaven I will darken,' supplies the exact 'moon shall not give its light' phrase Mark shares with Isaiah 13. A fourth witness in the darkening cluster, demonstrating Hays' recurrence.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'They will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory' directly cites Daniel 7:13, 'one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven.' This is the christological centerpiece of the discourse; Mark adds 'power and glory' from the dominion granted in 7:14, and the title 'Son of Man' is the load-bearing self-designation throughout Mark.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'With great power and glory' renders the gift to the son of man of 'dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples should serve him.' Mark fuses 7:13's coming-on-clouds with 7:14's enthronement glory, so the Son of Man's parousia carries the universal dominion of Daniel's vision.

echoes.text: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Gather the elect from the four winds' echoes Zechariah 2:6, 'I have spread you abroad as the four winds of heaven, declares the LORD,' a regathering-of-the-dispersed oracle. The eschatological ingathering of the scattered people from the four winds is the conceptual core of Mark's angelic harvest of the elect.

echoes.text: If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of the heavens, from there Yahweh your God will gather you, and from there he will bring you back.
echoes.note: 'If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the LORD will gather you' undergirds gathering the elect 'from the ends of the earth to the ends of the sky.' Deuteronomy's covenant promise of regathering the exiled from the extremities of earth and heaven matches Mark's double horizon precisely.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that the Lord will set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant that is left of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: Isaiah's promise that the LORD will 'assemble the banished of Israel and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth' supplies the messianic-age ingathering behind Mark's gathering of the elect. The 'four corners/four winds' regathering is a recurrent restoration motif, here applied to the Son of Man's harvest.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that a great trumpet will be blown; and those who were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and those who were outcasts in the land of Egypt, shall come; and they will worship Yahweh in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'A great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost... will come and worship the LORD' from the Isaiah Apocalypse provides the trumpet-summoned ingathering of the scattered; Matthew's parallel makes the trumpet explicit. Mark's angelic gathering coheres with this Isaianic regathering even without naming the trumpet.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn. In that day there will be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon. The land will mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of […]
echoes.note: 'They will look on him whom they have pierced' and the mourning of the tribes lies behind 'they will see the Son of Man'; the seeing-and-mourning at the coming one is more explicit in Matthew 24:30 and Revelation 1:7 but may color Mark's 'they will see.' Faint in Mark, marked contested.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son. In that day the lamentation in Jerusalem shall be very great, as the mourning for the pomegranate grove cut down in the plain. And the land shall lament in separate families, the […]

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him' parallels the Son of Man sending out his angels at the parousia. The accompanying-holy-ones motif of the day of the LORD coheres with Mark's angelic retinue; included for recurrence of the Zecharianic day-of-the-LORD material in this pericope.

echoes.text: He lays the beams of his rooms in the waters. He makes the clouds his chariot. He walks on the wings of the wind.
echoes.note: 'He makes the clouds his chariot, riding on the wings of the wind' is part of the OT cloud-rider theophany tradition (cf. Isaiah 19:1; Psalm 18:9-12) that informs the Son of Man's coming 'in clouds.' The divine-prerogative of cloud-borne arrival lends figural weight to Daniel 7's cloud-coming as Mark applies it.

pericopes.text: “Now from the fig tree, learn this parable. When the branch has now become tender, and produces its leaves, you know that the summer is near; even so you also, when you see these things coming to pass, know that it is near, at the doors. Most certainly I say to you, this generationwill not pass away until all these things happen. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid, you animals of the field; for the pastures of the wilderness spring up, for the tree bears its fruit. The fig tree and the vine yield their strength.
echoes.note: The fig-tree parable ('the fig tree puts forth... you know summer is near') faintly recalls Joel's restoration imagery, 'the fig tree and vine give their full yield,' as a sign-bearing tree marking the season's turn. The fig tree elsewhere in Mark (11:13-21) carries judgment symbolism; here its budding signals nearness, a season-discernment topos. Contested.

echoes.text: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.
echoes.note: 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away' draws on Isaiah 51:6, 'the heavens will vanish like smoke, the earth wear out like a garment... but my salvation will be forever.' The contrast between the perishing cosmos and the enduring divine word is distinctively Isaianic and high in volume.

echoes.text: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: 'The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever' is the closest source for the permanence of God's word over against transient creation. Mark transfers the abiding-word of Isaiah 40 to 'my words,' an implicit christological claim; the verbal contrast (pass away / not pass away vs. wither / stand forever) is strong.

echoes.text: Of old, you laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same. Your years will have no end.
echoes.note: 'They will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment... but you are the same' grounds 'heaven and earth will pass away.' The Psalm's contrast of the perishable heavens-and-earth with the unchanging LORD supplies the theological warrant Mark applies to the abiding word.

echoes.text: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
echoes.note: 'All the host of heaven shall rot away and the skies roll up like a scroll' reinforces 'heaven and earth will pass away,' connecting this declaration to the cosmic-dissolution imagery already cited at 13:25. Recurrence of Isaiah 34 across the discourse supports its faint presence here.

echoes.text: But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'All these things' coming to pass before 'this generation' passes resonates with Daniel's assurance that 'the saints shall receive the kingdom... forever, forever and ever'; the certainty that the decreed events will be accomplished is Danielic. Faint, included for the apocalyptic guarantee that frames 'most certainly I say.'

pericopes.text: But of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. Watch, keep alert, and pray; for you don’t know when the time is. “It is like a man, traveling to another country, having left his house, and given authority to his servants, and to each one his work, and also commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch. Watch therefore, for you don’t know when the lord of the house is coming, whether at evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning; lest coming suddenly he might find you sleeping. What I tell you, I tell all: Watch.”

echoes.text: It will be a unique day which is known to Yahweh; not day, and not night; but it will come to pass, that at evening time there will be light.
echoes.note: 'A unique day... known to the LORD' on which the timing is hidden faintly parallels 'of that day or hour no one knows... but only the Father.' Zechariah's day-of-the-LORD whose timing belongs to God alone coheres with Mark's reservation of the hour to the Father; contested.

echoes.text: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished. I heard, but I didn’t understand: then I said, my lord, what shall be the issue of these things? He said, Go your way, […]
echoes.note: Daniel is told 'the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end' — the timing of the consummation is withheld even from the seer. Mark's 'no one knows the day or hour' continues this Danielic concealment of the appointed time, the necessary counterpart to the timetable expounded throughout the chapter.

echoes.text: I will stand at my watch, and set myself on the ramparts, and will look out to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer concerning my complaint. Yahweh answered me, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it. For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
echoes.note: The watchman who stations himself to keep watch (2:1) and the vision that 'awaits its appointed time... if it seems slow, wait for it' (2:3) supplies the watching-for-a-delayed-coming posture behind the doorkeeper commanded to keep watch and the repeated 'watch.' The waiting-watchman for an appointed-yet-delayed arrival is the Habakkuk pattern.

echoes.text: For the Lord said to me, “Go, set a watchman. Let him declare what he sees. When he sees a troop, horsemen in pairs, a troop of donkeys, a troop of camels, he shall listen diligently with great attentiveness.” He cried like a lion: “Lord, I stand continually on the watchtower in the daytime, and every night I stay at my post.
echoes.note: 'Go, set a watchman... he calls, Upon a watchtower I stand continually by day, and at my post whole nights' provides the prophetic figure of the sentinel keeping watch through the night-watches. Mark's doorkeeper told to 'keep watch' and the listing of evening/midnight/cockcrow/morning watches draw on this watchman tradition.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple' parallels the master who returns 'suddenly,' lest he find the servants sleeping. The sudden, unannounced arrival of the lord coheres with Malachi's suddenly-coming Lord; faint and contested, but Malachi is a recurrent source in Mark.

echoes.text: Son of man, speak to the children of your people, and tell them, When I bring the sword on a land, and the people of the land take a man from among them, and set him for their watchman; if, when he sees the sword come on the land, he blow the trumpet, and warn the people; then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet, and doesn’t take warning, if the sword come, and take him away, his blood shall be on his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet, and […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's watchman charged with sounding the alarm and held accountable if he fails to keep watch supplies the responsibility-of-the-sentinel theme behind 'commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch.' Faint relative to Isaiah 21 and Habakkuk 2; included for the recurrent watchman motif.

echoes.text: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.
echoes.note: The parable of the man who goes abroad, leaves his house, and assigns each servant authority over his work faintly recalls the trusted-steward-over-an-absent-master's-household pattern (e.g., Joseph over Potiphar's house). A diffuse OT household-management topos rather than a specific text; low confidence.

echoes.text: in the twilight, in the evening of the day, in the middle of the night and in the darkness. Behold, there a woman met him with the attire of a prostitute, and with crafty intent.
echoes.note: The four night-watches (evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning) draw on the OT/Second-Temple reckoning of the night's divisions; Proverbs' 'in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness' attests the watch-segmented night. Marked contested as a cultural-temporal echo rather than a quoted text.

pericopes.text: It was now two days before the feast of the Passover and the unleavened bread, and the chief priests and the scribes sought how they might seize him by deception, and kill him. For they said, “Not during the feast, because there might be a riot of the people.”

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: Mark times the whole Passion by 'the Passover and the unleavened bread,' invoking the foundational deliverance festival of Exodus 12 as the calendrical and theological frame. The recurrence of Passover language across the chapter (vv. 1, 12, 14, 16) raises the volume, and the coherence is total since Mark presents Jesus' death as a new exodus. The availability is secure as the institution narrative of Israel's central feast.

echoes.text: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: The chief priests and scribes who 'sought how they might seize him by deception, and kill him' enact the rulers who 'take counsel together against the Lord and against his anointed.' Mark has already cited Psalm 2 at the baptism, so recurrence supports a faint conspiratorial echo, though there is no verbal quotation here.

echoes.text: For I have heard the slander of many, terror on every side, while they conspire together against me, they plot to take away my life.
echoes.note: The plot to take Jesus' life 'by deception' resonates with the lament psalmist's complaint that his enemies 'scheme together against me, plotting to take my life.' The motif of conspiratorial counsel against the righteous sufferer belongs to the psalmic matrix Mark draws on throughout the Passion, but the link is thematic rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: While he was at Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at the table, a woman came having an alabaster jar of ointment of pure nard—very costly. She broke the jar, and poured it over his head. But there were some who were indignant among themselves, saying, “Why has this ointment been wasted? For this might have been sold for more than three hundred denarii, and given to the poor.” They grumbled against her. But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want to, you can do them good; but you will not always have me. She has done what she could. She has anointed my body beforehand for the burying. Most certainly I tell you, wherever this Good News may be preached throughout the whole world, that which this woman has done will also be spoken of for a memorial of her.”

echoes.text: For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.
echoes.note: Jesus' saying 'you always have the poor with you' reproduces Deuteronomy's declaration that 'the poor will never cease out of the land,' which grounds the command to open one's hand to the needy. The verbal volume is high and the coherence sharp: Jesus does not dismiss the poor but cites the very text that mandates perpetual generosity, contrasting that standing obligation with the unrepeatable moment of his own burial.

echoes.text: While the king sat at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance.
echoes.note: The woman's costly nard (nardos) poured on the reclining Jesus closely matches the bride's line, 'while the king sat at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.' The rare term nard and the banquet setting give real verbal volume, and the figural reading of the beloved anointing the king coheres with Mark's messianic scene, though Mark does not cite it.

echoes.text: Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets, and said to him, “Put your belt on your waist, take this vial of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth Gilead. When you come there, find Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi, and go in, and make him arise up from among his brothers, and carry him to an inner room. Then take the vial of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, ‘Thus says Yahweh, “I have anointed you king over Israel.”’ Then […]
echoes.note: The pouring of oil over the head as an act that designates a king (Jehu anointed by Elisha's servant) supplies background for reading this anointing as royal/messianic. The connection is conceptual, drawing on Israel's anointing rites generally rather than a specific verbal parallel.

echoes.text: Then Samuel took the vial of oil, and poured it on his head, and kissed him, and said, “Isn’t it that Yahweh has anointed you to be prince over his inheritance?
echoes.note: Samuel pouring a flask of oil on Saul's head and kissing him as the Lord's anointed offers the paradigmatic royal anointing on the head that Mark's scene quietly evokes (Christos = 'anointed'). The echo is thematic, suggesting kingship, with no direct verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: They buried him in his own tombs, which he had dug out for himself in the city of David, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odors and various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumers’ art: and they made a very great burning for him.
echoes.note: Jesus interprets the anointing as preparation 'for the burying,' resonating with Israelite burial customs of anointing the dead with spices, as at Asa's funeral with its bed of spices. This supplies the cultural background for the burial reading, though it is a custom-echo rather than a cited text.

pericopes.text: Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went away to the chief priests, that he might deliver him to them. They, when they heard it, were glad, and promised to give him money. He sought how he might conveniently deliver him.

echoes.text: I said to them, “If you think it best, give me my wages; and if not, keep them.” So they weighed for my wages thirty pieces of silver.
echoes.note: Judas going to the priests who 'promised to give him money' to deliver Jesus evokes the shepherd-prophecy where the people 'weighed out thirty pieces of silver' as the price of the rejected shepherd. Mark, unlike Matthew, does not specify the sum, so the volume is lower, but the motif of betraying the shepherd for a priced payment coheres with Mark's shepherd-citation in v. 27.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: The intimate associate who turns to hand Jesus over begins the betrayed-friend motif that Mark develops at the table (v. 18); Psalm 41's 'my close friend who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me' is the controlling subtext. Here the link is anticipatory and thematic, with the verbal force concentrated in the meal scene that follows.

echoes.text: Someone told David, saying, “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” David said, “Yahweh, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”
echoes.note: Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor who defected to Absalom, is the classic Old Testament type of the intimate betrayer, traditionally paired with Psalm 41 in readings of treachery against the anointed. Judas' defection coheres with this Ahithophel pattern, though the echo is typological rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: On the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover, his disciples asked him, “Where do you want us to go and prepare that you may eat the Passover?” He sent two of his disciples, and said to them, “Go into the city, and there you will meet a man carrying a pitcher of water. Follow him, and wherever he enters in, tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says, “Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?”’ He will himself show you a large upper room furnished and ready. Get ready for us there.” His disciples went out, and came into the city, and found things as he had said to them, and they prepared the Passover.

echoes.text: and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening.
echoes.note: The disciples prepare 'on the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover,' directly enacting Exodus 12's prescription that the lamb be killed at twilight on the appointed day. The volume is high and the coherence total as Mark stages the Last Supper as a Passover meal, drawing the institution narrative into the Passion frame.

echoes.text: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
echoes.note: The instruction to 'prepare' the Passover and to eat it in a guest room invokes the Exodus regulation that the lamb be eaten roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs that same night. The preparatory action presupposes the full Exodus rubric, supplying the meal's content even where Mark abbreviates.

echoes.text: When you have departed from me today, then you shall find two men by Rachel’s tomb, in the border of Benjamin at Zelzah; and they will tell you, ‘The donkeys which you went to seek have been found; and behold, your father has stopped caring about the donkeys, and is anxious for you, saying, “What shall I do for my son?”’ “Then you shall go on forward from there, and you shall come to the oak of Tabor; and three men shall meet you there going up to God to […]
echoes.note: Jesus' detailed prediction that the disciples will meet a man carrying a water jar who leads them to a prepared place mirrors Samuel's sequence of precise sign-predictions to Saul ('you will meet... you will come... you will find'). The form of foreknown encounters fulfilled to the letter resonates, though there is no verbal citation.

pericopes.text: When it was evening he came with the twelve. As they sat and were eating, Jesus said, “Most certainly I tell you, one of you will betray me—he who eats with me.” They began to be sorrowful, and to ask him one by one, “Surely not I?” And another said, “Surely not I?” He answered them, “It is one of the twelve, he who dips with me in the dish. For the Son of Man goes, even as it is written about him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.”

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: Jesus' words 'one of you will betray me—he who eats with me' and 'he who dips with me in the dish' draw their pathos directly from 'my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.' The shared scene of table fellowship turned to treachery gives high coherence, and the deliberate emphasis on shared eating supplies strong verbal volume for this load-bearing subtext.

echoes.text: For it was not an enemy who insulted me, then I could have endured it. Neither was it he who hated me who raised himself up against me, then I would have hidden myself from him. But it was you, a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend. We took sweet fellowship together. We walked in God’s house with company.
echoes.note: The lament over betrayal by 'a man my equal, my companion and familiar friend, with whom I kept pleasant company... in the house of God' parallels the intimate-betrayer motif of the meal. Its recurrence alongside Psalm 41 in the suffering-righteous tradition makes it a strong secondary subtext for the betrayed table-companion.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: Jesus' self-designation 'the Son of Man goes, even as it is written about him' presupposes the scriptural Son-of-Man figure that Mark will name explicitly in v. 62, framing his death as the destined path of that figure. The phrase 'as it is written' signals a scriptural script even though no single text is quoted, with Daniel 7 as the governing Son-of-Man matrix.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth. He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people? They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he […]
echoes.note: The notion that 'the Son of Man goes as it is written' — a suffering and death foreordained in Scripture — coheres with the Servant who is led to slaughter according to God's purpose. Mark gives no quotation here, but the Servant Song is a leading candidate for the scriptural 'writing' about the Son of Man's fated suffering.

pericopes.text: As they were eating, Jesus took bread, and when he had blessed, he broke it, and gave to them, and said, “Take, eat. This is my body.” He took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave to them. They all drank of it. He said to them, “This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many. Most certainly I tell you, I will no more drink of the fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it anew in the Kingdom of God.”

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: 'This is my blood of the covenant' formally echoes Moses' words at Sinai, 'Behold the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you,' as he dashes sacrificial blood on the people. The verbal correspondence (haima tes diathekes) is exact and the coherence high: Jesus enacts a covenant-ratifying blood rite that recapitulates and surpasses Sinai. This is the load-bearing intertext of the cup-word.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The blood 'poured out for many' draws on the Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and 'bore the sin of many,' where the rare 'many' (rabbim/polloi) language is distinctively Isaianic. The combination of pouring-out unto death and vicarious 'for many' gives strong volume and coheres with Mark's ransom saying at 10:45, making Isaiah 53 a controlling subtext.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
echoes.note: The covenant sealed in Jesus' blood evokes Jeremiah's promised 'new covenant' that the Lord will make with the house of Israel, written on the heart. Even in Mark's shorter 'blood of the covenant' reading, the eschatological covenant-renewal theme makes Jeremiah 31 a natural subtext; the explicit 'new' is firmer in the parallel traditions, lowering the volume slightly here.

echoes.text: As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I have set free your prisoners from the pit in which is no water.
echoes.note: Zechariah's 'because of the blood of my covenant with you, I will set your prisoners free' joins covenant-blood to eschatological release, matching Jesus' cup-word that looks ahead to the Kingdom (v. 25). The shared phrase 'blood of the covenant' in a deliverance context makes this a plausible secondary allusion within the same covenant-blood cluster.

echoes.text: They shall take some of the blood, and put it on the two door posts and on the lintel, on the houses in which they shall eat it.
echoes.note: Within a Passover meal, the saving power of the lamb's blood smeared on the doorposts stands behind the cup of Jesus' blood that delivers 'many.' The Passover-blood and covenant-blood motifs fuse in Mark's scene, so Exodus 12 supplies the festal-blood resonance alongside the explicit Sinai citation.

echoes.text: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.
echoes.note: Jacob's blessing of Judah, who 'washes his garments in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes,' was read messianically in Second-Temple tradition and links wine, blood, and the coming ruler. Jesus' 'fruit of the vine' and 'blood' in a kingdom-context may faintly evoke this royal vine-and-blood imagery, though the connection is associative.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
echoes.note: Jesus' vow to drink the fruit of the vine 'anew in the Kingdom of God' evokes the eschatological banquet on Zion where the Lord makes 'a feast of well-aged wines' for all peoples. The messianic-feast horizon coheres with Mark's kingdom-cup, supplying the festal-wine background for the eschatological pledge.

echoes.text: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the one treading grapes him who sows seed; and sweet wine will drip from the mountains, and flow from the hills. I will bring my people Israel back from captivity, and they will rebuild the ruined cities, and inhabit them; and they will plant vineyards, and drink wine from them. They shall also make gardens, and eat their fruit.
echoes.note: The promise that in the restored kingdom 'the mountains shall drip sweet wine' and replanted vineyards yield abundance supports the eschatological vine-imagery of Jesus' pledge to drink anew in the Kingdom. The link is thematic, part of the prophetic vision of restored vintage in the age to come.

pericopes.text: When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

echoes.text: Praise Yah! Praise, you servants of Yahweh, praise Yahweh’s name. Blessed be Yahweh’s name, from this time forward and forever more. From the rising of the sun to the going down of the same, Yahweh’s name is to be praised. Yahweh is high above all nations, his glory above the heavens. Who is like Yahweh, our God, who has his seat on high, Who stoops down to see in heaven and in the earth? He raises up the poor out of the dust. Lifts up the needy from the […]
echoes.note: 'When they had sung a hymn' refers to the Hallel psalms sung at Passover, the fixed liturgical conclusion of the seder. The volume rests on established liturgical practice rather than a quoted line, but the coherence is strong: Mark places the praise of God's deliverance on Jesus' lips immediately before Gethsemane, and Psalm 118 in particular (already cited at 12:10-11 and the triumphal entry) frames his approaching vindication.

echoes.text: David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and wept as he went up; and he had his head covered, and went barefoot: and all the people who were with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up.
echoes.note: Jesus going out to the Mount of Olives in the night of betrayal evokes David ascending the Mount of Olives weeping as he flees Absalom's conspiracy, with Ahithophel's treachery in view. The geographical and situational parallel (the anointed crossing Olivet amid betrayal) supports a faint Davidic typology.

echoes.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
echoes.note: The Mount of Olives is the site where, in Zechariah, the Lord's feet stand on the day of eschatological battle and deliverance. Mark's repeated staging of decisive moments on Olivet (chs. 11, 13, 14) may quietly trade on this prophetic geography, though the link is locational rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: Jesus said to them, “All of you will be made to stumble because of me tonight, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ However, after I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee.” But Peter said to him, “Although all will be offended, yet I will not.” Jesus said to him, “Most certainly I tell you, that you today, even this night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” But he spoke all the more, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” They all said the same thing.

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: Mark introduces with 'it is written' and quotes 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered,' a formal citation of Zechariah's sword-against-the-shepherd oracle. The volume is maximal and the coherence total: God himself strikes the shepherd, the disciples are the scattered flock, and the surrounding Zecharian context (the refining of the remnant) frames the Passion. Mark adapts the verb to a divine-passive/first-person form fitting his theology.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's image of the flock 'scattered because there is no shepherd,' wandering over the mountains, reinforces the shepherd-and-sheep motif of the citation. Mark elsewhere casts the crowds as sheep without a shepherd (6:34), so this prophetic scattered-flock tradition coheres strongly and supplies depth to the Zechariah quotation.

echoes.text: It shall happen that in all the land,” says Yahweh, “two parts in it will be cut off and die; but the third will be left in it. I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”
echoes.note: The continuation of the struck-shepherd oracle — the remnant passed through fire, refined, and restored as God's people — coheres with Jesus' immediate promise of restoration after he is 'raised up' (v. 28). Reading the quotation in its Zecharian context illuminates the scattering-then-regathering pattern Mark builds into Peter's failure and recovery.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.
echoes.note: The shepherd-flock imagery and the dark valley of the night's events faintly evoke the shepherd psalm, though here the shepherd is struck rather than protecting. The connection is associative within the broader shepherd motif rather than a cited parallel.

pericopes.text: They came to a place which was named Gethsemane. He said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I pray.” He took with him Peter, James, and John, and began to be greatly troubled and distressed. He said to them, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here, and watch.” He went forward a little, and fell on the ground, and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass away from him. He said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible to you. Please remove this cup from me. However, not what I desire, but what you desire.” He came and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “Simon, are you sleeping? Couldn’t you watch one hour? Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Again he went away, and prayed, saying the same words. Again he returned, and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they didn’t know what to answer him. He came the third time, and said to them, “Sleep on now, and take your rest. It is enough. The hour has come. Behold, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Arise, let us be going. Behold, he who betrays me is at hand.”

echoes.text: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him for the saving help of his presence. My God, my soul is in despair within me. Therefore I remember you from the land of the Jordan, the heights of Hermon, from the hill Mizar.
