echoes.note: Jesus' words 'My soul is exceedingly sorrowful' closely echo the refrain 'Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me?' of the downcast psalmist. The verbal correspondence (perilypos / he psyche mou) is strong, and the coherence is high: Mark voices Gethsemane's anguish in the idiom of the lament psalms, casting Jesus as the suffering-yet-hoping righteous one.

echoes.text: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him: my Savior, my helper, and my God.
echoes.note: The repeated refrain 'Why are you cast down, O my soul?' continues into Psalm 43, the twin lament of 42, and undergirds Jesus' 'my soul is sorrowful even to death.' Its recurrence as a fixed refrain strengthens the allusion, and the psalmist's longing for God's deliverance coheres with Jesus' prayer that the hour might pass.

echoes.text: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him, the saving help of my countenance, and my God.
echoes.note: The third occurrence of the cast-down-soul refrain reinforces that Mark frames Jesus' sorrow through this specific psalmic complaint. The triple repetition across Psalms 42-43 mirrors the threefold prayer of Gethsemane, deepening the recurrence and coherence of the allusion.

echoes.text: God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the vine?” He said, “I am right to be angry, even to death.”
echoes.note: Jonah's 'I am angry enough to die' (lit. 'sorrowful unto death') supplies a verbal precedent for Jesus being grieved 'even to death.' The phrase 'unto death' as an intensifier of grief makes this a plausible secondary verbal echo, though Jonah's resentment differs sharply from Jesus' obedient sorrow.

echoes.text: For in the hand of Yahweh there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.
echoes.note: Jesus' plea 'remove this cup from me' draws on the prophetic 'cup' of God's wrath and judgment, here Psalm 75's cup of foaming wine that the wicked must drink to the dregs. The metaphor of drinking a divinely appointed cup of suffering gives real volume and coheres with Mark's earlier cup-saying (10:38-39).

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
echoes.note: Isaiah's 'cup of his wrath,' the 'cup of staggering' that Jerusalem has drunk to the dregs, is a leading source for the cup Jesus prays to have removed. The strong prophetic-cup tradition of divine judgment-wine coheres with Jesus drinking the cup on behalf of the 'many,' reinforcing the wrath-cup reading.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, to me: take this cup of the wine of wrath at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it. They shall drink, and reel back and forth, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them. Then took I the cup at Yahweh’s hand, and made all the nations to drink, to whom Yahweh had sent me: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and its kings, and its princes, to make them a desolation, an […]
echoes.note: Jeremiah's cup of wrath, which the nations must drink at God's hand, belongs to the same prophetic cluster that informs Jesus' 'cup.' Its recurrence across the prophets establishes the cup as a fixed symbol of appointed judgment, supporting the figural reading of Gethsemane's prayer.

echoes.text: Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me with a willing spirit.
echoes.note: The saying 'the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak' resonates with the penitential psalm's prayer for a willing/steadfast spirit ('uphold me with a willing spirit'). The spirit-versus-weak-flesh contrast may draw on this psalmic anthropology, though the link is conceptual rather than a direct citation.

echoes.text: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and […]
echoes.note: The agonized obedience of the son who submits to the father's will ('not what I desire, but what you desire') faintly recalls the Aqedah, where Abraham obeys God's command to offer his beloved son. The figural resonance of obedient surrender of a son's life coheres with Mark's beloved-Son theology, though there is no verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: Jesus' announcement that 'the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners' continues Mark's Danielic Son-of-Man thread, here in its suffering aspect. The title carries the Daniel 7 background even as Mark inverts the figure's exaltation into delivery to sinners, anticipating the explicit citation at v. 62.

pericopes.text: Immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas, one of the twelve, came—and with him a multitude with swords and clubs, from the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders. Now he who betrayed him had given them a sign, saying, “Whomever I will kiss, that is he. Seize him, and lead him away safely.” When he had come, immediately he came to him, and said, “Rabbi! Rabbi!” and kissed him. They laid their hands on him, and seized him. But a certain one of those who stood by drew his sword, and struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. Jesus answered them, “Have you come out, as against a robber, with swords and clubs to seize me? I was daily with you in the temple teaching, and you didn’t arrest me. But this is so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled.”

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: Judas, 'one of the twelve,' identifying Jesus with a kiss completes the intimate-betrayer motif governed by Psalm 41's friend who shared bread and 'lifted his heel.' The treacherous gesture of affection from a close companion gives the arrest its psalmic depth, consummating the theme opened at the meal.

echoes.text: Joab said to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand. So he struck him with it in the body, and shed out his bowels to the ground, and didn’t strike him again; and he died. Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri.
echoes.note: Joab's murderous kiss of Amasa — 'he took him by the beard with his hand to kiss him' before stabbing him — is the Old Testament archetype of the deadly false kiss that Judas reenacts. The pairing of a feigned greeting-kiss with betrayal gives this a strong typological coherence, though Mark does not cite it.

echoes.text: Faithful are the wounds of a friend; although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.
echoes.note: The proverb 'the kisses of an enemy are deceitful' (LXX) supplies a wisdom commentary on Judas' kiss, contrasting the faithful wounds of a friend with an enemy's profuse kisses. The conceptual fit is exact, but the connection is gnomic rather than a quoted source.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: Jesus' protest that they come 'as against a robber' and his arrest among the violent faintly anticipate the Servant 'numbered with the transgressors.' The motif of the innocent treated as a criminal coheres with Mark's Servant-shaped Passion, though here it is allusive and undeveloped.

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: The arrest that precipitates the disciples' flight ('they all left him, and fled,' v. 50) enacts the scattering of the sheep foretold by the struck-shepherd oracle just quoted in v. 27. The narrative fulfills the citation, tying the arrest scene back to Zechariah's prophecy.

pericopes.text: They all left him, and fled. A certain young man followed him, having a linen cloth thrown around himself, over his naked body. The young men grabbed him, but he left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked.

echoes.text: and he who is courageous among the mighty will flee away naked on that day,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: The young man who 'left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked' closely matches Amos' oracle that 'he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day.' The distinctive image of fleeing naked in a day of judgment gives real verbal volume, and the coherence fits Mark's depiction of total abandonment as the day of reckoning falls on Jesus' followers.

echoes.text: She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!” He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.
echoes.note: The flight in which a garment is left behind in the grasping hands recalls Joseph fleeing Potiphar's wife, who 'caught him by his garment... and he left his garment in her hand, and fled.' The shared motif of escaping by abandoning the seized cloth supports a faint verbal echo, though the contexts differ.

echoes.text: I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, and he said, “Strike the tops of the pillars, that the thresholds may shake; and break them in pieces on the head of all of them; and I will kill the last of them with the sword: there shall not one of them flee away, and there shall not one of them escape. Though they dig into Sheol, there my hand will take them; and though they climb up to heaven, there I will bring them down. Though they hide themselves in the […]
echoes.note: The wider Amos context of inescapable judgment, where none can flee the Lord's hand, reinforces the day-of-reckoning resonance of the naked flight. This strengthens the Amos 2:16 reading by establishing the prophet's recurring theme of futile flight in the day of judgment.

pericopes.text: They led Jesus away to the high priest. All the chief priests, the elders, and the scribes came together with him. Peter had followed him from a distance, until he came into the court of the high priest. He was sitting with the officers, and warming himself in the light of the fire.

echoes.text: My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my plague. My kinsmen stand far away.
echoes.note: Peter following 'from a distance' while Jesus is led to the high priest faintly echoes the lament psalmist's complaint that 'my friends and companions stand aloof from my affliction, and my kinsmen stand far off.' The motif of associates keeping their distance from the suffering righteous one coheres with Peter's hesitant, fearful following.

echoes.text: You have taken my friends from me. You have made me an abomination to them. I am confined, and I can’t escape.
echoes.note: The psalmist's 'you have caused my companions to shun me' belongs to the same lament tradition of friends who withdraw in the hour of suffering. Peter warming himself among the officers, distanced and soon to deny, fits this isolation motif, though the connection is thematic.

pericopes.text: Now the chief priests and the whole council sought witnesses against Jesus to put him to death, and found none. For many gave false testimony against him, and their testimony didn’t agree with each other. Some stood up, and gave false testimony against him, saying, “We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another made without hands.’” Even so, their testimony did not agree.

echoes.text: Don’t deliver me over to the desire of my adversaries, for false witnesses have risen up against me, such as breathe out cruelty.
echoes.note: The council seeking testimony as 'false witnesses rose up against him, breathing out violence' is precisely Mark's scene of those who 'gave false testimony against him.' The volume is strong (pseudomartyres), and the coherence is high: Mark casts Jesus as the persecuted righteous one of the psalms, hemmed in by lying witnesses, confident in God's vindication.

echoes.text: Unrighteous witnesses rise up. They ask me about things that I don’t know about.
echoes.note: 'Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things that I do not know' matches the false testimony and incoherent accusations leveled at Jesus. The recurrence of the false-witness motif across the lament psalms (27, 35) strengthens the allusion and frames the trial as the persecution of the innocent sufferer.

echoes.text: for they have opened the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of deceit against me. They have spoken to me with a lying tongue. They have also surrounded me with words of hatred, and fought against me without a cause.
echoes.note: The psalmist surrounded by 'lying tongues' and 'words of hatred' who 'attack me without cause' coheres with the conspiratorial false testimony of Mark's council. As another suffering-righteous psalm prominent in the Passion tradition, it reinforces the false-accusation matrix Mark draws on.

echoes.text: Then the presidents and the satraps sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion nor fault, because he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him. Then these men said, We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God.
echoes.note: The plotters who seek a charge against the blameless Daniel and find none parallel the council that 'sought witnesses against Jesus... and found none.' The motif of conspirators unable to fault the righteous man until they manufacture a charge resonates, though the link is situational rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Then the two elders stood up in the midst of the people, and laid their hands upon her head. And she weeping looked up toward heaven: for her heart trusted in the Lord. And the elders said, As we walked in the garden alone, this woman came in with two maids, and shut the garden doors, and sent the maids away. Then a young man, who there was hid, came to her, and lay with her. And we, being in a corner of the garden, saw this wickedness, and ran to them. […]
echoes.note: Susanna's ordeal by false witnesses whose testimony does not finally agree offers a Second-Temple type of the righteous condemned on perjured evidence that fails to cohere. Mark's note that the witnesses' testimony 'did not agree' echoes this exposure-of-false-witness pattern, supplying a deuterocanonical parallel.

pericopes.text: The high priest stood up in the midst, and asked Jesus, “Have you no answer? What is it which these testify against you?” But he stayed quiet, and answered nothing. Again the high priest asked him, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?”

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: Jesus' silence — 'he stayed quiet, and answered nothing' before his accusers — directly enacts the Servant who 'was oppressed and afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter... so he opened not his mouth.' The volume is high and the coherence total: Mark portrays Jesus' refusal to answer as the deliberate fulfillment of the silent Servant.

echoes.text: But I, as a deaf man, don’t hear. I am as a mute man who doesn’t open his mouth. Yes, I am as a man who doesn’t hear, in whose mouth are no reproofs.
echoes.note: The psalmist who, surrounded by accusers, becomes 'like a deaf man... like a mute man who does not open his mouth' offers a psalmic parallel to Jesus' silence under interrogation. This lament-psalm motif of the righteous keeping silence before false charges reinforces the Isaianic Servant-silence Mark foregrounds.

echoes.text: I was mute. I didn’t open my mouth, because you did it.
echoes.note: 'I was mute; I did not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it' supplies a further psalmic instance of the sufferer's silent submission to God's hand. The connection deepens the lament-psalm coloring of Jesus' silence, though Isaiah 53 remains the controlling text.

echoes.text: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: The high priest's question 'Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?' joins the titles 'anointed' and 'son' that Psalm 2 fuses ('the Lord and his anointed... you are my Son'). Mark's Christology trades on this royal-messianic psalm, lending the interrogation its scriptural charge even without quotation.

pericopes.text: Jesus said, “I am. You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of the sky.”

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: Jesus' 'you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power' fuses the enthronement oracle 'Sit at my right hand,' which Mark has just expounded at 12:36. The volume is maximal and the coherence climactic: the accused declares his coming vindication as the one seated at God's right hand, making this the decisive scriptural self-claim of the Gospel.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'Coming with the clouds of the sky' quotes Daniel's vision of 'one like a son of man' who comes 'with the clouds of heaven' and is given everlasting dominion before the Ancient of Days. Mark fuses this with Psalm 110 into a single declaration, so that the Son of Man both sits enthroned and comes in glory; the conflation is the theological summit of Mark's Christology.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: Jesus' bare 'I am' (ego eimi) in answer to the high priest may carry an overtone of the divine self-naming 'I AM' of the burning bush, especially given Mark's other ego-eimi sayings. The reading is contested, since the phrase functions primarily as a plain affirmative, but the loaded context invites the figural divine-name resonance.

echoes.text: Let your hand be on the man of your right hand, on the son of man whom you made strong for yourself.
echoes.note: 'Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you made strong for yourself' uniquely joins 'son of man' with God's 'right hand,' the two elements Jesus combines. As a psalm that already braids these motifs, it may stand among the scriptural matrix behind the fused declaration.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
echoes.note: Zechariah's oracle that 'they shall look on him whom they have pierced' anticipates the council 'seeing' the vindicated Son of Man, a connection drawn explicitly elsewhere in the NT. The verb of seeing the rejected-yet-coming one resonates with Jesus' 'you will see,' lending an eschatological-recognition overtone.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

pericopes.text: The high priest tore his clothes, and said, “What further need have we of witnesses? You have heard the blasphemy! What do you think?” They all condemned him to be worthy of death. Some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to beat him with fists, and to tell him, “Prophesy!” The officers struck him with the palms of their hands.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: The spitting, blindfolding, and beating — 'some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to beat him' — enact the Servant who said 'I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting.' The specific cluster of spitting and striking the face gives high volume and coherence, casting the abuse as fulfillment of the third Servant Song.

echoes.text: “‘He who is the high priest among his brothers, upon whose head the anointing oil is poured, and that is consecrated to put on the garments, shall not let the hair of his head hang loose, nor tear his clothes;
echoes.note: The high priest tearing his clothes at the alleged blasphemy ironically transgresses the Levitical rule that the high priest 'shall not tear his clothes.' Mark's readers attuned to Torah would register the violation, sharpening the irony that the one charged with blasphemy is condemned by a priest breaking his own consecration law. The allusion turns on the prohibition's reversal.

echoes.text: Now you shall gather yourself in troops, daughter of troops. He has laid siege against us. They will strike the judge of Israel with a rod on the cheek.
echoes.note: Micah's 'they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek with a rod' (LXX 5:1) offers a prophetic image of the smitten ruler that resonates with the blows to Jesus' face. The motif of striking Israel's appointed judge/ruler coheres with Mark's mocked-king theme, though it is a faint secondary echo to Isaiah 50:6.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh. His delight will be in the fear of Yahweh. He will not judge by the sight of his eyes, neither decide by the hearing of his ears; but with righteousness he will judge the poor, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the […]
echoes.note: The taunt 'Prophesy!' mockingly tests the messianic gift of discerning judgment that Isaiah ascribes to the shoot of Jesse, who judges not by what his eyes see. The irony of demanding prophecy from the blindfolded Messiah plays on this expectation, though the connection is thematic and undeveloped.

echoes.text: Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near, and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, “Which way did the Spirit of Yahweh go from me to speak to you?”
echoes.note: Zedekiah striking the prophet Micaiah on the cheek and challenging his prophetic word ('How did the Spirit pass from me to speak to you?') parallels the officers striking Jesus and jeering 'Prophesy!' The pattern of slapping and taunting a true prophet supplies a faint Old Testament precedent.

pericopes.text: As Peter was in the courtyard below, one of the maids of the high priest came, and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him, and said, “You were also with the Nazarene, Jesus!” But he denied it, saying, “I neither know, nor understand what you are saying.” He went out on the porch, and the rooster crowed. The maid saw him, and began again to tell those who stood by, “This is one of them.” But he again denied it. After a little while again those who stood by said to Peter, “You truly are one of them, for you are a Galilean, and your speech shows it.” But he began to curse, and to swear, “I don’t know this man of whom you speak!” The rooster crowed the second time. Peter remembered the word, how that Jesus said to him, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” When he thought about that, he wept.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: Peter's threefold denial, capping the abandonment by the inner circle, extends the Passion's betrayed-by-intimates theme rooted in the psalm of the friend who lifted his heel. While Judas is the primary referent, Peter's failure broadens the motif of the righteous sufferer forsaken even by his closest companions.

echoes.text: Because of all my adversaries I have become utterly contemptible to my neighbors, A fear to my acquaintances. Those who saw me on the street fled from me.
echoes.note: The psalmist who has become 'a horror to my acquaintances; those who see me in the street flee from me' resonates with Peter's recoil and the disciples' flight from association with Jesus. The lament motif of acquaintances disowning the afflicted one colors Peter's denials, though without verbal citation.

echoes.text: My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my plague. My kinsmen stand far away.
echoes.note: Peter's denial that he 'knows' Jesus enacts the lament theme of friends and kinsmen who 'stand far off' from the sufferer's affliction. The repeated psalmic image of withdrawn intimates frames Peter's failure as a further instance of the righteous one's abandonment, deepening Mark's lament-shaped Passion.

pericopes.text: Immediately in the morning the chief priests, with the elders and scribes, and the whole council, held a consultation, and bound Jesus, and carried him away, and delivered him up to Pilate. Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” He answered, “So you say.” The chief priests accused him of many things. Pilate again asked him, “Have you no answer? See how many things they testify against you!” But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate marveled.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: Jesus' refusal to answer Pilate's repeated questions ('Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate marveled') enacts the Servant who 'was oppressed and afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.' The volume is high because Mark twice underscores the silence (vv. 4-5) precisely where defense is expected, and the Servant coherence runs through the whole passion. This is the load-bearing intertext of the trial.

echoes.text: But I, as a deaf man, don’t hear. I am as a mute man who doesn’t open his mouth. Yes, I am as a man who doesn’t hear, in whose mouth are no reproofs.
echoes.note: The suffering psalmist becomes 'like a deaf man' who 'hears not, and in whose mouth are no reproofs,' opening not his mouth before his accusers. The same psalm supplies later passion details (friends standing far off, v. 11), and its portrait of the afflicted righteous one mute before those who 'seek my hurt' coheres with Jesus' silence before Pilate.

echoes.text: I was mute. I didn’t open my mouth, because you did it.
echoes.note: 'I was mute, I opened not my mouth, because you have done it' offers a further psalmic instance of the righteous sufferer's deliberate silence under affliction interpreted as God's doing. The link is conceptual rather than verbal but belongs to the same cluster of silent-sufferer texts available behind Mark's twice-noted silence.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed. He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me.
echoes.note: The third Servant Song's defendant who 'set my face like a flint,' confident that 'he who vindicates me is near' and asks 'who will contend with me?', frames the silent, composed bearing of the accused before a hostile tribunal. Its juridical setting coheres with Jesus standing wordless before Pilate's questions.

pericopes.text: Now at the feast he used to release to them one prisoner, whom they asked of him. There was one called Barabbas, bound with those who had made insurrection, men who in the insurrection had committed murder. The multitude, crying aloud, began to ask him to do as he always did for them. Pilate answered them, saying, “Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?” For he perceived that for envy the chief priests had delivered him up. But the chief priests stirred up the multitude, that he should release Barabbas to them instead. Pilate again asked them, “What then should I do to him whom you call the King of the Jews?” They cried out again, “Crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Why, what evil has he done?” But they cried out exceedingly, “Crucify him!” Pilate, wishing to please the multitude, released Barabbas to them, and handed over Jesus, when he had flogged him, to be crucified.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: Pilate's 'handing over' (paredoken) of Jesus to be crucified continues the Servant motif that 'the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all' and that he was 'given up' for transgressions; the Greek paradidomi recurs across Mark's passion as the technical Servant-handing-over verb. The crowd's choice of a murderer-insurrectionist over the innocent one sharpens the substitution coherence.

echoes.text: He shall take the two goats, and set them before Yahweh at the door of the Tent of Meeting. Aaron shall cast lots for the two goats; one lot for Yahweh, and the other lot for the scapegoat. Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot fell for Yahweh, and offer him for a sin offering. But the goat, on which the lot fell for the scapegoat, shall be presented alive before Yahweh, to make atonement for him, to send him away for the scapegoat into the […]
echoes.note: The release of Barabbas alongside the condemnation of Jesus has long been read figurally against the Day of Atonement's two goats: one released, one bearing sin to death. The pairing of a freed prisoner and a doomed one invites the scapegoat typology, though Mark makes no explicit citation and the connection rests on conceptual coherence.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The innocent 'righteous one' delivered up while a guilty insurrectionist goes free echoes the Servant who 'bore the sin of many' and was 'numbered with transgressors.' The contrast between Barabbas the murderer and the sinless Jesus dramatizes the vicarious exchange the Servant Song announces.

pericopes.text: The soldiers led him away within the court, which is the Praetorium; and they called together the whole cohort. They clothed him with purple, and weaving a crown of thorns, they put it on him. They began to salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” They struck his head with a reed, and spat on him, and bowing their knees, did homage to him. When they had mocked him, they took the purple off of him, and put his own garments on him. They led him out to crucify him.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: The soldiers' mockery — striking Jesus' head, spitting on him, and abusing him — closely tracks the third Servant Song: 'I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled out the beard; I hid not my face from shame and spitting.' The combination of striking and spitting (v. 19) is distinctive enough, and Isaiah 50 is so embedded in Mark's passion, that the allusion registers strongly.

echoes.text: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”
echoes.note: The mock-coronation — purple robe, thorn-crown, the sarcastic 'Hail, King of the Jews,' and homage — enacts the psalmist who is 'scorned by men and despised by the people,' mocked by all who see him. Psalm 22 is the controlling passion psalm in Mark 15, and the derisive royal homage coheres tightly with its portrait of the righteous sufferer made an object of contempt.

echoes.text: You know my reproach, my shame, and my dishonor. My adversaries are all before you. Reproach has broken my heart, and I am full of heaviness. I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; for comforters, but I found none.
echoes.note: 'You know my reproach, and my shame and my dishonor... reproaches have broken my heart' supplies the other great passion psalm's vocabulary of public humiliation. Mark draws heavily on Psalm 69 (esp. v. 21), so the soldiers' degrading mockery resonates with this psalm's catalogue of shame as well.

echoes.text: With outrage and torture let us put him to the test, That we may learn his gentleness, And may prove his patience under wrong.
echoes.note: The plotters in Wisdom resolve to 'test him with insult and torture, that we may find out how gentle he is, and make trial of his forbearance.' The soldiers' systematic insult and physical abuse of the mock-king enacts precisely this testing of the righteous one through outrage; the Wisdom passage is a key Second-Temple template for the mocked-righteous-sufferer that Mark's scene embodies.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
echoes.note: The piercing thorn-crown and abuse of the one who is 'King' faintly anticipate Zechariah's 'they shall look on me whom they have pierced' and the mourning for a smitten royal figure. The link is thematic and contested, resting on the broader Zecharian shepherd-king matrix Mark uses elsewhere.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

pericopes.text: They compelled one passing by, coming from the country, Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to go with them, that he might bear his cross. They brought him to the place called Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, “The place of a skull.”

echoes.text: Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. He took in his hand the fire and the knife. They both went together.
echoes.note: The compelled bearing of the cross-beam out to the place of execution has been read figurally against Isaac, who 'carried the wood of the burnt offering... laid it on Isaac his son,' as the son bears the wood of his own sacrifice. The connection is typological and unmarked in Mark, resting on the Aqedah's availability as a beloved-son-to-sacrifice pattern.

echoes.text: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
echoes.note: Simon of Cyrene compelled to 'bear' (airo) the cross can echo the Servant who 'has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows,' the burden-bearing language at the heart of the Song. The link is faint and lexical, but it belongs to the Servant coherence that pervades the chapter.

pericopes.text: They offered him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he didn’t take it.

echoes.text: They also gave me gall for my food. In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.
echoes.note: The drink offered at the cross — here 'wine mixed with myrrh' — and again the vinegar of v. 36 derive from the psalmist's complaint, 'they gave me also gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.' Matthew sharpens the link to 'gall,' but Mark's offered drugged/bitter wine already evokes the psalm's hostile offering. Psalm 69 is one of the two governing passion psalms here, so the volume and coherence are high.

echoes.text: Give strong drink to him who is ready to perish; and wine to the bitter in soul: Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more.
echoes.note: 'Give strong drink to him who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress, let him drink and forget his poverty' provides a sapiential rationale for offering a numbing draught to the dying. The custom of a stupefying wine to the condemned may stand behind the gesture Jesus refuses, though the connection is conceptual.

echoes.text: and they lay themselves down beside every altar on clothes taken in pledge; and in the house of their God they drink the wine of those who have been fined.
echoes.note: The motif of drinking 'the wine of the condemned' in a context of injustice offers a faint prophetic resonance with the bitter cup pressed on the crucified. The link is associative and contested.

pericopes.text: Crucifying him, they parted his garments among them, casting lots on them, what each should take.

echoes.text: They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.
echoes.note: 'They parted his garments among them, casting lots on them, what each should take' reproduces the psalm nearly verbatim: 'they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.' This is a formal-level allusion (near-quotation of LXX Psalm 21:19) embedded in the crucifixion narration itself, and it is the clearest single proof that Mark narrates the cross through Psalm 22. Volume and explicitness are maximal.

pericopes.text: It was the third hour, and they crucified him. The superscription of his accusation was written over him, “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” With him they crucified two robbers; one on his right hand, and one on his left. The Scripture was fulfilled, which says, “He was numbered with transgressors.”

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: Crucifixion between 'two robbers,' one on the right and one on the left, fulfills the Servant 'numbered with transgressors' — a link Mark (or the early textual tradition) makes explicit in v. 28, 'The Scripture was fulfilled, which says, He was numbered with transgressors.' This is a formal citation of Isaiah 53:12, even if v. 28 is text-critically secondary; the scene itself enacts the Servant being reckoned among the lawless.

echoes.text: For dogs have surrounded me. A company of evildoers have enclosed me. They have pierced my hands and feet.
echoes.note: 'A company of evildoers encircle me; they have pierced my hands and feet' resonates with the crucifixion act and the criminals flanking Jesus. The LXX reading and the surrounding-by-the-wicked motif cohere with the scene, though Mark does not cite it directly here.

pericopes.text: Those who passed by blasphemed him, wagging their heads, and saying, “Ha! You who destroy the temple, and build it in three days, save yourself, and come down from the cross!” Likewise, also the chief priests mocking among themselves with the scribes said, “He saved others. He can’t save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him.” Those who were crucified with him insulted him.

echoes.text: All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”
echoes.note: The passersby who 'blasphemed him, wagging their heads' and the chief priests' taunt 'He saved others, he cannot save himself... let him come down' directly enact the psalm: 'All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me, they wag their heads: He committed himself to the Lord; let him deliver him, let him rescue him, since he delights in him.' Both the head-wagging gesture and the 'let God save him' challenge are present, making this a high-volume, double-feature allusion.

echoes.text: Let us see if his words be true, And let us try what shall befall in the ending of his life. For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries. With outrage and torture let us put him to the test, That we may learn his gentleness, And may prove his patience under wrong. Let us condemn him to a shameful death; For he will be visited according to his words.
echoes.note: The mockers' logic — 'let the Christ come down... that we may see and believe' and 'he saved others, he cannot save himself' — closely matches Wisdom's ungodly: 'Let us see if his words are true... for if the righteous man is God's son, he will help him and deliver him from his adversaries. Let us condemn him to a shameful death, for he will be protected, according to what he says.' This deuterocanonical righteous-sufferer text is the strongest non-Psalmic intertext for the mockery, supplying the taunt's 'son of God / let God deliver him' shape.

echoes.text: I have also become a reproach to them. When they see me, they shake their head.
echoes.note: 'I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they wag their heads' supplies a second head-wagging derision text reinforcing Psalm 22:7. Psalm 109 is an imprecatory suffering psalm whose mocking accusers cohere with the crowd's gestures, raising the recurrence of the head-wagging motif.

echoes.text: All that pass by clap their hands at you. They hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men called The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?
echoes.note: 'All who pass along the way clap their hands at you; they hiss and wag their heads at daughter Jerusalem' applies the passers-by-wagging-the-head gesture to the destroyed temple/city. Mark's mockers — who taunt the destroyer-of-the-temple as they pass by and wag their heads — fold the temple-destruction theme into the head-wagging derision, making Lamentations a coherent secondary echo.

echoes.text: For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.
echoes.note: 'Zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me' resonates with the temple-destruction taunt hurled at Jesus ('you who destroy the temple'). The passion psalm's fusion of temple-zeal and reproach coheres with the mockery's content.

echoes.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning?
echoes.note: The taunt that God will not save the sufferer anticipates and frames the cry of dereliction (v. 34); the mockers unwittingly voice the psalm's opening abandonment that Jesus will quote. The recurrence of Psalm 22 across the scene strengthens this proleptic echo.

pericopes.text: When the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day,” says the Lord Yahweh, “that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day.
echoes.note: Darkness over the whole land from the sixth to the ninth hour (noon to mid-afternoon) enacts the day-of-the-Lord oracle: 'I will make the sun go down at noon, and darken the earth in broad daylight.' The midday darkening is distinctive and eschatologically loaded, and Amos's following line about turning feasts into mourning over an 'only son' coheres with the death of the beloved Son.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.” Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days. They didn’t see one another, neither did anyone rise from his place for three days; but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.
echoes.note: The plague of darkness over the land of Egypt — 'a darkness to be felt' for three days — supplies the exodus-judgment template for supernatural midday darkness. The coherence is strong (a divine darkness signaling judgment and deliverance) and the motif is widely available, reinforcing the cosmic-sign reading of the cross.

echoes.text: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.
echoes.note: Joel's day-of-the-Lord darkening — 'the sun and the moon are darkened' — belongs to the prophetic cluster of cosmic gloom at divine judgment that Mark draws on (cf. Mark 13:24, quoting Joel/Isaiah). The crucifixion darkness signals the eschatological day breaking in, cohering with Joel's imagery.

echoes.text: That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,
echoes.note: 'A day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness' adds another day-of-the-Lord text to the matrix of judgment-darkness behind the noon gloom. The link is general but reinforces the prophetic recurrence of cosmic darkening at the day of wrath.

echoes.text: For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.
echoes.note: 'The sun will be dark at its rising' in Isaiah's oracle of cosmic upheaval contributes to the same prophetic darkening-of-the-luminaries tradition. Its availability strengthens the eschatological coloring of the crucifixion darkness, though it is not specifically cited here.

pericopes.text: At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” which is, being interpreted, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

echoes.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning?
echoes.note: Jesus' cry 'Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?' — interpreted 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' — is a formal quotation of the psalm's opening line, given in Aramaic (a Targum-like rendering of the Hebrew). This is the climactic citation that retrospectively unlocks the whole chapter's reliance on Psalm 22, and it is the highest-volume, most explicit OT use in Mark 15.

echoes.text: But don’t be far off, Yahweh. You are my help: hurry to help me. Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of the dog. Save me from the lion’s mouth! Yes, from the horns of the wild oxen, you have answered me.
echoes.note: The same psalm Jesus cites turns from abandonment to a plea for help and ends in vindication and praise; readers who hear v. 1 are meant to hear the whole arc. The trajectory toward deliverance frames the dereliction cry as something other than final despair, supplying the coherence of the broader psalm.

pericopes.text: Some of those who stood by, when they heard it, said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” One ran, and filling a sponge full of vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Let him be. Let’s see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”

echoes.text: They also gave me gall for my food. In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.
echoes.note: 'One ran, and filling a sponge full of vinegar... gave it to him to drink' directly enacts 'in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.' The Greek oxos ('sour wine/vinegar') matches LXX Psalm 68:22 exactly, making this the chapter's second strong contact with Psalm 69 and a near-quotation of the offered drink.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The bystanders' guess that Jesus is 'calling Elijah' and the wait to 'see whether Elijah comes' trade on the expectation, from Malachi, that 'Elijah the prophet' would come before the great day of the Lord. The Elijah-redivivus hope is the Second-Temple backdrop that makes the misheard 'Eloi' into a question about eschatological rescue.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Elijah's translation to heaven without dying underlies the popular belief that he could return to intervene; the bystanders imagine him coming 'to take him down.' The link is to the Elijah-rescue tradition rather than a verbal parallel, but it grounds the crowd's expectation.

pericopes.text: Jesus cried out with a loud voice, and gave up the spirit. The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.

echoes.text: “You shall make a veil of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cherubim. The work of the skillful workman shall it be made. You shall hang it on four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold; their hooks shall be of gold, on four sockets of silver. You shall hang up the veil under the clasps, and shall bring the ark of the testimony in there within the veil: and the veil shall separate the holy place from the most holy for you.
echoes.note: The veil (katapetasma) of the temple torn in two evokes the curtain Exodus commands to be made, separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy and screening the divine presence. Mark's tearing of this barrier at Jesus' death signals access to God and/or judgment on the sanctuary; the specific cultic vocabulary makes the allusion firm.

echoes.text: and Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother, not to come at all times into the Most Holy Place within the veil, before the mercy seat which is on the ark; lest he die: for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat.
echoes.note: The veil 'before the mercy seat' that only the high priest may pass on the Day of Atonement defines what the torn curtain guarded. Its rending at the moment of death coheres with an atonement reading — the way into the holiest opened — making Leviticus 16 a coherent secondary intertext to the Exodus veil.

echoes.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the lower part of the mountain. Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked […]
echoes.note: The tearing open of the sacred boundary recalls Sinai's theophany where God descends in cloud and the mountain is wrapped in awe; some read the rent veil as a renewed theophanic disclosure paralleling the heavens 'torn' (schizomenous) at Jesus' baptism, the same verb. The Sinai echo is faint but coheres with Mark's tearing-open inclusio.

echoes.text: Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence,
echoes.note: 'Oh that you would tear open (LXX) the heavens and come down' uses the same dramatic rending language for divine self-disclosure that Mark applies to the heavens at the baptism and arguably to the veil here. The verbal resonance of 'tearing' for God breaking through reinforces the theophanic reading.

pericopes.text: When the centurion, who stood by opposite him, saw that he cried out like this and breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”

echoes.text: For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries.
echoes.note: The centurion's confession 'Truly this man was the Son of God' answers the mockers' Wisdom-shaped taunt: 'if the righteous man is God's son, God will help him.' What the ungodly proposed as a test, the Gentile soldier declares as truth at the moment of death, so the deuterocanonical righteous-son motif frames the irony of the climactic recognition.

echoes.text: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Yahweh. All the relatives of the nations shall worship before you. For the kingdom is Yahweh’s. He is the ruler over the nations.
echoes.note: The psalm Jesus quotes ends with 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord; all the families of the nations shall worship.' The Gentile centurion's confession at the cross can be read as the first-fruits of that promised turning of the nations, cohering with the psalm's universal-worship climax.

pericopes.text: There were also women watching from afar, among whom were both Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome; who, when he was in Galilee, followed him, and served him; and many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.

echoes.text: My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my plague. My kinsmen stand far away.
echoes.note: The women 'watching from afar' echoes the lament 'My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my kinsmen stand far off.' Mark's distinctive note that the followers observe 'from a distance' (apo makrothen) matches the psalm's portrait of the afflicted righteous one abandoned to watch alone, fitting the chapter's suffering-psalm weave.

echoes.text: You have taken my friends from me. You have made me an abomination to them. I am confined, and I can’t escape.
echoes.note: 'You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them' adds a second psalm of the friendless sufferer whose acquaintances are removed far off. Its bleak isolation coheres with the women keeping their distance at the cross.

pericopes.text: When evening had now come, because it was the Preparation Day, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathaea, a prominent council member who also himself was looking for the Kingdom of God, came. He boldly went in to Pilate, and asked for Jesus’ body. Pilate marveled if he were already dead; and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he had been dead long. When he found out from the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph. He bought a linen cloth, and taking him down, wound him in the linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb which had been cut out of a rock. He rolled a stone against the door of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary, the mother of Joses, saw where he was laid.

echoes.text: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
echoes.note: Burial by Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy and prominent councillor who lays Jesus in his own rock-cut tomb, fulfills 'they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence.' The Servant's honorable burial 'with a rich man' coheres precisely with the rich Joseph's intervention, sealing the chapter's Servant frame.

echoes.text: If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree; his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him the same day; for he who is hanged is accursed of God; that you don’t defile your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.
echoes.note: The urgency to take the body down and bury it before nightfall on the Preparation Day reflects the law that a man hanged on a tree 'shall not remain all night... you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God,' lest the land be defiled. This statute drives the same-day burial and carries the theology of the curse borne on the tree.

echoes.text: Afterward Joshua struck them, put them to death, and hanged them on five trees. They were hanging on the trees until the evening. At the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down off the trees, and cast them into the cave in which they had hidden themselves, and laid great stones on the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.
echoes.note: Joshua's taking down of the hanged kings at sunset and laying them in a cave, sealed with great stones, offers a narrative precedent for the same-day removal of a hanged body and burial behind a rolled stone. The link is conceptual but coheres with the Deuteronomic same-day-burial command and the stone at the tomb.

echoes.text: After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre (that is, Hebron), in the land of Canaan.
echoes.note: Abraham's burial of Sarah in a purchased cave-tomb hewn for the family establishes the patriarchal pattern of honorable interment in a rock-cut sepulchre. The dignity of Jesus' rock-tomb burial faintly recalls this venerable practice, though there is no verbal contact.

pericopes.text: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, bought spices, that they might come and anoint him. Very early on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb when the sun had risen. They were saying among themselves, “Who will roll away the stone from the door of the tomb for us?” for it was very big. Looking up, they saw that the stone was rolled back. Entering into the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were amazed. He said to them, “Don’t be amazed. You seek Jesus, the Nazarene, who has been crucified. He has risen. He is not here. Behold, the place where they laid him! But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you.’” They went out, and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had come on them. They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.

echoes.text: Two other also appeared to him, young men notable in their strength, and beautiful in their glory, and splendid in their apparel, who stood by him on either side, and scourged him unceasingly, inflicting on him many sore stripes.
echoes.note: The 'young man' (neaniskos) sitting in the tomb dressed in a white/dazzling robe matches the Second-Temple convention of angelic figures appearing as young men in bright apparel; in 2 Macc 3 two glorious young men in splendid robes (and elsewhere five) appear at the temple. Volume is moderate (shared vocabulary of youthful angelic messengers in shining garb) and the convention is widely available in Jewish literature of the era, supporting an angelophany reading of Mark's 'amazement.'

echoes.text: And as they were there, close to Jerusalem, there appeared at their head one on horseback in white apparel, brandishing weapons of gold.
echoes.note: A heavenly horseman in white apparel leads the Maccabean army, reinforcing the deuterocanonical topos of angelic deliverers clothed in white. The echo is faint and corroborative rather than a direct source, supporting the figural identification of Mark's white-robed youth as angelic.

echoes.text: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire.
echoes.note: The dazzling-white garment recalls Daniel's vision where the Ancient of Days' clothing is white as snow, the apocalyptic register from which heavenly whiteness derives; Mark's restrained 'white robe' partakes of this imagery cluster. Coherence with Mark's transfiguration whiteness (9:3) supports the link, though the specific divine throne setting is absent here.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: Hosea's 'after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up' is the most plausible scriptural matrix for early Christian 'third day' resurrection language; though Mark does not say 'third day' here, the dawn-of-the-first-day raising participates in that pattern. Recurrence is high across the NT (1 Cor 15:4), but Mark 16's silence on explicit third-day phrasing keeps the volume low and the link contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: Three days and nights in the fish became a stock figure for death-and-deliverance, invoked elsewhere in the Jesus tradition (the sign of Jonah). The empty-tomb scene enacts the emergence-from-the-deep pattern figurally, but Mark 16 makes no verbal contact, so the connection is thematic and faint.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: 'You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor let your holy one see corruption' became the foundational psalm-text for resurrection proclamation (cited at Acts 2:27). The empty tomb dramatizes the body not seeing corruption, but Mark supplies no citation, so the resonance is conceptual and low-volume.

echoes.text: Terror and dread falls on them. By the greatness of your arm they are as still as a stone— until your people pass over, Yahweh, until the people pass over who you have purchased.
echoes.note: The women's 'trembling and astonishment' and fear follows the conventional human response to theophany and divine deliverance, as in the Song of the Sea where trembling seizes the nations. The pattern of fear before God's saving acts is widely available; the link is to a topos rather than a specific text.

echoes.text: I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; for the men who were with me didn’t see the vision; but a great quaking fell on them, and they fled to hide themselves.
echoes.note: Daniel's companions are seized by great trembling and flee at an angelic vision, closely paralleling the women who flee in trembling from the white-robed messenger. This fear-and-flight response to an angelophany is a coherent Second-Temple convention that Mark's ending deploys, though no shared wording fixes the source.

pericopes.text: Now when he had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. When they heard that he was alive, and had been seen by her, they disbelieved.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: The longer ending's notice that Jesus 'had risen early on the first day of the week' reasserts the third-day/restoration pattern crystallized in Hosea's revival oracle. The connection remains a low-volume conceptual echo, since the appended ending narrates rather than cites Scripture.

pericopes.text: After these things he was revealed in another form to two of them, as they walked, on their way into the country. They went away and told it to the rest. They didn’t believe them, either.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth,
echoes.note: Jesus 'revealed in another form' to the two travelers evokes the biblical pattern of divine/angelic visitants appearing in altered or unrecognized guise to wayfarers, as the LORD appears to Abraham as travelers. The motif of hospitality-with-a-stranger-who-is-more-than-he-seems is available in the patriarchal narratives, though the link here is thematic and faint.

pericopes.text: Afterward he was revealed to the eleven themselves as they sat at the table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they didn’t believe those who had seen him after he had risen. He said to them, “Go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who disbelieves will be condemned. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak with new languages; they will take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will in no way hurt them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover.”

echoes.text: You will tread on the lion and cobra. You will trample the young lion and the serpent underfoot.
echoes.note: The promise that believers 'will take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will in no way hurt them' directly recalls Psalm 91's pledge that the faithful will tread on the serpent and the adder and be guarded from harm. Volume is moderate (shared serpent-and-protection imagery) and the psalm's protective register coheres with the signs-following-believers theme, making this the strongest OT echo in the longer ending.

echoes.text: The nursing child will play near a cobra’s hole, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den.
echoes.note: The eschatological vision of the infant playing over the adder's den, harm undone in the messianic age, underlies the promise that serpents and poison will not hurt believers. The connection is to Isaiah's new-creation peace between humans and venomous creatures, a coherent backdrop for the signs, though no verbal citation is present.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.
echoes.note: The bronze-serpent episode, where looking to the lifted serpent neutralizes deadly snakebite, supplies a scriptural precedent for serpents made harmless to the faithful. The link is figural and low-volume, mediated by the wider tradition of God's people delivered from serpent venom.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The commission to 'go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation' echoes the Servant's mandate to be a light to the nations reaching to the end of the earth. The universalizing scope coheres with Isaianic mission theology, but the appended ending offers no quotation, keeping the volume low.

echoes.text: Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples.
echoes.note: The call to declare God's glory and salvation among all nations stands behind the worldwide preaching commission. The enthronement-psalm summons to proclaim to every people is a coherent matrix for the universal mission, though the contact is thematic rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: So then the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was received up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God. They went out, and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word by the signs that followed. Amen.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'Sat down at the right hand of God' is a formal allusion to Psalm 110:1, 'Sit at my right hand,' the most-cited OT verse in the NT and Mark's own christological touchstone (Mark 12:36; 14:62). Volume and recurrence are high, and the enthronement coheres with Mark's exaltation theology, making this an unmistakable, near-quotation reuse of the psalm.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Jesus being 'received up into heaven' echoes Elijah's bodily assumption, the paradigmatic OT ascent narrative that shapes early Christian ascension language. The motif of a prophet taken up to heaven is coherent and available, supplying the narrative grammar for Mark's ascension notice, though the wording is shared with the Elijah cycle only loosely.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: Enoch's being 'taken' by God, with the Second-Temple expansion of his heavenly ascent, contributes to the assumption tradition behind 'received up into heaven.' The echo is faint and corroborative of the broader taken-up-to-God pattern rather than a direct source.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The one like a son of man brought up to the Ancient of Days and given dominion provides an apocalyptic backdrop for Jesus' heavenly enthronement and the subsequent worldwide proclamation. Coherence with Mark's son-of-man enthronement language (14:62) supports the link, though the ascension verb here points more directly to Psalm 110 and the Elijah motif.
